note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from deeds; Pazhamozhi 111 lays the quarrelsome temper on those small by lineage. The conflict holds on the reading that குலத்துச் சிறியார் ranks by birth rather than naming the mean ones of a family.
teaches: Set beside the Kural, the verse shows the ethics books divided on whether baseness is inherited: the couplet ranks by deeds, Pazhamozhi traces a vice to the family one comes from.
list_adds: it attaches a specific behaviour, turning on peacemakers, to a birth group, the very link between birth and worth the couplet denies.

note: Kural 677 says the doer should learn the mind of one who knows the task from inside; Pazhamozhi 176 warns against the bystander who speaks fine words but does not know the task's hidden state.
teaches: The couplet tells the doer to take counsel; Pazhamozhi adds which counsel to refuse, that of the onlooker who talks subtly from outside, so the test of an adviser is inner knowledge, not subtlety.
list_adds: it sets the false adviser beside the true one the couplet names, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Thirikadugam 62 names the man who wrongly keeps a deposit placed with him as one who loses his line; Acharakkovai 95 lists a deposit among four things to be guarded like gold.
teaches: One verse says what keeping a deposit asks and the other what breaking it costs, and together they show the deposit as another's property that the period held as close as one's own body and family.

note: Pazhamozhi 270 has the ripe palm fruit fall at the foot of its parent tree, and 280 has the felled palm fall on the feller; both use a falling palm for a deed returning to its doer.
teaches: Together the two palm images show one law of return working both ways in the king's service: work done in measure comes back like ripe fruit to its tree, and treachery comes back like a felled trunk on the axeman.

note: Pazhamozhi 201 says small drops gathered make a flood; Pazhamozhi 203 says the licks of a jackal do not dry the sea, so petty thefts do not hurt great wealth.
teaches: Side by side, the two verses show that the book's arithmetic of small amounts runs only toward growth: daily drops add up to a flood, but daily thefts are not allowed to add up to loss, because the scale of the whole decides which small things count.

note: Kural 633 names the minister's skill of dividing others; Pazhamozhi 305 shows one way of dividing, by giving allied brothers something to quarrel over.
teaches: The couplet lists division as a skill of office, the proverb verse shows it worked through flattering speech, so the minister's art is seen in practice.
list_adds: it turns the couplet's bare word பிரித்தல் into a scene with a speaker, a boast and its effect.

note: Both use grass fed to a bullock that will not work: the Naladiyar's small bullocks never take the yoke however much cut grass they eat, and Pazhamozhi 209's grass is fed to a sluggish ox.
teaches: The Naladiyar uses the ox to show that the base cannot be improved by feeding, while Pazhamozhi uses it to show the feeder's loss, so the one image condemns the base man's nature in one book and the owner's choice of keeper in the other.
list_adds: it moves the image from the base man who has come into wealth to the wealth a householder hands to a man of no family, making the image a counsel on custody.

note: Kural 1122 calls the bond between the lover and the girl the bond of body and life, using the word நட்பு; Pazhamozhi 124 says friends take each other as a whole body, more than the god who took Uma as half.
teaches: Both measure the closest bond by the body, but the Kural's lovers are body and life, two in one frame, while Pazhamozhi uses the divine half-woman to claim that friendship joins two wholes completely, setting friendship above even the god's marriage.
list_adds: its proverb from the god's half-body adds a ranking the couplet lacks: friendship is placed above the divine marriage, not only likened to lovers.

note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh can hold to grace; Pazhamozhi 343 traces the flesh-eater back through killing to rage, and says he did not walk in grace.
teaches: The Kural states the incompatibility of flesh and grace, and Pazhamozhi gives its order in a life: anger first, then killing, then eating.
list_adds: its chain of rage, killing and eating sets the diet among its causes, and the curd proverb casts grace as the good thing spoiled.

note: Kural 700 warns that intimacy which, presuming on old ties, does what is improper brings ruin; Acharakkovai 82 applies the same warning to sitting near the women, even with great intimacy (மிகக்கிழமை).
teaches: The pair show the period's fear of presumed closeness reaching its sharpest point in the women's place, where the Acharakkovai grounds the bar not in the king's anger but in a claim about women's changing liking.
list_adds: It names the one occasion where even the closest intimacy gives no right and adds a reason drawn from women rather than from the ruler.

note: Both use the reaped millet stubble of the hill farmer: in Kuruntokai 133 the stubble cropped by parrots puts out leaves again in the rain, as the girl lives on after his first taking of her beauty; in Ainkurunuru 286 the stubble bears pods for his ever-yielding land while her own glow is taken.
teaches: The same stubble is a figure of the girl's own survival in Kuruntokai 133 but of the man's endless plenty in Ainkurunuru 286, set against her fading, so the image of renewal cuts both ways: what revives on his hills need not revive in her.

note: Naladiyar 121 sets flesh-eaters among those who do not turn to renunciation; Pazhamozhi 342 says one who has renounced and then eats flesh undoes the whole crossing.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes flesh-eating a mark of the unrenounced, and Pazhamozhi adds that renunciation once achieved can still be sunk by it.
list_adds: its proverb of the sea and the hoofprint ranks the craving overcome against the small appetite kept, a contrast of scale the quatrain does not draw.

note: Kural 706 says the face, like crystal, shows what is strongest in the heart; Pazhamozhi 144 applies this to deceit held under concealment (ஒளிப்பினும்).
teaches: The pair extends the Kural's claim from feeling that shows freely to intent that is actively hidden, and holds that concealment does not stop the face's showing.
list_adds: it narrows the couplet to கள்ளம் and adds the condition of hiding, with the flood's dampness as the sign that runs ahead.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 63 says small gifts given without calling them of small use bear great fruit; Pazhamozhi 341 says nothing is of no use to something, since even a crab saved a man.
teaches: The two refuse the judgment 'too small to matter' from both sides, of the gift one gives and of the companion one keeps.

note: Naladiyar 342 shows the base man refusing with excuses when urged toward the faultless; Pazhamozhi 363 says those who will not take up aram should be made to take it, as a mother feeds a refusing infant.
teaches: The Naladiyar treats refusal of the good as a mark of baseness and leaves it there; Pazhamozhi treats the refuser as a child to be fed by force, so refusal becomes a ground for compulsion rather than contempt.
list_adds: its mother-and-infant image adds a remedy and a motive, the other's lasting good, to the quatrain's bare portrait of refusal.

note: Kural 700 says the intimacy that does improper things on the ground of old acquaintance brings ruin; Pazhamozhi 280 says those trusted for their truth who turn to falsehood against the king fell the palm onto themselves.
teaches: The pair names two kinds of capital a servant can spend against himself: the Kural's long familiarity and Pazhamozhi's reputation for truth, and in both the very ground of trust becomes the instrument of the fall.
list_adds: its palm that falls on the one who fells it makes the ruin self-inflicted by the servant's own act, where the couplet says only that the intimacy brings ruin.

note: Kural 691 tells those who attach themselves to kings to stay like fire-warmers, neither far nor near; Pazhamozhi 157 calls those who seek wealth through kings a crow on a pestle.
teaches: The Kural offers a way to keep a safe place by the king, and Pazhamozhi doubts that such a place can be kept: the courtier's perch moves with every stroke.
list_adds: its proverb makes court dependence itself unstable and sets it against wealth won by effort, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Naladiyar 261 says no one counts on the wealth of the worthless, as bats shun the cracked wood-apple; Pazhamozhi 221 lists the faults of the ungiving and calls leaving them leaving an old field's stack.
teaches: The quatrain says people do not approach such wealth; Pazhamozhi adds a counsel, that walking away costs nothing, so shunning the miser becomes a choice, not an instinct.
list_adds: it lists the miser's faults side by side (no giving, no strength, harsh speech, no help in trouble), making stinginess one of a cluster of failures.

note: Kural 891 ranks not slighting those able to act as the highest safeguard; Pazhamozhi 60 says calling the great small is neither wisdom, grace nor knowing, and brings harm.
teaches: The Kural values the restraint as self-protection; Pazhamozhi adds that the slight is also a failure of understanding, so the man who belittles the great is both unsafe and wrong about them.
list_adds: its threefold denial (not wisdom, not grace, not knowing) strips the slight of every merit before naming its harm, and the proverb says the slighted greatness itself survives.

note: Kural 126 says drawing in the five like a tortoise in one birth is a safeguard (ஏமம்) for seven; Pazhamozhi 388 mocks those who do not guard the five early and so make no safeguard (ஏமம்) for the road after the body.
teaches: Both use the same pair, guarding the five and the safeguard it earns, but the Pazhamozhi adds a deadline: the couplet promises a return across births, the proverb shows the loss of one who begins only when the body is falling.
list_adds: it joins the guarding of the five to the 'three' taken up, puts the act in youth (சிறுகாலை), and turns the couplet's promise into a jibe at the late starter.

note: Kural 283 says wealth got by stealth perishes even as it seems to grow; Pazhamozhi 340 applies the same doom to a deposit held back, saying base wealth does not stay.
teaches: Pazhamozhi counts the withheld deposit as stealth without any taking, so the Kural's rule on stolen gain reaches a thing that came into one's hand lawfully.
list_adds: it moves the couplet's claim from theft to trust, the thing placed in one's hand, and adds the time of return as the test.

note: Naladiyar 241 says the worthy feel shame and do not advance on humbled enemies, as the eclipse snake does not seize the crescent moon; Pazhamozhi 277 says those who serve a fallen king do not mock him, as no one slights a young snake.
teaches: Set side by side, the two snakes give two different grounds for sparing the fallen: in the Naladiyar the strong one is the snake and holds back from shame, in Pazhamozhi the fallen king is the snake and is spared from fear, so restraint before the weak may be nobility or prudence.
list_adds: it turns the quatrain's image around, making the humbled one the snake, so the same restraint is grounded in the danger of the weak rather than the shame of the strong.

note: Kural 611 forbids slackening because a task seems hard; Pazhamozhi 152 forbids it because a single effort seems too small to help.
teaches: Together they close both exits from effort: the Kural answers the excuse that the task is too great, Pazhamozhi the excuse that one's part is too small.
list_adds: it names the opposite excuse to the couplet's and gives the cost, not surviving even the day.

note: Naladiyar 98 calls giving to those who will give back a profitable loan; Pazhamozhi 372 shows the same giving as bait cast to land a larger fish.
teaches: The Naladiyar names the return-seeking gift a loan between equals; Pazhamozhi adds the disproportion, a small gift aimed at a large catch, so the fault is not only expecting return but calculating a profit on it.
list_adds: its angler's image adds the ratio of small outlay to large gain that the quatrain's loan does not state.

note: Kural 801 defines old friendship as friendship that does not cut down the liberties intimacy gives; Pazhamozhi 129 says a span of respect is better than a cubit of friendship when intimacy is presumed upon without care.
teaches: The Kural asks the friend to bear the liberties of intimacy; Pazhamozhi sets a limit from the other side, that intimacy which forgets care and respect is worth less than a little regard, so the liberties of old friendship do not cancel the duty of regard.
list_adds: its proverb ranks two measures, respect and friendship, where the couplet only defines one.

note: Kural 819 calls bitter the bond with those whose words and deeds differ; Pazhamozhi 125 says between true friends the words and their meaning are one, and twisting them is betrayal.
teaches: The Kural tests the speaker for a gap between word and deed; Pazhamozhi tests the hearer for a gap between word and meaning, so the demand for oneness falls on both sides of a friend's speech.
list_adds: its proverb of acceptance turned to weapon carries the fault to the listener who re-tells, a party the couplet does not consider.

note: Kural 692 says not desiring what kings desire brings lasting prosperity through them; Acharakkovai 85 says that even great charity, weddings, enterprise and houses must not outdo the king's, or lasting wealth (மன்னிய செல்வம்) is lost.
teaches: The pairing turns the Kural's general restraint into a ceiling on display, and shows that in the period even a subject's virtue, charity included, could not be allowed to outshine the king.
list_adds: It names four kinds of display, charity first among them, so the limit is placed on virtue as well as on luxury.

note: Kural 695 says not to listen in or press for anything, but to hear a secret when it is released; Acharakkovai 78 says not to take counsel with others or listen in, and if near, to stand turned away as if busy with something else.
teaches: The Kural states the inner restraint; the Acharakkovai gives the posture that makes it visible, standing turned away, so not listening must also be seen not to listen.
list_adds: It adds a staged posture of attention elsewhere to the bar on listening, which the couplet does not have.

note: Kural 861 says avoid opposing the strong but favour enmity against the weak; Pazhamozhi 300 says even if the great fight the strong, enmity with the low brings them nothing. The tension holds if புன்பாட்டவர், men of low standing, are the Kural's மெலியார்.
teaches: Where the Kural measures an enemy by strength and picks the weak, Pazhamozhi measures by worth and warns that the petty, though small, can flood one like a light shower.
list_adds: its proverb gives the low enemy a capacity for harm the couplet denies the weak, so the choice of enemy turns on standing and risk, not strength alone.

note: Kural 155 says the world keeps the forbearing like wrapped gold; Pazhamozhi 256 says the slow to anger rule the world and people shelter under them like a food tree.
teaches: The couplet gives the forbearing esteem; the pairing turns esteem into rule, so forbearance is shown as a ground of authority and not only of reputation.
list_adds: its image reverses the couplet's direction: the forbearing are not kept by others like gold but keep others under their shade.

note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even without means; Pazhamozhi 376 says those long used to giving still relieve dependents when they have nothing to give.
teaches: Read together, the Kural gives the reason, knowledge of what is due, and Pazhamozhi gives the source, long habit of giving, so the giving that survives poverty is both understood and practised into the body like a horse's training.
list_adds: its thin-but-harnessed horse adds that the capacity shows only when put to work, a point the couplet's bare statement lacks.

note: Purananuru 92 is Avvai's song to Anji calling her words a child's babble he graciously hears; 352 measures the friend's sweetness against a famous bard's new tune for Anji's praise.
teaches: The praise songs for Anji, which Avvai offers modestly as babble, had become in akam a byword for sweetness, showing that puram performances were known to the love poets' audience as celebrated pieces of music.

note: Elathi 12 says it is good neither to desire nor to look at five places, among them the killing ground and the ground where men gamble; Acharakkovai 98 says the wise do not enter the gamblers' hall or the ground of unceasing din, and that entering brings harm.
teaches: Both books treat the gambling place as a place to avoid, but the Jain Elathi bars even desiring or seeing it alongside the killing ground, while the Acharakkovai bars entering it for the harm it brings, so the pair show a moral and a prudential reason for the same avoidance.

note: Naladiyar 193 says a starving tiger will eat even a small frog and urges taking lowly work in need; Pazhamozhi 70 says the starving tiger will not graze grass and that the exalted keep their station in want. The conflict holds on reading 193 as counsel to stoop for a while.
teaches: The same starving tiger is made to argue both ways, so the pair shows where the line falls: the tiger may stoop to small meat but not to grass, stooping within one's kind but never out of it.
list_adds: it makes the tiger's refusal the proof that poverty must not move the high from their station, the opposite lesson from the same animal.

note: Kural 768 says that even without striking power or endurance an army gains stature by its படைத்தகை; Pazhamozhi 325 uses the same word for men of good name who lack the drive to march on the enemy.
teaches: The couplet treats bearing as a real asset of a weak army; Pazhamozhi turns it on men, so that bearing without ஊற்றம் becomes their measure, and the concession reads, on this reading, as a limited or ironic praise.
list_adds: its list of generosity, conduct and intelligence as the virtues of reputation sets the warrior's drive apart from them, showing that the civil virtues do not make a fighting man.

note: The logician's perception grasps name, class, quality and action and sits among ten means; Aravanar's Buddhist logic keeps two means and takes name, class, quality and action out of perception.
teaches: The epic stages the theory of knowledge as a reply across two kaathais: what the Vedic logician packs into seeing, the Buddhist teacher moves into inference, so the dispute is over where conceptual labels enter knowledge.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 17 names winning over those who are not one's allies as sweeter than doing good to the land; Pazhamozhi 296 says an old enemy never becomes a friend and should not be kept close.
teaches: Within the ethics group itself the two verses disagree on the reconciled enemy, one ranking his winning over among the sweetest things and the other counting him a sprout that will rise against one.

note: Kural 698 says not to slight one as younger or as kin but to act by the light he stands in; Acharakkovai 68 says not to speak slightingly even of an undiscerning child.
teaches: Read together, the young one the Kural warns against slighting can be a mere child of the great house, so the rule against belittling youth reaches down to the child who cannot yet understand.
list_adds: It makes the child's undiscerning state the extreme case, not only youth, and ties the rule to the place where one is not intimate.

note: Kural 920 names double-minded women, toddy and dice as the company of those Fortune has abandoned; Acharakkovai 37 bars even looking at another's wife, toddy, theft, gambling and killing.
teaches: The Kural's sanction is loss of fortune in this life, while the Acharakkovai adds public scorn and hell, and it shifts the sexual fault from the courtesan to another's wife, so the same cluster of vices is judged on different grounds.
list_adds: It adds theft and killing to the Kural's three, so pleasures and crimes stand in one list, and it bars them at the level of sight.

note: Kural 505 makes one's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness; Pazhamozhi 36 tells the hearer not to be like the small and to walk by his own conduct, which none knows apart from him.
teaches: The Kural gives the touchstone; Pazhamozhi places it inside the man, so the one who must test the deeds first is the doer.
list_adds: it sets the small man's three failures (not watching himself, not knowing his forebears, not joining the right path) before turning the touchstone on the hearer.

note: The queen's dream of the falling umbrella and sceptre is fulfilled in the king's lowered umbrella and slack sceptre at the verdict.
teaches: The omen comes first in the queen's private dream and is fulfilled the same hour in public, so the fall of justice is shown as already decided before Kannaki speaks.

note: Acharakkovai 1 names eight virtues as the seed from which ஆசாரம் grows; Acharakkovai 96 says ஆசாரம் comes in any case to those who hold to their own work like the ant, the weaver bird and the crow.
teaches: The book that opened by rooting conduct in inner virtues nears its close by rooting it in diligence, so ஆசாரம் is given two sources, character and steady work, and the second is learned from animals.

note: Naladiyar 130 asks the heart how long it thinks it will live while it clings to home and pines for children; Pazhamozhi 394 bids the heart not to die speaking fondly of the house, since wives and children are many bonds.
teaches: Both speakers argue with their own heart about house and children, and together they show the form: the Naladiyar shows the heart its brief span and the good deeds that alone remain, the Pazhamozhi pictures the deathbed scene of one still talking of home.
list_adds: it names wives and children together as many bonds in a proverb, and sets the scene at death, where the quatrain asks a question about years.

note: Kural 448 says a ruler without the guard of those who rebuke perishes even with no enemy; Pazhamozhi 263 says the elders' counsel that saves him is painful at first.
teaches: The pair names the cost of the Kural's safeguard: the rebuke that keeps the king from ruin must be borne as pain before it is known as protection, which is why kings are tempted to do without it.
list_adds: it adds the cost to the hearer, painful first, which the couplet's plain statement of necessity leaves out.

note: In Akananuru 167 the man tells his heart, which is pressing him to leave for wealth, that after a sweet night with his wife in the tall house he would lie sleepless in a ruined village hall, and gives up the journey; in Natrinai 366 he tells his heart that whoever leaves her washed, flower-tied hair and soft bed in the north wind that shakes the sparrow's nest is a fool.
teaches: The two give the same refusal two arguments: Akananuru 167 sets the home against the terror of the road, while Natrinai 366 never reaches the road and argues from the season alone, a cold wind that even a bird's home must withstand, so the stay-at-home decision could rest either on fear or on a general law of the world (உலகியல்).

note: Kural 888 says a family with inner enmity wears itself down like gold rubbing a file; Pazhamozhi 112 says provoking the defiant within one's own house is pulling the axle-pin from inside the cart.
teaches: Together they show inner enmity as both a slow wearing and a sudden collapse, and Pazhamozhi places its cause with the householder who provokes it, not with the enmity alone.
list_adds: its proverb makes the head of the house the agent of the ruin, sitting inside what he dismantles, where the couplet speaks of the family as a whole.

note: Thirikadugam 62 names the man who wrongly keeps a deposit among three whose line is lost; Pazhamozhi 340 traces how keeping begins, by delaying the return in the hope that the owner will not claim it.
teaches: The pair shows the sin and its root: the Thirikadugam punishes the kept deposit, and Pazhamozhi locates the fault already in stalling when the owner asks.

note: Naladiyar 126 likens attaching to one thought worthy who is not to opening a casket for sandal and finding a snake; Pazhamozhi 385 likens seekers who attach to patrons unable to satisfy them to axle grease that soaks away.
teaches: The Naladiyar's failed attachment brings danger, Pazhamozhi's brings slow waste, so the pair shows two costs of attaching without examining: harm from the unworthy and loss to the incapable.
list_adds: it moves the quatrain's failed choice of a friend into the suppliant's choice of a patron, and names the seeker's own great desire as the cause.

note: Kural 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, aram plots the plotter's; Pazhamozhi 346 says plotting against one's benefactor is cutting the branch one sits on.
teaches: The Kural leaves the return to aram, while Pazhamozhi needs no agent: the benefactor is the plotter's own support, so the ruin is self-inflicted at once.
list_adds: it narrows the couplet to the one who cared for the plotter and joins others to the plot, and its proverb makes the retribution mechanical.

note: Naladiyar 33 says the fool breaks down when the fruit of past deeds arrives, while those who see it as old desert are freed of confusion; Pazhamozhi 238 says those who do not see their suffering as their old deed rage at the foes who cause it.
teaches: The quatrain turns the knowledge of old deeds against grief, and Pazhamozhi turns it against anger at enemies, recasting the foe as a servant carrying out an order, so the same doctrine is shown ending both despair and revenge.
list_adds: its proverb of the servant who burns the town on orders gives the enemy a role, the agent of one's own deed, that the quatrain does not consider.

note: 234 says the five got out of the lac house because there is no place without escape for one due to escape; 239 says the Chola's son survived burning and came to rule, for nothing is beyond those who keep their life.
teaches: Both proverbs follow an escape from fire, one from the epic and one from Tamil royal memory, and the second carries the story past survival to kingship, so the chapter makes surviving the fire the first step of a fortune still unfolding.

note: Kural 515 says work is not to be given to anyone but one who knows and can do it, merely because he is favoured; Pazhamozhi 172 says not to ask whether a man is kin but to look only at learning.
teaches: The couplet bars favour as a ground; Pazhamozhi names the commonest favour, kinship, and adds a concession the couplet lacks, that even a disobedient learned agent costs no more than the salt fed to a working ox.
list_adds: its proverb weighs the risk of the learned stranger against kin and finds the risk cheap, a cost-reckoning the couplet does not make.

note: Naladiyar 255 praises the worthy who will not speak their learning even when asked, knowing it would not be taken in; Pazhamozhi 23 shows the chatterer scorning those whose learning keeps their tongues in check.
teaches: The pair exposes the cost of the worthy's silence that the Naladiyar praises: the low read restraint as emptiness and mock it, so the learned man's silence protects his learning but not his standing.
list_adds: it sets the restrained learned and the chattering intruder in one scene, so the silence the quatrain commends is seen from the scoffer's side.

note: Both foster mothers ask யாங்கு வல்லுநள்கொல் தானே of a girl who refused milk held up in a fine vessel at home: Akananuru 105 follows the question with the raiders' road of Ezhini's bowmen, Kuruntokai 356 with the scalding muddy water she must gulp.
teaches: The shared formula of the refused milk and 'how will she manage' is a stock frame of the foster mother's lament, and the two poems show its slot filled differently: the long poem measures the girl's leaving by the road's dangers, the short one by what she must now drink, so the same frame can carry either fear or tenderness.

note: Naladiyar 365 ranks striving in austerity first and dwelling with loved ones as the middle way; Pazhamozhi 390 condemns those who stand in the middle, choosing neither household nor its absence.
teaches: The word 'middle' moves: for the Naladiyar the middle is the household, a lesser but honest life, while for the Pazhamozhi the middle is indecision between the two lives, and only that is worthless, so neither life is shamed, only failing to commit.
list_adds: it drops the ranking of the two lives and puts the fault in the gap between them, with the image of a pole-carrier who drops both loads.

note: Naladiyar 37 says the gains of human birth should not be spent serving the body; Pazhamozhi 365 says the hard-won human birth should be used for aram as far as one can before disease, age and Death arrive together.
teaches: The Naladiyar argues from what human birth is for; Pazhamozhi adds the deadline, so the rare birth has both a purpose and a closing time, and aram is measured by capacity, ஆற்றும் துணையும்.
list_adds: it couples the rarity of the birth with the three that end it, which the quatrain, speaking of gains and the body, does not name.

note: 149 says no one does for another what that other must do; 159 applies it to the man who waits to have his task done later by someone else.
teaches: 159 supplies the evidence for 149's flat denial: the helper one waits for will not even heat water, so he will not leap into fire for one.

note: Kural 414 offers listening to one who has not studied, the ஆயினும் keeping study first; Pazhamozhi 5 says outright that hearing is better than learning.
teaches: The two rank the same pair in opposite order: the Kural makes hearing the fallback for the unlearned, Pazhamozhi makes it the cure for the learned man's narrowness.
list_adds: its frog-in-the-well image gives a reason for ranking hearing above study, that one's own text is a single well, which the couplet lacks.

note: Purananuru 142 says Pekan is foolish (மடம்) only in giving, like rain on salt land, never foolish in battle; Pazhamozhi 74 says knowing foolishness (அறிமடம்) is an ornament to the worthy, citing the mantle given to a peacock.
teaches: The puram poem already calls Pekan's giving மடம் and limits it to the gift; the ethics verse adds அறி, knowing, and so makes the patron's folly a chosen virtue rather than a lapse.
list_adds: it pairs Pekan's mantle with Pari's chariot as one kind of act and gives the whole class a name, அறிமடம்.

note: Naladiyar 70 says no one bites back a raging dog; Pazhamozhi 57 says no one gores back a cow. Both make a beast of the insulter to show that retaliation is beneath a person.
teaches: The two images differ in what they make of the insulter: the Naladiyar's biting dog is vicious, Pazhamozhi's goring cow is merely artless, so the unlearned are excused where the low are condemned.
list_adds: it puts a cow in the dog's place and the unlearned in the place of the low, softening the judgement on the offender.

note: Kural 700 says intimacy that does the improper because 'we are old friends' brings ruin; Acharakkovai 66 names கழிகிழமை, overstepping intimacy, among the things those who would last in service avoid.
teaches: The Kural states the danger of presuming on an old bond; the Acharakkovai puts that danger among gate, gift and dress, showing that presuming on intimacy is one of several small encroachments on a lord's dignity.
list_adds: It sets excessive intimacy beside anger at the gate, carelessness at gifts and dressing like the lord, so the couplet's single fault becomes one of a family of encroachments.

note: Kural 848 describes the man who neither does what he is told nor sees for himself; Pazhamozhi 28 says the senseless cannot be set firm and gives as the condition that learning has not gone in. The link rests on an uncertain reading of 28.
teaches: The couplet names the double failure of the unteachable, and the Pazhamozhi verse places its cause earlier, in learning that never entered, so telling fails because nothing is there to receive it.
list_adds: its image of the drum that answers a spoken cue supplies the responsive learner the couplet leaves out, so the fool is measured against an instrument.

note: Both verses forbid pleading 'I have no kin' as a reason to fail; 153 answers it with unwearied effort, 156 with the image of the long-armed man's great shoulders.
teaches: The pair shows the heading's single counsel argued two ways, by the promise of success and by the sign of strength in one's own body, so the lack of kin is answered both by outcome and by capacity.

note: Naladiyar 310 says that where old acquaintance stands as a post (பழமைகந் தாக) one may ask what intimacy allows; Pazhamozhi 129 speaks of friends who lean on old acquaintance as a post (பழமை கந்தாக) and closes that a span of respect beats a cubit of friendship.
teaches: The two use the same phrase of old acquaintance as a tethering post: the quatrain lets one lean on it to ask for help, while Pazhamozhi warns that leaning on it while dropping care wears the friendship out, so the post is a support with a limit.
list_adds: its proverb ranks a little respect above much intimacy, a measure the quatrain does not apply to the same post of old acquaintance.

note: Naladiyar 63 says unguarded words burn the speaker without end; Pazhamozhi 58 says returned abuse sets fire to one's own house.
teaches: Both place the burn of an angry word on the speaker, and Pazhamozhi widens it from the speaker's self to his household, the house as the thing consumed.
list_adds: its proverb names the house, not the speaker's mind, as what the retort burns, widening the harm beyond the self.

note: Kural 1009 says others take the wealth gathered by giving up love and virtue; Pazhamozhi 214 says wealth draws attackers when its holder lacks firmness, though the wealth itself is good.
teaches: Losing wealth to others has two causes in the pair: a vice in how it was gathered and a weakness in who holds it, so even rightly gained wealth is not safe in weak hands.
list_adds: it adds a condition the couplet lacks, that the wealth may be நன்மையின் மாண்ட and still be lost, because the danger lies in the owner's want of resolve.

note: Naladiyar 113 says that in trouble few kin claim the relation; Pazhamozhi 352 says those of one family do not part from a man in trouble.
teaches: On the same test, trouble, the two works give opposite verdicts on kin, one of shared family loyalty and one of kin as fair-weather clingers, so the ethics group has no settled view.
list_adds: it narrows kin to ஒருகுடியார் and puts the desertion on outsiders, where the quatrain puts it on kin themselves.

note: Thirikadugam 36 names the flesh-eater who claims compassion; Pazhamozhi 343 says those who eat flesh do not walk in grace.
teaches: Both deny the meat-eater's claim to grace, one by exposing his self-serving reasoning and the other by tracing the habit back to anger.

note: Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; Pazhamozhi 10 uses the same image for the misdeed of a learned man known in his town.
teaches: The image of the moon's spot passes from birth to learning, so the two together make visibility of fault the cost of any eminence, inherited or earned.
list_adds: it carries the couplet's image from lineage to the learned who live conspicuously, and makes their breach of their own texts the fault seen.

note: Kural 247 grants as plain fact that this world is not for those without wealth; Pazhamozhi 327 brings that fact into the house and sets money beside a woman's modesty and the body's food as a precondition of the household's work.
teaches: Read together, the couplet's premise about wealth and this world becomes a rule of the house: money is one of three things a household life cannot do without.
list_adds: its run of three 'not without' clauses ranks money with modesty and food, so wealth stands as one of the household's basic needs rather than a worldly power.

note: Kural 30 says those called அந்தணர் are the virtuous, kind to every living being; Acharakkovai 92 trusts the word of the அந்தணர் and distrusts that of the புலையர் on the day of a rite.
teaches: The Kural derives the name அந்தணர் from conduct, while the Acharakkovai uses it as a birth-group set against the புலையர், so the pair show the same word serving as a moral title in one book and a caste rank in the other.
list_adds: It pairs the அந்தணர் with the புலையர் as opposites, a contrast of birth that the Kural's definition by kindness does not make.

note: Kural 90 says a guest wilts when the host's face changes; Acharakkovai 54 puts a smile first among five honours given with food to a guest.
teaches: The Kural says what the wrong face does to a guest, and the Acharakkovai sets the right face at the head of a sequence of welcome, so the host's smile is the first act of hospitality, before word, water, mat and bed.
list_adds: It orders the welcome from face to word to body to rest, so the smile the Kural defends by a negative image becomes the first of five steps that accompany food.

note: Kural 874 says the world rests on the greatness of one who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship; Pazhamozhi 296 says old enmity never becomes friendship. On the reading that 874 means turning enemies into friends, the two conflict.
teaches: The two disagree over whether enmity can be converted: the Kural praises the man who makes a friend of a foe, while the Pazhamozhi holds that the old foe, like a tuber, only waits for rain.
list_adds: its tuber image gives a reason for the denial, that enmity lies dormant and revives with its season, which the couplet's praise does not face.

note: Naladiyar 280 counts guarding wealth among its bitter sufferings; Pazhamozhi 368 says why guarding is vain: those who eye wealth outnumber those who keep it, as birds take grain under the watcher's eye.
teaches: The Naladiyar finds custody painful; Pazhamozhi finds it futile, since the covetous are always more than the keepers, and under its heading on aram this futility is the argument for giving wealth rather than keeping it.
list_adds: its pairing of grain and wealth makes the watcher's failure an image of all custody, where the quatrain lists custody as one of four pains.

note: Thirikadugam 42 says the vellala family behaves toward brahmins as toward fire even when familiar with them; Acharakkovai 84 says fire, like the king, harms one who slights it as familiar.
teaches: The two books use one image, fire that burns the familiar, for two superiors, the brahmin and the king, showing that the period's rule against contempt bred by familiarity covered ritual and political rank alike.

note: Kural 1076 makes carrying on (உய்த்து) secrets the mark of the base; Pazhamozhi 180 says that even pleasant friends cannot refrain from passing on (உயவாது) what they heard, then restricts the rule to the base.
teaches: Read with the Kural, the verse shows the trait the couplet confines to the base is near-universal, so keeping secrets from the base is a minimum measure, not a sufficient safeguard.
list_adds: it widens the couplet's claim from the base to everyone, even agreeable friends, before narrowing it again in the proverb, a turn the couplet lacks.

note: Kural 33 asks for aram without ceasing, as far as one is able; Pazhamozhi 367 allows that one may not manage it on many days and asks for it on some days with the best things.
teaches: Where the Kural measures aram by constancy within capacity, Pazhamozhi concedes the lapse and moves the measure to the quality of the gift, so a few days of the best is accepted where the couplet asks for every day.
list_adds: it trades frequency for quality, some days with the best things, which the couplet's 'without ceasing' leaves no room for.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 98 says the base, though bound and scoured, show their dirt; Pazhamozhi 110 says suffering does not tame the wicked, as unfit clay makes no wall.
teaches: Both deny that working on the base changes them, and together they cover the two methods of correction, scouring from outside and mixing in from within, each failing on the material.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 62 counts that want of close friends is learned in ruin (கெழியின்மை கேட்டா லறிக); Pazhamozhi 134 says the ruined have no friends.
teaches: The counted verse makes ruin a means of knowing; Pazhamozhi adds the crowd of eaters who vanish and puts the fact in the Kali age, so a test of friends becomes a judgement on the time.

note: Kural 987 asks one to do good even to those who have done harm; Acharakkovai 40 asks only that one not wound elders and young kin at their meal, even if they have done great harm.
teaches: Set beside the Kural's universal demand, the Acharakkovai's rule is narrower in scope (kin, at the meal) and lower in demand (not harming rather than doing good), so the code fixes a minimum where the Kural sets an ideal.
list_adds: It joins forbearance to a seating rule (not sitting above them), so restraint toward kin is part of the precedence of the table.

note: Saying 8 ranks serving the learned above learning; saying 46 denies the name of learning to what is learnt without submission.
teaches: Across two tens, the book first puts reverence for teachers above learning and then makes it the condition of learning, so reverence moves from the greater good to the thing without which learning does not exist.

note: Pazhamozhi 273 says the king's servant should ask the king for nothing; 274 says he should not seek help elsewhere either, for that is like sucking the cow's throat while the udder is there.
teaches: Taken together the verses leave the servant no one to ask: not the king, whom he must not petition, and not others, who are a dry source, so all his provision must come unasked from the master he serves.

note: Kural 489 says to do the hard deed at the very moment the rare chance comes; Pazhamozhi 287 applies this to answering an enemy who has struck, and calls delay folly.
teaches: The Kural's general rule of the moment is given a hostile case, where the passing chance is the attacker himself, gone like a snake once it has bitten.
list_adds: it turns the couplet's abstract rare moment into a concrete one with a cost, the snake's fang that cannot be taken once it has fled.

note: Purananuru 196, a bard to the Pandya Nanmaran, says that saying yes to what one can and no to what one cannot are both proper ways of a giver's friendship, while false promises and false refusals wound the asker and lessen the giver's fame.
teaches: The bard's complaint to a king and the ethics verse state the same rule about refusal, which shows the norm of the honest 'no' is older than the ethics works and was first argued from a suppliant's side.

note: Kural 1268 has a man serving in the king's war wish the king victory so that he may feast at home with his wife by evening; Akananuru 24 is such a man in the king's camp at the end of the rains, measuring the camp's sleepless night against his wife's lonely one.
teaches: The couplet states the soldier-husband's wish as a sentence; the poem gives the night that produces it, the blunted tusks, the drums and the cold rain, so the Kural's two clauses read as the end of a long vigil.

note: Kural 221 calls every gift but one to the destitute a measured loan; Pazhamozhi 383 says even lavish giving with no eye to return is wage labour if it looks to fame.
teaches: The Kural strips the name of giving from gifts that expect a material return; Pazhamozhi strips it also from gifts that expect only fame, so the wage can be praise as well as goods.
list_adds: it adds fame as a hidden return and names lack of discernment as the giver's fault, which the couplet's loan does not cover.

note: Kural 691 asks those who serve kings to be like people warming at a fire, neither too far nor too near; Pazhamozhi 276 warns the favourite who answers the king's fierce love with his own and acts without perceiving what lies hidden.
teaches: Together they show that the danger of being too near comes most from the king's own affection: the Kural's fire burns those who press close, and Pazhamozhi shows the courtier being drawn close by love and forgetting to keep distance.
list_adds: it gives the too-near case a cause the couplet leaves out, the king's love itself, and closes it with a proverb of self-betrayal.

note: Naladiyar 269 likens the giving of fools to rain poured into the sea while the paddy withers; Pazhamozhi 220 says leaving the hunger of kin and lovers unrelieved while helping strangers is like the black palmyra.
teaches: Both make misdirected giving a vice, not a virtue: the Naladiyar faults giving where there is no need, Pazhamozhi names the need passed over, the hunger of one's own kin.
list_adds: it names who is passed over, those who came with love and one's kin, where the quatrain gives only the image of the parched field.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 64 says the world passes over the elder who grew old unlearned and praises the young one who learned; Pazhamozhi 6 also has a young man outdo his elders, but by birth, not study.
teaches: Both set the able young against the doubting old, but the counted work credits learning and Pazhamozhi credits lineage, so youth's claim rests on two different grounds.

note: Naladiyar 6 says no one here has leapt clear of Death and escaped (கூற்றம் குதித்துய்ந்தார் ஈங்கில்லை) and urges the wealthy to give; Pazhamozhi 391 closes on the same words as a proverb after a list of wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth and birth.
teaches: The same saying about leaping Death serves two ends: the Naladiyar draws from it a duty to give wealth now, the Pazhamozhi uses it to cancel every advantage of fortune and birth at once, showing the saying was a common proof for different counsels.
list_adds: it sets six goods (wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth, birth) before the saying, so the proverb strikes a whole inventory, where the Naladiyar names wealth alone.

note: Verse 16 says the elders are to be worshipped as gods; verse 72 says that in a great house or a temple one does not bow even to them.
teaches: The god-like worship verse 16 owes to elders gives way where a greater object of worship is present, so the book ranks reverence by place and the elder's claim is not absolute.

note: Elathi 12 says it is good neither to desire nor to look at five places, among them the killing ground and the gambling ground; Acharakkovai 37 bars looking at five things, among them killing and gambling.
teaches: Both works bar the eye, but the Elathi bars the places where killing and gambling happen while the Acharakkovai bars the acts themselves and gives hell as the reason, so the ban on looking is applied once to sites and once to deeds.

note: The idyll's king answers both those who seek justice and those who seek their needs, with a clear sight that discerns between them; the couplet says a ruler not easy of access who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself.
teaches: The couplet names access and examined judgment as two duties whose lack ruins a king, while the idyll shows them as one daily audience in which judgment and gifts are granted together and discernment joins them, so justice and giving were seen as a single court function.

note: Kural 129 says the scar (வடு) burned by the tongue never heals; Pazhamozhi 39 says one must do nothing that leaves a scar (வடு) on oneself, since a word does not wear away.
teaches: The pair turns the tongue's unhealing scar both ways: the Kural's falls on the one spoken to, Pazhamozhi's on the one spoken of, and both last for the same reason.
list_adds: it moves the scar from the wound of harsh speech to the reproach a deed earns, and sets it against stone for duration.

note: Pazhamozhi 139 counts love given to the shameless as wasted; 140 goes on to say what to do when a friend turns unfriendly: break with him.
teaches: Read in order, the two verses move from loss to action: once the love is seen to be moonlight in a forest, the next counsel is to stop shedding it and answer the break with a break.

note: Kural 729 holds the learned who fear an assembly of the good lower than the unlearned; Pazhamozhi 20 advises the learned to fear the unlearned who bandy words among them.
teaches: The Kural's demand for fearlessness in assembly has an exception: before the good, fear is a failing, but before the shameless unlearned, against whom even gods are powerless, wariness is wisdom.
list_adds: it names the one opponent in an assembly a learned man should fear, and its proverb grounds that fear in shamelessness rather than skill.

note: Kural 448 says a ruler without rebukers perishes even with no one to ruin him; Pazhamozhi 117 says one who will not take the words of the great and does not guard himself makes others into thieves.
teaches: The Kural's ruin needs no enemy; Pazhamozhi adds that the unguarded man's ruin creates its own agents, so the thief is partly his making.
list_adds: it carries the couplet's claim from the king to anyone and its proverb shifts guilt from the thief to the man who would not heed counsel.

note: Verse 16 names the five peerless elders and says to worship them as gods; verse 62 names the three acts of ஆசாரம் owed to elders.
teaches: Verse 16 gives the rank and verse 62 the bodily acts by which god-like worship of elders is performed, so the book's worship of elders turns out to be bowing, timely attendance and rising.

note: 205 says the bard does not want even the three kings' gifts if given without regard (பெட்பின்றி); Kural 1057 says the heart rejoices on seeing those who give without scorn.
teaches: The Kural states the receiver's joy at a gift given without contempt; 205 turns it into a condition of acceptance, so the manner of giving decided whether a bard would take the gift at all, not only how he felt about it.

note: Kural 442 bids one cherish those who can remove present affliction and guard against what has not come; Pazhamozhi 262 describes guardians restrained in mind, speech and body and says without them life perishes.
teaches: Together they show that the Kural's guarding helpers are, for the Pazhamozhi, first of all men disciplined in all three channels, so the ascetic's threefold restraint becomes the qualification of the king's protectors.
list_adds: it sets the guardians' power beside their threefold self-restraint as its ground and closes with the stark cost of lacking them.

note: Kural 759 calls wealth the sharpest steel for cutting down enemies' pride (செருக்கறுக்கும்); Pazhamozhi 196 says wealth given cuts off (அறுத்தல்) the senseless better than a spear.
teaches: The pair shows how the Kural's metaphor works in practice: wealth wounds not by being held but by being handed over, so the sharpest blade is a payment that leaves the opponent nothing to resist.
list_adds: its proverb sets the gift and the spear side by side and ranks the gift above force, a contrast the couplet only implies.

note: Kural 715 praises the restraint of not speaking first among elders; Pazhamozhi 19 applies the same rule of order to a dispute two have begun, where the later speaker pushes ahead of his turn.
teaches: The pair shows the Kural's rule of precedence is also a rule of relevance: speaking out of turn is not only immodest but misses the point at issue, as the bandage misses the torn knee.
list_adds: the proverb gives a reason the couplet lacks: speech before its turn lands on the wrong place.

note: Kural 458 says that even the worthy, good of mind in full, are protected by good company; Pazhamozhi 90 reverses the same phrase to say the base, good of company in full, never become good of mind.
teaches: Held together they show the house view that company acts on the mind has a limit: it guards a good mind already there and cannot make one in the base.
list_adds: its salt-sea image and inverted wording set an exception beside the couplet: for the base, company runs one way only and leaves the mind as it was.

note: Kural 890 says living with those not in accord is like dwelling with a snake in a hut; Pazhamozhi 253 uses the same image for a king who keeps aspirants to leadership on his own level.
teaches: The couplet leaves open who the discordant companions are; the pairing names them in a court, ambitious men the king himself has raised, so the snake is one he brought in.
list_adds: it carries the household image into the king's domain and makes the king's own act of raising men the cause of the danger.

note: Naladiyar 273 says the fool who hoards and dies is mocked by his own stored wealth; Pazhamozhi 219 says those who keep their wealth and die guard the outer fence while the inner is lost.
teaches: The two verses use the same phrase of keeping and dying and give the hoarder two judges, his wealth's mockery and his own lost next birth.
list_adds: it adds the next birth as the thing lost, where the quatrain stops at the mockery of the wealth that outlived him.

note: Acharakkovai 42 treats the menstrual days as days of no touch and sets the twelve days after the bath apart for the wife; Sivavakkiyar 134 says the monthly pollution is what grows into the body once the months stop, so no birth is free of it.
teaches: The ritual rule and the Siddhar's attack both join menstruation to conception, but one draws a line of pollution across the cycle while the other uses the same cycle to deny that any body stands outside pollution.

note: The Kural commands making wealth as the sharpest weapon; the hero leaving for wealth that is hard to earn counts what the going costs the girl he leaves.
teaches: The Kural's bare imperative to make wealth is weighed here against a girl's quoted plea not to stay long, showing that the duty the maxim states without condition was, in akam, always paid for by someone left behind.

note: Kural 204 says that if one plots another's ruin, virtue plots the ruin of the plotter; Pazhamozhi 46 says one who looks on another's ruin sees his own soon after, and rebukes the heart for a cruel word.
teaches: Both make inner intent enough to set the return in motion, but the Kural names virtue as the agent while Pazhamozhi names no agent and only the speed of the return.
list_adds: it sets the counsel inside a dialogue with one's own heart and swaps the Kural's agent, அறம், for a bare law of time.

note: Innaa Narpathu 10 counts, as its first painful thing, reciting a song where none grasp its meaning as painful; Pazhamozhi 25 says counsel spoken among dull men is lost like flour sifted in the sea.
teaches: The counted work names the speaker's pain and the proverb names the speech's loss, so together they show that speaking to those who cannot take it in hurts the speaker and achieves nothing for the hearer.

note: Naladiyar 195 says good and bad lineage are words with nothing behind them; Pazhamozhi 34 treats excellent descent from an old line as a real distinction. The conflict holds on reading 34's விழுத்தொடையர் and தொல் வந்தார் as birth.
teaches: The pair shows the ethics group divided on whether lineage is a fact before conduct: the Jain quatrain empties the word, the proverb collection banks on it.
list_adds: its abundance image treats birth and conduct as two goods to be summed, where the quatrain allows only austerity, learning and effort to make a line.

note: Kural 880 says those who do not break the pride of hostile men are as good as dead; Pazhamozhi 299 sets the limit, that once the enemy is killed further rage is waste.
teaches: Together they bound hostility at both ends: one must break the enemy, but anger that outlives the enemy is water poured on a reaped field.
list_adds: its harvest proverb adds an end point the couplet lacks, measuring anger by whether anything is left for it to do.

note: Naladiyar 351 says the petty-minded grow more practised in wrong as they age; Pazhamozhi 93 says some grow old without understanding, like trees that flower without fruit.
teaches: Together they deny that age brings wisdom from two sides: the Naladiyar says age deepens folly, Pazhamozhi that it can simply pass without yield, so telling the fool is one more seed that will not sprout.
list_adds: it sets old age among the failures of plant growth, flower without fruit and seed without sprout, so the old fool becomes a natural kind of barrenness.

note: Kural 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores; Pazhamozhi 216 says the drum-proclaimed wealth of such a man is a dog's coconut.
teaches: The Kural says he has nothing; the proverb sharpens this to having something he cannot open, so the miser is not poor but locked out of his own possession.
list_adds: its proverb replaces the couplet's abstract 'nothing' with an image of possession without access, and the drum carries the claim to royal wealth.

note: Kural 442 bids one cherish as support those who remove an affliction that has come and guard against one to come; Pazhamozhi 149 says one need not seek helpers at all, since each is his own physician.
teaches: The Kural's helper is a physician to the king, and Pazhamozhi takes the same healing image back for the self, so the two disagree on whether one's trouble can be cured from outside.
list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's healer into the striver himself, denying that another can do one's own work.

note: Kural 534 says the fearful have no fortress; Pazhamozhi 320 says the incapable are caught through fear though shut behind walls, like a timid bird that betrays itself in the dark.
teaches: The couplet states that walls do not help the fearful; Pazhamozhi shows how, since fear itself gives them away, as the bird's start reveals it, so the failure is exposure from within, not weak defences.
list_adds: it supplies the mechanism through the bird image, the fear that makes its holder visible, which the couplet's flat 'no fortress' does not give.

note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander like a shielded flame; Pazhamozhi 138 makes the same steadiness the mark of the highest friend, who finds no rift even when looking, against the lowest, who believe.
teaches: The pair moves resistance to slander from a private virtue to a test of friendship: the Naladiyar's steady heart protects itself, Pazhamozhi's protects the bond between two other people.
list_adds: it sets the steady man against his opposite and names what the credulous one's belief costs, the friendship's later pain.

note: Kural 806 says those who keep bounds do not give up an old bond even when ruin comes; Pazhamozhi 64 has the great keep feeling for long-standing associates who go astray, yet their house perishes.
teaches: The pair shows the limit of old loyalty: the great do not cast the old associate off, they grieve for him, but their constancy cannot stop the ruin his crooked conduct brings.
list_adds: it sets the loyal great man's grief beside the old associate's ruin, so the couplet's constancy is shown to be powerless to save.

note: Verse 42 names the days a husband keeps to his wife after her bath; verse 43 lists hours and calendar days on which the couple do not come together.
teaches: Taken together the two verses make marital union a matter of the ritual calendar, with days prescribed by the wife's cycle and others barred by the moon, the gods and the hours.

note: Kural 99 asks why one who sees the sweetness sweet speech yields would use harsh words; Pazhamozhi 191 asks the same of those who can tell good speech from mean, and answers that only mean speech brings trouble.
teaches: The two rest one choice on two motives: the Kural on the good that sweet speech brings, Pazhamozhi on the danger harsh speech brings back to the speaker, so the case for sweet speech is both gain and safety.
list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's rhetorical question into a rule about risk, that sweet speech never endangers, which the couplet does not state.

note: Kural 1047 says a man in poverty is looked at as a stranger even by his own mother; Pazhamozhi 68 calls it a painful wrong for a man to set a poor kinsman apart among his many kin.
teaches: The Kural records estrangement from kin as one of poverty's miseries; Pazhamozhi names the kinsman who does the estranging as at fault, so the same fact appears once as the poor man's suffering and once as the kin's wrong.
list_adds: its proverb of a line drawn within a row makes the poor kinsman's exclusion a breach of the group's own unity, which the couplet states only as the poor man's loss.

note: Kural 359 says one who knows the support and lives so that supports perish is freed from clinging pains; Pazhamozhi 397 shows a flame living on wick, bowl and ghee and says that, its supports gone, the self cuts off birth.
teaches: The Kural's abstract play on சார்பு gets a working model in the lamp: the flame is not destroyed by being blown out but goes out when what feeds it is gone, so release is shown as starvation of support, not an act of force.
list_adds: it lists the flame's three supports, wick, bowl and ghee, and adds the water proverb, so the couplet's one word becomes a concrete chain of dependence.

note: Kural 1078 says the base yield their use only when crushed like sugar-cane; Pazhamozhi 110 asks whether the wicked ever come under control because they have suffered and answers no. The conflict holds on the reading that the Kural's crushing and Pazhamozhi's suffering are both pressure applied to the base.
teaches: The pair splits on whether pressure works on the base: the Kural finds something sweet to be pressed out, Pazhamozhi finds clay that no binder will make into a wall.
list_adds: its proverb puts the fault in the material itself, so that no admixture of hardship helps, against the couplet's cane that yields under force.

note: Both close on உடைத்து, 'the world holds such': Kural 277 those bright outside like the kunri seed and black within, Pazhamozhi 194 thieves like peacocks who seem attached by day and rob by night.
teaches: Pazhamozhi moves the Kural's hidden-black ascetic into the household: the false outside belongs to dependants who live with one, and the betrayal is a theft of food and clothing in the hours of sleep.
list_adds: it gives the couplet's single colour image a sequence of acts, night theft and daylight show of attachment, which makes the deceit something one can watch for.

note: Naladiyar 9 says the man who only guards his wealth without using or giving it will be thought of as one who has lost it; Pazhamozhi 217 says the non-giver's wealth is a loss like losing an eye with its beauty.
teaches: Both verses answer the miser's fear of loss by calling his keeping the real loss, and the proverb adds that it is a double loss of use and of looks.
list_adds: it grounds the claim in the fall of rulers of the whole earth, an argument from impermanence the quatrain does not make, and turns the miser's own word இழவு against him.

note: Kural 510 says that doubting one already trusted brings endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 121 says raising a man to intimacy and casting him off without cause is a deed of smallness.
teaches: The Kural counts the cost of withdrawing trust to the one who withdraws; Pazhamozhi judges the character of the act, a child's play with a grove, so the error is both costly and mean.
list_adds: its proverb names the fault as whim and smallness, a moral judgement beside the couplet's prudential one.

note: Kural 103 praises help given by those who do not weigh the return; Acharakkovai 88 says those who would live rightly do not even speak of the return on help they gave.
teaches: The Kural's giver does not reckon the return before giving; the Acharakkovai adds that he does not mention it after, so the pair carry the refusal to weigh from the act into speech.
list_adds: It groups silence about one's help with not faulting food and not praising one's own vows, so the rule becomes part of a discipline of the tongue about one's own goods.

note: 34 quotes dharma: there is expiation for killing cows' udders, destroying unborn children or wronging elders, but none for killing a benefit; Kural 110 says those who killed any good may escape, but not one who killed a good done to him.
teaches: The Kural compresses into a rule what the Purananuru presents as a known saying with its list of lesser crimes, and the poet turns it on himself, so the maxim was already used to bind a bard to praise his patron: gratitude here is the poet's own obligation, not only the patron's claim.

note: Kural 375 says that in making wealth the favourable can turn bad and the unfavourable good; Pazhamozhi 235 says that for those who are to prosper even what was judged bad turns out good, for the fortunate have no evil day.
teaches: The couplet leaves it open which way a thing will turn, and Pazhamozhi decides it by the person: the same reversal runs only toward good for one with fortune, so the pair shows the couplet's instability resolved by whose lot it is.
list_adds: it makes the reversal depend on the person's fortune and ties it to the reckoning of good and bad days, which the couplet does not mention.

note: Naladiyar 229 says that when those taken as one's own prove otherwise, one should honour them all the more and keep it within; Pazhamozhi 139 calls heart's friendship given to the shameless moonlight shed in the forest.
teaches: Read together, the Naladiyar's counsel to keep honouring the false friend meets its limit in shamelessness: where the other has no shame within, the honour reaches no one, and Pazhamozhi counts it wasted.
list_adds: its proverb names the outcome the quatrain leaves out, that continued regard for the shameless lights an empty forest.

note: Both use a damaged great building that keeps its function: Naladiyar 147's decayed house still has a dry corner, Pazhamozhi 60's assembly hall stays a hall when cut into. The reading of 60's proverb is uncertain.
teaches: The same image works from two sides: the Naladiyar uses it for what the well-born still do in hardship, Pazhamozhi for how others must still regard the great when their standing is damaged.
list_adds: it turns the quatrain's image of the well-born man's own constancy into a warning to those who would belittle him.

note: Kural 894 says the weak doing harm to the strong is beckoning Death; Pazhamozhi 47 says the strong tormenting the weak find the victims' tears fall on them as Death.
teaches: The pair makes Death the outcome on both sides of an unequal fight: the weak who strike the strong invite it by their act, the strong who strike the weak receive it from their victims' tears.
list_adds: it reverses the couplet's direction, making the strong the doer and the weak's tears, not the strong man's arm, the bearer of Death.

note: Kural 717 says the learning of the learned shines among those able to examine words faultlessly; Pazhamozhi 7 says it is visible only to the very learned and closed to common people.
teaches: The Kural names the audience where learning shines; Pazhamozhi adds that outside it learning is not dimmer but unseen, as a snake's feet are hidden from all but snakes.
list_adds: its proverb makes judgement of learning a matter of kind knowing kind, and shuts out the common people the couplet does not mention.

note: Kural 517 says to examine who will finish a task by what means and then leave it to him; Pazhamozhi 158 shows the task handed out of sloth to those without firm grip, while the master too lets go.
teaches: The Kural's letting go is safe only after examination; Pazhamozhi shows the same handing-over done from sloth, so delegation is a virtue or a ruin depending on why it is done.
list_adds: it names the motive, sloth, and the double loss of grip, which the couplet's rule of choosing assumes away.

note: Naladiyar 218 asks what use is a close friend who gives not even a fly's foot of help; Pazhamozhi 136 names the friend kept as a reserve who gives none at need and adds that he first set one in danger.
teaches: The pair separates two failures the word 'useless friend' joins: the Naladiyar's friend merely gives nothing, while Pazhamozhi's raises one into peril and then withdraws, so the worst friend is the one whose help began.
list_adds: the ladder proverb adds the stage the quatrain lacks, being helped up and then stranded, which makes a half-given help worse than none.

note: Kural 454 says understanding seems to be in the mind but lies in one's company; Pazhamozhi 148 makes company the test by which others, sages included, are known.
teaches: The Kural's claim about where understanding lives becomes, in the Pazhamozhi, a rule of evidence: if a person's nature is in their company, then the company is what an observer should read, even of a sage.
list_adds: it extends the couplet to the judging of முனிவர் and sets company above witnesses and inquiry as proof.

note: Naladiyar 350 says small bullocks fed cut grass never learn the yoke, and the base, though rich, are known by their deeds; Pazhamozhi 96 says forest men of cruel deeds granted a place in the country do not behave well.
teaches: The Naladiyar's care is feeding and wealth, Pazhamozhi's is a ruler's grant of settlement; together they show the period's ethics denying reform by provision whether the provider is a herdsman or a lord.
list_adds: it moves the claim from private wealth to a ruler's act of settlement and pins it on a people of a named way of life.

note: Both set understanding against ornaments: in 26 ornaments come after the cloth of understanding, in 33 priceless jewels come and go with fortune while understanding stays.
teaches: Read together the chapter makes jewels doubly inferior to understanding, dependent on it for their sense and on fortune for their keeping.
list_adds: 33 adds time to 26's order of dressing, so the ornament is not only secondary but unstable.

note: Kural 463 says the wise do not undertake a deed that loses the capital for the sake of gain; Pazhamozhi 232 says those who did no great good deeds before cannot have great wealth later, for without capital there is no profit.
teaches: The same trader's logic of capital and profit is prudence in the Kural and fate in Pazhamozhi, where the capital is earlier good deeds, so the pair shows the merchant's rule being moved from a counsel about risk to an account of merit.
list_adds: its proverb replaces the couplet's money capital with good deeds done before, so the capital cannot be raised now by any present skill.

note: Kural 964 says those fallen from their position are like hair fallen from the head; Pazhamozhi 71 says the great keep their worth when their standing is gone, like the timber of a fallen mansion.
teaches: The pair splits on whether worth lies in place or in substance: the Kural's fallen hair is worthless off the head, the Pazhamozhi's timber is still building stuff off the ruin.
list_adds: its salvage image gives the fallen great a further use, where the couplet's hair has none once it leaves its place.

note: Verse 32 lists ten places barred for spitting and excretion; verse 34 says where these are allowed, a screened or secluded place, and sets the stake at refusing even Indra's throne.
teaches: Together they give the rule's two sides, the barred places and the permitted one, and verse 34 adds that the screening is also an act of mind, so the code of bodily acts reaches into intention.

note: Kural 698 forbids belittling a king as young or as close kin; Pazhamozhi 277 forbids mocking a king who has lost his greatness and his kin and stands alone, for no one slights a snake as small.
teaches: The pair extends the Kural's bar on belittling from youth and kinship to ruin and isolation, and the proverb's இளைது echoes the couplet's இளையர: in both, smallness of age or fortune is no licence, but Pazhamozhi grounds this in the power still in him, the Kural in the light of his station.
list_adds: it moves the couplet's case from a young king in his strength to a fallen king without kin, and gives a reason by fear of the snake where the couplet gives one by the dignity of the office.

note: Naladiyar 195 says austerity, learning and effort make a lineage; Pazhamozhi 6 says a lineage gives half its craft without learning.
teaches: The pair disagree on which way the gift runs: for the Naladiyar learning makes the family, for Pazhamozhi the family half-supplies the learning.
list_adds: its named royal story stakes the claim for inherited capacity on a king's judgement, against the quatrain's denial that birth names anything.

note: Kural 158 says those who wrong one out of excess are to be defeated by one's own rightness; Pazhamozhi 50 says the superior should not rise against the low who wrong him at all, since it is a great weapon spent on a jackal.
teaches: The couplet still frames forbearance as a way of winning, while Pazhamozhi treats the contest with the low as not worth entering, so forbearance becomes economy of the superior's strength rather than victory.
list_adds: its proverb sets a measure of proportion, great means against a small target, that the couplet's language of victory does not.

note: Innaa Narpathu 4 counts doing harm to the very strong as painful; Pazhamozhi 302 counsels keeping silent before the strong.
teaches: The counted verse names the pain of provoking the strong, the proverb verse the policy that avoids it and turns force on the weak instead, so the two give cause and remedy.

note: Kural 753 calls wealth an unfailing lamp that cuts darkness wherever one goes; Pazhamozhi 197 says the rich see well even in the sea, while the same affairs bring the poor to grief.
teaches: Together the two make wealth a means of sight as well as of power: the Kural's lamp travels to any land, and Pazhamozhi carries it into the sea, the place where sight should fail, and adds the poor man for whom the same road is dark.
list_adds: it sets the rich man's ease against the poor man's trouble in the same affairs, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Naladiyar 256 says the learned keep silent for fear of a lapse while others chatter, like green and dry palm leaves; Pazhamozhi 9 says those ignorant of the learned man's restraint praise themselves, like a pot that is not full.
teaches: The quatrain gives the learned man's motive for silence; Pazhamozhi names what the noisy lack, knowledge of that restraint and attention to themselves, so the two halves of the contrast each get a cause.
list_adds: it narrows the others' chatter to self-praise and traces it to heedlessness, which the leaf image leaves unexplained.

note: Kural 619 grants that the deity may deny the end but says effort still pays the wage of bodily strain; Pazhamozhi 227 asks what effort can do at all once the deity has settled the end.
teaches: Both start from the same concession, that தெய்வம் can deny the goal, and part over what is left: the Kural keeps a wage for effort, while Pazhamozhi leaves it nothing, so the pair locates the precise point where the two works divide on effort and fate.
list_adds: its proverb of a pit dug in vain makes effort's labour itself the loss, where the couplet saves that labour as a wage.

note: Verse 6 lists புலை among five sights barred in எச்சில்; verse 80 bars addressing புலையர் by kinship terms, and both close on நன்கறிவார்.
teaches: Verse 80's plural personal form with a verb of address shows the book uses this root for persons, which weighs toward reading புலை in verse 6 as the outcaste person rather than an impure thing.

note: Pazhamozhi 218 says the miser's fear of sin is idle; 219 says that those who give nothing toward the next birth keep their wealth and die.
teaches: The second verse supplies the consequence the first only implies: a fear of sin that does not give leaves the next birth unprovided.

note: Kural 443 says making the great one's own is the rarest of things; Pazhamozhi 257 shows Lanka's younger prince joining Rama and gaining Lanka.
teaches: The couplet ranks the act as rare; the pairing gives its reward in one epic case, and shows the bond with the great outweighing even the bond with a brother.
list_adds: it proves the couplet's claim by a story, and the story's cost, leaving a brother, is something the couplet's general claim does not face.

note: Naladiyar 70 tells the high not to answer the low, as no one bites back a biting dog; Pazhamozhi 107 sets the base man's slighting talk as a dog barking at the moon.
teaches: Read together the dog moves from biting to barking out of reach: the Naladiyar asks the great to refrain from answering, and Pazhamozhi shows the insult never reaches them anyway.
list_adds: its proverb puts the insulted great man out of the dog's range, so restraint is backed by the insult's harmlessness, which the quatrain does not claim.

note: Naladiyar 347 says a gem-set golden sandal is still for the foot, so the base are known by their deeds though rich; Pazhamozhi 72 says a gem rolled in mud is still a gem to those who know.
teaches: Together they make one rule from both directions: wealth does not lift the base and mire does not lower the noble, so neither fortune changes what a person is.
list_adds: it gives the case the quatrain leaves out, the noble brought low, and adds that only the discerning see the worth through it.

note: Naladiyar 68 says the anger of the low keeps spreading and never dies; Pazhamozhi 111 shows it spreading onto those who come to part the fighters.
teaches: Pazhamozhi gives the Naladiyar's spreading anger its concrete path, from the quarrel to the peacemakers themselves, so that intervention becomes one of the ways it spreads.
list_adds: its proverb shows the attempt to settle the quarrel as what overturns it, a turn the quatrain's general claim lacks.

note: Pazhamozhi 281 says that even when an angry king does what one does not want, one should not act on one's resentment, for no one wakes a sleeping tiger; Acharakkovai 69 says one does not sulk or contradict even if the great one says the crow is white.
teaches: Pazhamozhi bars acting on resentment when the king wrongs one; the Acharakkovai extends the bar to speech and face when he speaks falsely, so the attendant's silence covers both injury and untruth.

note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Sirupanchamoolam 39 says giving treasury, accounts and stores to men without understanding is setting a crow to guard rice.
teaches: The couplet locates the fault in the master's fondness; the verse measures the appointee (understanding that does not match his size) and shows the result as the guard eating what he guards.

note: Naladiyar 70 and Pazhamozhi 49 share the proverb that no one bites back a dog that bites; the Naladiyar applies it to low words, Pazhamozhi to harm done (நலிதல்).
teaches: The shared proverb carries non-retaliation from insult to injury: the Naladiyar asks the high not to answer low words, Pazhamozhi asks the worthy not to answer actual torment.
list_adds: it moves the proverb from speech to deed and names the offender's lack of worth (நீர்த்தகவு இல்லார்) as the reason the worthy hold back.

note: Kural 562 tells the king to raise the rod sharply and bring it down lightly; Pazhamozhi 250 says kings need a little harshness, since even a cool stick raises the body.
teaches: Both refuse a choice between mildness and terror, and the pairing shows two ways to split it: the couplet splits the act into threat and blow, the quatrain sets a small severity inside just rule.
