list_adds: it adds the cost of failing at the other end, that even allies scorn a king who is not just, so severity is fenced by contempt on both sides.

note: Kural 672 sorts tasks into those to be done slowly and those to be done at once; Pazhamozhi 164 says work with intimates must be carried patiently, since haste ruins it.
teaches: The couplet leaves open how to tell the slow task from the urgent one; Pazhamozhi supplies one test, the closeness of the people involved, and the cost of getting it wrong, that the work turns into trouble.
list_adds: it places the slow kind of task in the circle of one's intimates and adds the condition of keeping to the spoken word, which the couplet does not name.

note: Kural 745 praises a fort that is hard to take, holds stored food and is easy for those inside to hold; 44 tells a besieged king that sitting secure behind shut gates and a long wall is shameful while his elephants starve and his people cry for milk and water. On the reading that both judge the king who holds out in a fort, they disagree.
teaches: The Kural values the fort as a means of holding out, while Kovur Kizhar sees the same holding out from inside, through starving beasts and infants, and calls it neither aram nor maram, so the pair shows the fort's strength and its moral cost as two views of one siege.

note: In Akananuru 146 the wife refuses the bard sent to plead for the husband who goes to the courtesans' street; Pazhamozhi 333 sets the same refusal of the bard in four lines and closes it with the proverb that a feigned sleeper cannot be woken.
teaches: The ethics work takes the akam wife's refusal of the bard and turns it into a general judgement, that a husband who strays knowingly is beyond persuasion, where the Sangam poem left the charge in images and pity.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 92 lists not learning in youth as one of four faults; Pazhamozhi 1 says why it is a fault: the chance does not return in old age.
teaches: The counted verse names the fault and moves on; the proverb supplies its logic, that learning is a toll only collectable while the road is still ahead.

note: Ainthinai 14 has the friend say the man came 'like those who ask after a beast' (மாவினவு வார்போல) with something else to ask; Thinaimalai 9 has the man himself call his asking after a beast deceit.
teaches: The ruse is seen through from both sides, the friend naming it as a likeness and the hero confessing it as a trick, which shows the beast question as a convention both parties knew and played along with rather than a deception that worked.

note: Kural 694 says to suppress whispers before the great; Acharakkovai 75 says that in the house of the great one does not take in whispered words, nor look at the women, nor let the garment slip.
teaches: The Kural forbids whispering in the presence of the great; the Acharakkovai also forbids receiving a whisper, so the listener is as guilty as the speaker.
list_adds: It sets the whisper beside the gaze on the women and the slipping garment, so the couplet's rule on speech becomes one of several guards on eye, ear and body in the great house.

note: 248 says a king who lets things slip is scorned, since all scorn the weak; 250 says an unjust king is scorned by his own allies and yet needs some severity.
teaches: Together they place the king between two contempts, for weakness and for injustice, and make a small severity within just rule the way between them.

note: Both use death, old age and disease as the spur: Naladiyar 92 to share wealth while it is in hand, Pazhamozhi 365 to do aram while one can.
teaches: The same triad backs sharing wealth in the Naladiyar and the use of a rare human birth in Pazhamozhi, which ends the triad with death as a stupor that puts one to sleep, so the urgency rests on the rare chance as well as on the threat.
list_adds: it puts the rarity of human birth before the triad of disease, old age and Death, joining a reason of opportunity to the quatrain's reason of threat.

note: Kural 316 forbids doing to another what one has felt to be painful; Pazhamozhi 44 gives the same self-measure as its proverb and names what blocks it, the sense of the other as different (வேற்றுமை).
teaches: Read together, the self-measure of pain is the remedy and the sense of otherness is the disease: the Kural gives the rule, Pazhamozhi names what makes people break it.
list_adds: it adds the cause of the harm, a felt difference from the other, and narrows the case to harm with no gain at all.

note: Kural 92 ranks sweet speech above glad giving; Pazhamozhi 338 says a gift of food, clothes, medicine and shelter is spoiled if the sweet word is withheld at parting.
teaches: Read together, sweet speech is not only the higher of two separable goods but the finishing part of a gift, so its absence cheapens what was given.
list_adds: it names the costly gifts one by one and then the missing word, so the proverb measures the meanness by the gap between a slaughtered buffalo and the spice.

note: Verse 37 bars looking at five wrongs; verse 38 bars even thinking of four more.
teaches: Read in sequence, the two verses move the ban inward from the eye to the mind, and both name hell as the end, so the code treats sight and thought as stages of the same fault.

note: The queen of 246 refuses the widow's life of greens and alli; the widow of 248 lives it and pities the lilies that now feed her.
teaches: Placed side by side, the two poems show that the widow's diet was a known, codified life that one woman could choose to bear and another could scorn as worse than the pyre.

note: Kural 618 says lacking fortune is no one's disgrace; Pazhamozhi 236 says that men who reach a generous king and still get nothing are not to be called dull or small, since gain comes by one's lot.
teaches: The couplet's general absolution becomes a defence of a particular figure, the empty-handed petitioner at court, and the pair shows the Kural's line on blame used to protect a man from the court's contempt rather than to urge him to work.
list_adds: it places the couplet's point at a king's court and adds a proverb of earned luck, so the failure is ascribed to unearned penance, not only excused.

note: 206 bars entrusting wealth to untested kin and eminent men; 208 bars handing it carelessly to worthless men; both turn on wealth put into another's hands.
teaches: Read together, the two verses show the danger of entrusting wealth from both sides: the keeper may be untested though respectable, or plainly base, and in each case the owner's own lapse is the fault.

note: 251 says no rival word can rise under a king's command, as no tree grows under a tree; 253 says keeping would-be leaders on equal footing is living with a snake.
teaches: 251 states the fact of single authority and 253 the danger of breaking it, so together they explain why a king keeps the ambitious beneath him.

note: Kural 1009 says others take wealth amassed without love or virtue; Pazhamozhi 373 names the taker, the seizing king, and sets the small gift to the destitute against the hoard.
teaches: The Kural leaves the taker as 'others'; Pazhamozhi makes him the king who drives the hoarder out, and pairs the lost hoard with rain in the wilderness, so the choice is between feeding royal power and feeding the destitute.
list_adds: it sets two ends of wealth side by side, the hoard going to the king and a single gift going to the starving, which the couplet's one fate does not contrast.

note: Kural 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who hoard and lose do not know the joy of giving; Pazhamozhi 378 asks whether those who hide wealth fearing it will dwindle have not seen the well refill.
teaches: Both ask the hoarder 'do they not know', but the Kural points to the joy he misses and Pazhamozhi to the fact he misjudges, that drawing renews the source, so the hoarder is wrong about both pleasure and arithmetic.
list_adds: its well proverb supplies the hoarder's own reason, fear of dwindling, and answers it with a fact of nature the couplet does not use.

note: Kural 579 ranks highest the disposition to show kindly regard and bear with those whose way is to hurt; Pazhamozhi 86 sets that regard at one moment, when an open and dangerous enemy is in distress.
teaches: The pairing fixes when the Kural's demand is hardest: not under the enemy's attack but at his fall, when sparing him is a choice and he may still bite.
list_adds: the snake proverb names the enemy as still dangerous and the assembly of the worthy as the place he is spared, a setting and a risk the couplet leaves out.

note: Kural 397 says every land and town is the learned man's own; Pazhamozhi 4 says the same and closes with the proverb that he needs no food for the road.
teaches: The Kural states belonging and asks why anyone stays unlearned; Pazhamozhi turns belonging into maintenance, the learned eat wherever they go.
list_adds: the proverb carries the couplet's claim of belonging into the traveller's practical case, provision for the journey.

note: Kural 1002 says the delusion of clinging without giving brings a மாணாப் பிறப்பு; Pazhamozhi 219 says those who give nothing for the coming birth hoard by attachment and die.
teaches: The Kural names the bad birth as the fruit of hoarding; Pazhamozhi makes giving the provision for that birth, so not giving is a failure to pack for a journey.
list_adds: it frames giving as something owed to the birth that follows (படரும் பிறப்பு) and names the attachment (பற்று) that holds the wealth, and its proverb sets outer guarding against inner loss.

note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander like a flame in a lamp; Pazhamozhi 40 says undeserved reproach is a disease that, untreated by excellence of character, destroys a man.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes the pure immune to slander; Pazhamozhi denies immunity and asks for treatment, so worth must act against blame rather than merely survive it.
list_adds: its medical frame of disease, medicine and wasting gives reproach a course and a cure, where the quatrain gives only the steady flame.

note: Kalittokai 143's woman asks why the king who guards the world's lives as his own does not guard hers; Purananuru 186 says the world lives by its king and the king must know he is its life.
teaches: The deserted woman takes the puram doctrine that the king is the people's life and finds its edge: a king can guard every life from war and want but not from a lover's leaving, so the akam poem marks a limit of royal protection that the puram counsel does not state.

note: Naladiyar 110 says what was set in the early mark neither shrinks nor grows and comes as due; Pazhamozhi 160, on the reading that the smearer rewrites the leaf, says a faulty written fate can be remade.
teaches: The two give opposite answers to what one should do before a fixed fate: the Naladiyar counsels calm acceptance, Pazhamozhi effort that rewrites the leaf, and both reject grieving or idle worship.
list_adds: its proverb casts fate as a palm-leaf document that a later hand can correct, against the quatrain's mark that cannot change.

note: Both speak of guarding ஈட்டிய ஒண்பொருள், earned bright wealth: the Naladiyar calls that guarding bitter suffering and wealth the dwelling of suffering, while Pazhamozhi 208 counts guarding it oneself a duty and handing it carelessly to others a folly.
teaches: On the same phrase the Jain quatrain makes custody of earned wealth a burden to be shed, by giving it away, while Pazhamozhi makes it a charge never to be delegated, so the two disagree on whether keeping earned wealth is worth its care.
list_adds: its crow proverb makes the careless handing over the fault, where the quatrain's list of sufferings makes the guarding itself the fault.

note: Naladiyar 164 says those who have angered the great do not escape even in a strong fortress, as the snake in its crevice dreads the thunder; Pazhamozhi 282 asks why those who cannot protect themselves are angry with kings at all.
teaches: The pair runs the danger the other way: the Naladiyar speaks of those who have provoked the great and find no shelter, Pazhamozhi of those who themselves feel anger at the king, and both conclude that against royal power the weak have no refuge.
list_adds: it shifts the quatrain's case from another's wrath to one's own anger, and its kongu tree makes the refuge something the angry man climbs himself.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 90 says a woman without a bond goes as she pleases though guarded; Pazhamozhi 336 says the same of confinement and closes it with the dog's tail.
teaches: The counted verse sets the woman beside desire and hidden murder as natures that outrun control; the proverb makes the same point by a household image of a crookedness force cannot straighten.

note: Naladiyar 314's fool, with one overheard sutra, walks unabashed (நாணாது) into the gathering of the good and shows his petty understanding; Pazhamozhi 22's man, knowing neither honour nor shame, sits among the wise and questions them.
teaches: Both trace the intrusion to a lack of shame rather than of learning alone, and Pazhamozhi adds that the shameless man need not even recite: questioning the wise is enough to make him laughable.
list_adds: it pairs மானம் with நாண் as what is missing and turns the exposure into ridicule through its proverb.

note: Both proverbs rest on a public commitment: the man who strapped on the drum beats it, the man who made friends before the village feeds them; 84 applies this to those who came for shelter, 85 to friends who prove faulty.
teaches: Taken together the two verses ground loyalty not in the worth of the person protected but in the protector's own visible pledge, so the other's unworthiness is ruled out twice as an excuse.

note: Kural 960 says one who wants lineage must want humility toward all; Pazhamozhi 88 shows the great families in the act, keeping kin-like company with those below them.
teaches: The Kural states humility as the condition of lineage; Pazhamozhi gives its form and its effect, the lesser carried along like string with the flower.
list_adds: it turns the couplet's general humility into one practice, keeping the lesser as kin, and adds what the lesser gain from it.

note: Kural 727 likens the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in a பேடி's hand amid enemies; Pazhamozhi 24 likens the same fear to a man who strings his bow at home and shoots a pot.
teaches: The two martial images complete each other: the Kural shows the weapon useless in the field, Pazhamozhi shows it used where no enemy is, so fear of the assembly is both impotence before the learned and bravado before the mean.
list_adds: it adds the self-praise in a mean assembly to the fear the couplet names, so the coward's display is seen alongside his failure.

note: Kural 692 says not desiring what kings desire brings lasting gain through them; Acharakkovai 68 opens with not taking pleasure in what the great take pleasure in.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule and its reward; the Acharakkovai shows what it looks like in the house, joined to not bringing low men in and not slighting the house's child, so not rivalling the lord's pleasures is part of guarding his household.
list_adds: It joins the rule to two others about the great man's house, so restraint of desire is placed among household courtesies rather than left as a maxim.

note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to water filling the village tank; Pazhamozhi 374 uses the tank to say discerning giving from long-gathered wealth does not quickly drain it.
teaches: The Kural's tank is wealth open to all; Pazhamozhi's tank is wealth that lasts though drawn on, so the same image answers the giver's fear of exhaustion, on condition that a capable man gives with discernment.
list_adds: it adds to the tank image the time it took to fill and the skill of the one who gives from it, so lasting depends on how the wealth was gathered and how it is given.

note: Naladiyar 357 says the worthy bear many faults from one who did them a kindness; Pazhamozhi 345 has the giver bear the anger of the kinsman he fed.
teaches: The pair runs patience both ways along a gift: the receiver bears the benefactor's faults in the Naladiyar, and the giver bears the receiver's rage in Pazhamozhi.
list_adds: it reverses the quatrain's direction and grounds the forbearance in kinship made by giving, with the ghee proverb as its sign.

note: Kural 379 asks why those who welcome good fortune grieve at bad, on the ground of fate; Acharakkovai 89 says those of true vision do not grieve over what has passed or what is beyond their control.
teaches: The Kural grounds calm in fate, whereas the Acharakkovai limits it to the unattainable, the past and the uncontrollable and grounds it in vision, so the pair show calm resting either on what governs events or on seeing which events one can still change.
list_adds: It splits the Kural's single good and bad fortune into three cases, each scoped to what cannot be changed.

note: The invocation's demons who lost their god's refuge are, in the story, the demons who complain to Neelakesi that the sage stopped their offerings.
teaches: The phrase 'removing refuge in the god' turns out to mean ending blood offerings, so the demons' grievance is the loss of sacrifice, the poem's first act against killing.

note: Kural 929 says giving reasons to a drunk is like searching with a torch for a man under water; the Innaa line says the business a drunkard himself speaks of is painful.
teaches: Together they close talk with the drunk in both directions: reasons cannot reach him, and his own account of affairs cannot be relied on.

note: Kural 824 warns of deceivers whose faces smile while their hearts are bitter, so the face hides malice; Pazhamozhi 144 says the deceitful are known on sight because the face tells what the heart intends even when they conceal it.
teaches: Read together they disagree on whether a deceiver's face can be trusted to betray him: the Kural fears the face that masks, the Pazhamozhi trusts the face to leak, so the reader must ask whether the skill lies in the face or in the one who reads it.
list_adds: its flood image claims the sign comes before the deed and cannot be held back, a confidence the couplet denies.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 3 says the use of kin is known when one is ruined; Pazhamozhi 350 says what that use is, removing the distress, and calls it a medicine at home.
teaches: The counted verse gives the test of kin and the proverb verse its content, so ruin both reveals kin and is the thing good kin cure.

note: Kural 226 makes relieving the hunger of the destitute the place to store wealth; Pazhamozhi 358 denies the hoard is a reserve and calls aram done at the fit place the reserve for the time of need.
teaches: Both turn the language of saving onto giving, but Pazhamozhi widens the deposit from the hungry poor to any aram placed with discernment, and its proverb names when the store is drawn on, at the time of exhaustion.
list_adds: it joins enjoying wealth, giving it on both sides and choosing the fit occasion as one use set against the hoard, where the couplet names a single act.

note: Kural 889 says inner enmity as small as a split sesame seed holds ruin; Pazhamozhi 307 says division is in everyone and an able man can use it to kill a hundred.
teaches: The couplet warns the house of its own small crack, the proverb verse tells the enemy to widen it, so the same fact of universal division is a danger at home and a weapon abroad.
list_adds: it moves the couplet's warning into offence and gives a scale to the ruin, one able man against a hundred.

note: Naladiyar 111 opens with nearly the same two lines as Pazhamozhi 225: refusing what one cannot give is no disgrace and the way of the world; it then says keeping the asker waiting till hope dies is worse than killing gratitude, where Pazhamozhi says the hope-killer has no world to go to.
teaches: The shared lines show one maxim closed two ways, measured against ingratitude in the Naladiyar and against the next world in Pazhamozhi, so the same fault is given a moral rank and a cosmic penalty.
list_adds: the two verses share their first lines; what Pazhamozhi adds is its proverb, which turns the Naladiyar's comparison of faults into a sentence on the hope-killer's afterlife.

note: Naladiyar 167 says those who keep close to kings enjoy their wealth without needing to be worthy; Pazhamozhi 272 says whomever the king esteems the people esteem as well.
teaches: The pair shows royal nearness conferring not only goods but public standing: the Naladiyar's unworthy favourite gets the king's wealth, and Pazhamozhi adds that he gets the town's regard too, poured on from the king like ghee from a filled pot.
list_adds: its proverb of the ghee-filled vessel makes honour a thing that passes from container to container, adding the public as a second recipient that the quatrain's image of shade-giving trees does not have.

note: 373 says the concealed hoard ends as provision for seizing kings; 386 says wealth that escapes its guard and is seized by a great king leaves those who did not give with no remedy.
teaches: 373 sets the hoard's end against the gift's use; 386 adds the hoarder's helplessness after the seizure, so the king's taking appears in the chapter twice, as the hoard's fate and as the moment past remedy.

note: Kural 1078 says the worthy are of use at a word and the base only when crushed like cane; Pazhamozhi 166 says to win help by affection, as forcing it is milking a cow with an arrow.
teaches: Read together, the two divide the means by the person: affection draws service from the ordinary helper while force kills what it wants, and the couplet marks the base as the exception who yield only under pressure.
list_adds: its paired images of the calf let in and the arrow loosed rank gentle means over force for ordinary dealings, which the couplet, speaking only of two extremes, does not do.

note: 79 says the fault of the exalted never stops being spoken of, like a brand on a grey bull; 80 says a single fault of the exalted is seen by all, like a lamp on a hill, while the small man's many go unseen.
teaches: Taken together, the fault of the great is exposed in both dimensions, lasting for all time in 79 and seen across all space in 80, which is why the heading asks more of them than of the small.

note: Kural 471 bids one weigh the strength of the deed, one's own, the opponent's and the allies' before acting; Pazhamozhi 154 weighs oneself, one's helpers and the gain, using the same verb தூக்கி.
teaches: Pazhamozhi adds the gain to the Kural's weighing of strengths and says what follows without it, so the reckoning is shown to be of purpose as well as of power.
list_adds: it replaces the enemy's strength with the gain in the reckoning and adds, through its proverb, the formless result of unweighed action.

note: Kural 423 says wisdom is seeing the true substance of what is heard from whatever mouth; Pazhamozhi 35 forbids scorning a good word from whatever mouth and proves it by low sources of prized things.
teaches: The Kural states the indifference to the speaker as a test of wisdom; Pazhamozhi shows its price, even the strictest abstainer taking what a dog has caught.
list_adds: it gives three low sources of good things, the spurge, the crow and the dog, and ends on a breach of a birth-group's diet as the extreme case.

note: Naladiyar 346 says the excellent never speak a boastful word even with an emperor's wealth; Pazhamozhi 315 asks the warrior who has killed the strutting foe not to tell his own valour.
teaches: The quatrain's restraint concerns wealth and the base man's swagger; Pazhamozhi carries it to the battlefield, where the deed is real and the praise of others is due, so silence is asked even of one who has earned praise.
list_adds: it moves the rule from wealth to valour and gives the reason in a proverb, that the deed shows itself as a theft cannot be bundled, where the quatrain gives only the contrast of excellent and base.

note: Kural 520 tells the ruler to look daily into those who do his work; Pazhamozhi 175 says raising untrustworthy men and leaving them far off is setting a tortoise loose in a pond and asking it to return.
teaches: The couplet prescribes daily oversight; Pazhamozhi shows what its absence looks like, an agent out of sight and in his own element, and adds that the fault is compounded when the agent lacked honesty of mind from the start.
list_adds: its proverb joins two errors the couplet keeps apart from choosing, raising the wrong man and sending him beyond sight.

note: Naladiyar 178 says enemies' anger cannot reach the weak who have joined good protection, like grass by a stump the plough avoids; Pazhamozhi 292 says the small who attack such dependents only rouse the protector.
teaches: The same situation is seen from both sides: the quatrain promises the protected weak their safety, and the Pazhamozhi warns their attacker that striking them wakes the great one behind them.
list_adds: its bear and wild dog image shows the attacker's fate, which the quatrain's stump and plough, concerned only with the sheltered grass, does not.

note: Kural 1110 uses the learner's growing sense of ignorance as a simile for love; Pazhamozhi 2 states the same thing of learning itself and makes it the engine of study.
teaches: The Kural borrows from learning a fact Pazhamozhi takes as a method: the lament 'I have not learnt' drives the next round of pondering and labour.
list_adds: it gives the simile's base in its own right and adds the practice it drives, reflection on one thing at a time, which the love couplet has no room for.

note: Pazhamozhi 389 says the body that does not renounce after the household is useless; 390 says those who choose neither household nor renunciation lose both.
teaches: Read together, the two verses give an order and a warning: household life first, renunciation after, and the one fault both condemn is the man who stops in between, holding neither.

note: Kural 81 says household life exists for tending guests and doing them good (விருந்தோம்பி வேளாண்மை); Pazhamozhi 151 uses the same pair of words and sets battle valour and freedom from sloth beside them.
teaches: The pairing shows the Kural's purpose of the household needs a means it does not name: hospitality is sustained only by toil, so giving to guests stands with valour as a fruit of effort.
list_adds: it puts hospitality, beneficence and sword-valour in one series closed by toil, making giving an outcome of effort rather than the end of the household alone.

note: Acharakkovai 83 says those who would live long do not tell the size of the king's army; in Patitruppattu 77 the poet, asked by travellers how large Poraiyan's army is, says he could not count it and describes its elephants.
teaches: Read together, the courtier's rule of silence and the bard's praise give the same answer to the same question: no figure is told, and the bard turns the forbidden number into the uncountable.

note: Naladiyar 108 says that when the knowing do blameworthy things it comes from their past deeds; Pazhamozhi 228 says the works of renowned wise men go by their fortune, so fate defeats understanding.
teaches: Together the two verses show fate overriding knowledge in two places, in the wise man's conduct (the Naladiyar) and in the outcome of his works (Pazhamozhi), so knowing what is right secures neither right action nor success.
list_adds: it moves the quatrain's moral puzzle to the success of undertakings and seals it with a proverb that sets fate against understanding outright.

note: Naladiyar 31 shows those who did no penance before clinging to the outer door of a house, unable to enter; Pazhamozhi 236 says for those who did penance curry falls even into their rice.
teaches: The two verses give both ends of one belief about past penance and present food: one man shut out at the door looking in, the other finding food falling into his plate, so the pair draws the full scale between beggary and luck as the fruit of earlier penance.
list_adds: its proverb shows the reward side that the quatrain leaves implied, and sets it at a king's court rather than at a rich man's house.

note: Kural 271 says the five elements within laugh at the deceiver's hidden conduct; Pazhamozhi 143 says the wrongdoer who thinks his deed screened by a mountain is pierced by others' eyes, sharper than arrows.
teaches: The pair names two witnesses the hider cannot escape, his own body within and other people's eyes without, so concealed wrong is seen from both sides at once.
list_adds: it moves the witness from the body's elements to the onlookers and gives the wrongdoer's false belief, the mountain, that the proverb answers.

note: Kural 1225 asks what good she did to morning and what harm to evening; Ainkurunuru 116 has evening come while they weep, having driven before it a morning like itself.
teaches: The Kural keeps a kind morning against a hostile evening, while the older poem, on one reading, lets the evening swallow the morning too, so the couplet's neat split of the day is a later tidying of a grief that had no safe hour.

note: Purananuru 73 has Nalankilli say the fool who scorned him will hardly escape, like a blind man stumbling on a sleeping tiger; Pazhamozhi 281 tells the king's wronged servant not to wake the sleeping tiger by acting on his grievance.
teaches: The pairing shows the same sleeping tiger from both sides: the Chola king boasts of being the tiger that the careless rouse to their death, and the ethics verse teaches the king's own servant to treat that tiger as a standing danger to be left asleep.

note: Naladiyar 80 forbids eating from the hands of those one should not eat from and speaking words mixed with falsehood; Pazhamozhi 83 grants that the worthy may have eaten from another's hand and says they speak the truth even so.
teaches: The Naladiyar guards truth by refusing the obligation that might bend it; Pazhamozhi allows the obligation and makes truth hold against it, a stronger and riskier claim.
list_adds: it sets the worthy man's truth beside the traitor's borrowed lie in battle, a contrast of two men under obligation that the quatrain's separate refusals lack.

note: Kural 620 says those who toil without flagging see even fate's back; Pazhamozhi 160 says folded hands before the one who fixed fate end no trouble.
teaches: Pazhamozhi names the rival of effort that the Kural leaves unstated, pious resignation, and replaces the Kural's battle image with a scribe correcting a leaf.
list_adds: it sets worship of the fixer of fate against effort, making resignation itself the error.

note: 290 asks the king to give this warrior toddy before he drinks himself; 298's warrior complains the king gave his men the dregs and drank the clear, and now does not send him first.
teaches: Together they show the order of drinking as the measure of the order of dying: 290 asks for the first cup on the strength of the family's dead, 298 reads a poor cup as the loss of the vanguard.

note: Naladiyar 241 says the worthy are ashamed to advance on a humbled enemy; Pazhamozhi 299 says rage after the enemy's death is fruitless.
teaches: The quatrain stops the worthy from pressing a fallen enemy out of shame, the proverb verse out of futility, so honour and plain economy reach the same restraint.
list_adds: it gives a practical reason, waste, beside the quatrain's reason of honour, and moves the case from a humbled enemy to a dead one.

note: Kural 560 says that when the guardian fails to guard, those of the six duties forget their books; Acharakkovai 47 lists affliction to the land's guardian among the days brahmins do not recite.
teaches: Both tie the reciting of the Veda to the king's state: the Kural through long neglect that makes the texts forgotten, the Acharakkovai through a single day of the king's distress that halts recitation at once.
list_adds: It sets the king's affliction among moon days, earthquake, thunder and impurity, so the ruler's distress counts as a cosmic disturbance rather than a failure of governance.

note: Kural 820 warns against those friendly at home who defame one in the assembly; Pazhamozhi 130 says those who chose friends after sifting do not blame them among many.
teaches: The Kural describes the false friend from the victim's side; Pazhamozhi describes the true friend from the speaker's side, and the pair makes the public gathering the place where a friendship is proved or broken.
list_adds: its proverb gives the true friend's reason for silence, the shameful dream one does not tell, where the couplet only names the false friend's fault.

note: Verse 63 bars speaking one's learning before elders; verse 71 bars displaying learning and three other excellences before the lord.
teaches: The same silence about one's learning is owed in the house to elders and at court to the lord, so the book treats display of learning as a breach of rank in both spheres.

note: Naladiyar 73 asks whether the harsh words of those who love are worse than strangers' smiling sweet words; Pazhamozhi 263 says good ministers press unwanted good on the king and check his evil, so elders' words are painful at first.
teaches: The pair carries the friend's welcome harshness up to the throne and adds time: the bitter word is painful only at first, and the minister must also push the king toward good he resists, not only rebuke.
list_adds: it moves the claim from friends to minister and king, adds the forward push to unwanted good beside the check on evil, and gives the time-order of pain then profit.

note: Naladiyar 161 warns not to offend even the faultless counting on their forgiveness, since once they turn away no one can undo it; Pazhamozhi 63 says a second offence after a first is not borne.
teaches: The quatrain warns against trading on forgiveness at all; Pazhamozhi shows when the trade fails, at the second offence, so together they mark forgiveness as real but single.
list_adds: it fixes the point at which the quatrain's turning away comes, the repetition, through the plantain that fruits once.

note: The Kural calls good children the ornament of a house's excellence; the verse makes bearing children of an old family the act by which the wife is mistress of the house.
teaches: Children move from ornament to office: what the Kural treats as the crown of a good home, Thirikadugam treats as a debt the wife owes in order to hold her title.

note: Kural 698 says the king is not to be slighted as young or as kin; Acharakkovai 84 sets the king among the snake, fire and the lion and says slighting any of them as young, weak or familiar brings harm.
teaches: The Kural asks respect for the light the king stands in, while the Acharakkovai asks it because he can harm, so the pair show two grounds for the same deference, the office and the danger.
list_adds: It ranks the king with a snake, fire and a lion, so his claim to respect is made one with their power to harm.

note: Pazhamozhi 153 promises that the unwearied never fail to reach their aim; Naladiyar 194 makes manliness standing firm even when the thing does not succeed.
teaches: The pair splits the reward of effort: Pazhamozhi gives the friendless striver success as his warrant, while the Naladiyar holds that persistence is the measure even when success does not come.
list_adds: it ties effort to the excuse of having no kin and guarantees success, where the quatrain detaches manliness from success.

note: Kural 839 calls the friendship of fools very sweet because parting from them brings no pain; Pazhamozhi 138 closes with the proverb that the friendship of fools is painful afterwards. The tension holds if the Kural's line is read plainly rather than as irony.
teaches: The two place the pain of a fool's friendship differently: the Kural finds none at the parting because there was no real bond, while Pazhamozhi finds pain later because the fool believes slander and breaks the bond.
list_adds: it ranks friends by how they take slander, highest against lowest, and so names the cause of the later pain, which the couplet does not.

note: Kural 788 says friendship removes distress at once, like the hand that catches a slipping garment; Pazhamozhi 127 says a friend's distress is not removed by words, as dew does not fill a tank.
teaches: The Kural gives the speed and instinct of true help; Pazhamozhi names what does not count as help, kindly words, and its dew-and-tank proverb shows that even sincere sympathy falls short of the deed.
list_adds: its proverb adds the negative case the couplet leaves out: words, however ungrudging, are dew and not water for the tank.

note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy for anyone and doing as spoken is hard; Pazhamozhi 176 says the bystander's subtle advice is easy while the doer who enters without inner knowledge perishes.
teaches: The couplet sets saying against doing in one person; Pazhamozhi splits them between two, the adviser at the edge of the board and the player in it, so the cost of easy speech falls on someone else.
list_adds: its dice-board proverb puts the speaker and the doer in different seats, which the couplet's single subject does not.

note: 211 says wealth let out of hand does not come back; 212 says a lender who let a loan lie and then asks for it is met with the borrower's anger.
teaches: 212 supplies the mechanism behind 211's maxim: lent wealth fails to return not only by loss but because asking for it turns the borrower hostile, so the loan costs the friendship as well as the goods.

note: Kural 269 says that even leaping past Death becomes possible for those who have gained the power of penance; Pazhamozhi 291 says that even those with the greatness of penance have never clapped Death on the back.
teaches: The two take opposite views of what penance can do against death: the Kural lets austerity overcome it, while the Pazhamozhi, using the demon great in penance who fell, denies that it protects the one who provokes the great.
list_adds: it sets the claim inside a story of a penitent who was destroyed in war, so the power of tapas is tested by a case rather than asserted.

note: Kural 861 says to avoid opposing the strong; Pazhamozhi 293 says what the weak should do when the strong are already against them: flee far and live by any means.
teaches: The couplet only advises against the contest; the Pazhamozhi carries the advice into defeat and allows any means of escape, since survival keeps future good open.
list_adds: it adds the step of flight and the proverb's promise of later fortune, which the couplet's balanced rule for strong and weak lacks.

note: Kural 451 says greatness fears small company and only smallness takes it as kin; Pazhamozhi 88 praises great families who conduct themselves as kin with those lesser than they. The conflict holds on the reading that 88's சிறியார் are the same small people the Kural warns against, not merely those of lower rank.
teaches: The two split on whether keeping company with the lesser degrades the great or raises the lesser: the Kural fears contamination, Pazhamozhi sees the flower lending itself to the string.
list_adds: its proverb reverses the direction of influence that the couplet assumes, making the great the ones who pass on their quality.

note: Kural 846 calls it folly to cover one's nakedness while leaving faults uncovered; Pazhamozhi 26 makes understanding the cloth without which ornaments are absurd.
teaches: Both use clothing to name what must be covered first, and together they make the senseless man's lack a nakedness that neither dress nor jewellery can hide.
list_adds: it sets gems, gold, sandal and garlands on the naked body, turning the couplet's single garment into a whole toilette that is wasted without understanding.

note: Kural 894 likens the weak doing harm to the strong to beckoning Death by hand; Pazhamozhi 62 likens the unlearned provoking the great to goading an elephant from behind an erukku shrub.
teaches: The Kural's weak man calls his death openly; Pazhamozhi's thinks he is hidden, so the pair adds a second folly to the first: misjudging one's cover as well as one's strength.
list_adds: the proverb adds the false shelter, the thin erukku, which the couplet's open gesture lacks, and names the provokers as the unlearned.

note: Naladiyar 65 says true patience is that of the strong who could punish all; Pazhamozhi 59 says punishing those who harmed one, though one could, brings no gain.
teaches: Both assume the power to punish, and together they show that forbearance counts as a virtue only when retaliation is open, and then gains what punishment cannot.
list_adds: it adds the outcome of the forgone punishment, no gain, and of the forbearance, renown and nobility, to the quatrain's test of strength.

note: Naladiyar 262 says the wise do not seek the base however rich, as no one picks cactus buds; Pazhamozhi 91 says those who live as kin of the worthy do not go over to the small though they are called superior.
teaches: The Naladiyar grounds the refusal in judgement of the base, Pazhamozhi in belonging: settled among the worthy, one does not change sides, and the sweetness on offer is jaggery in sand.
list_adds: it gives the refusal a cause the quatrain lacks, the bond of living as kin of the worthy, and admits the small some sweetness while denying it is edible.

note: 252, on a doubtful reading, says a ruler can unmake the men he raised; 253 warns that men raised to equal standing are a snake in the room.
teaches: Read together, 253 limits the confidence of 252: the raised follower stays in the ruler's hand only while he is not raised to the ruler's level.

note: Kural 695 tells the king's servant not to listen in or press after secrets; Acharakkovai 81 names the palace places, the back gate, the assembly and the women's quarters, where looking in is barred, and exempts those whose office lies there.
teaches: Together they show that the courtier's discretion is spatial as well as verbal: what the Kural states as restraint of curiosity the Acharakkovai maps onto doors and rooms, and ties to office rather than to trust.
list_adds: It turns a general rule about secrets into three named places and adds the exception for those whose work lies there.

note: Kural 249 likens aram done without அருள் to a muddled man's sight of truth; Pazhamozhi 370 calls அருள் the root of aram and its abandonment a loss of the greater for the lesser.
teaches: The Kural shows graceless aram as an empty act; Pazhamozhi names grace as aram's root and adds the cost of leaving it, the hare given up for a crow, so the fault is a bad exchange as well as a blindness.
list_adds: its hare-and-crow proverb ranks grace above whatever aram is done without it, a ranking of goods the couplet's simile of sight does not give.

note: Naladiyar 346 says the base man who gains a tiny fraction thinks himself Indra; Pazhamozhi 67 says those who extol such self-proclaimers call a hearth dog a tiger.
teaches: The quatrain describes the base man's inflated self-image; Pazhamozhi turns to the bystander who repeats it, so the pair shows the boast needs a flatterer to circulate and that the flatterer shares in the absurdity.
list_adds: it moves the fault from the boaster to the one who praises him and concedes that such praise is harmless, a qualification the quatrain does not make.

note: Kural 410 sets the learned against others as men against beasts; Pazhamozhi 27 says a thousand of the senseless together do not equal one excellent man.
teaches: The couplet makes the gap one of kind; the Pazhamozhi verse draws the consequence that numbers cannot close it, so a crowd of fools adds up to nothing.
list_adds: its moon and many stars turn the couplet's two-term comparison into one against a multitude, adding the argument from number.

note: Kural 656 forbids a deed the worthy condemn even to feed one's starving mother; Pazhamozhi 39 forbids a scarring deed even to save oneself from ruin.
teaches: The Kural tests the rule against duty to another, Pazhamozhi against self-preservation, and gives the reason both leave out: the word about the deed outlasts stone.
list_adds: its proverb supplies the reason behind the refusal, the lasting report, which the couplet leaves as a bare command.

note: Kural 978 says smallness adorns itself with self-admiration; the line says birth in a small house shows in pride.
teaches: The same mark of pride serves the Kural as a sign of small character and the Muthumozhikkanchi as a sign of small birth, which shows the ten tying character to family.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the work one does; Acharakkovai 56 says one does not leave the work of one's ancestral line even when famine makes one poor.
teaches: If செய்தொழில் in the Kural is occupation, the two clash: the Kural ranks people by their work and not their birth, while the Acharakkovai fixes the work by birth, so rank by work becomes rank by descent.
list_adds: It sets the bar on leaving hereditary work after plain rules of safety in fire, rain and forest, treating loyalty to one's descent as prudence of the same kind.

note: Pazhamozhi 304 sets someone on a stronger enemy's rear; 306 incites an outside power against one's natural enemy and keeps it friendly by favour.
teaches: The two verses together show a graded method: first find a rear threat, then keep the third power warm and let it take the burn, as the monkey's hand stirs the fire.

note: Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as one spoke is hard; Pazhamozhi 318 asks the man in the council of kings not to talk in turn and leave but to resolve to act, undeterred by the enemy's elephants.
teaches: The couplet locates the difficulty in doing; Pazhamozhi names what makes doing hard in war, fear of a strong enemy, and refuses the wait for a safer moment, so resolve is tied to accepting risk.
list_adds: it sets the contrast in the royal council before war and adds the waves proverb, which answers the excuse of waiting that the couplet does not consider.

note: Kural 620 says those who toil without flagging see even fate's back; Pazhamozhi 237 says effort is needless for the fortunate and fruitless for the unfortunate.
teaches: Both name ஆள்வினை and fate together and give opposite verdicts on the same contest, the Kural letting tireless labour outrun fate and Pazhamozhi denying labour any effect in either lot, on the plain reading of both.
list_adds: it splits people into two lots and denies effort a role in each, where the couplet speaks of the single toiler who prevails.

note: Both verses set the high-born beside those small by birth: in 87 the great go to the small and depend on them, in 88 the great take the small into their company.
teaches: Read together they show the edition's heading praising the great for crossing the birth-rank in both directions, as dependents and as patrons, while leaving the ranking itself in place.

note: Kural 586 counsels the king to use spies who go in the guise of renunciants and wanderers; 47 insists that the bard's wandering life, crossing many wastes from patron to patron, harms no one. On the reading that 47 answers a suspicion of the wandering bard, the two disagree about whether such travellers should be trusted.
teaches: The Kural's advice to disguise spies as wanderers is the very reason a real wanderer could fall under suspicion, and 47 gives the wanderer's side, a life of gifts and honour that 'knows no harm to others', so the pair shows the cost the state's craft laid on the travelling poet.

note: Kural 182 ranks backbiting with a false smile as worse than open wrongdoing; Pazhamozhi 115 asks why blame the backbiter at all, since he is past disgrace.
teaches: The Kural's ranking condemns the backbiter most severely, and Pazhamozhi warns that this condemnation does him no harm, since a man without shame is beyond the reach of blame.
list_adds: its proverb turns from judging the backbiter to judging the use of blaming him, adding a limit of blame the couplet does not raise.

note: Kural 452 says water changes with the land it runs on, as understanding takes the nature of company; Pazhamozhi 90 uses water the other way, the fresh flood that cannot sweeten the sea.
teaches: The same water image proves opposite things depending on which is larger: the Kural's water yields to the soil, while the base man is the sea that absorbs every good influence unchanged.
list_adds: it turns the couplet's image around, making the base the vessel that alters what flows in rather than being altered.

note: 168 says even one's own cart needs grease, so an agent takes his small share; 173 says wealth always clings to those who handle it, so careless handlers must not be chosen.
teaches: Together the two verses accept the handler's share as unavoidable and then limit it: the master budgets for the grease but chooses men who care for the work, so the cut stays a காணி and does not become flight with the goods.

note: Pazhamozhi 263 praises ministers who afflict the king to tell him his good and stop his evil; Pazhamozhi 265, in the same heading, says the experienced never think of anything that would anger him.
teaches: Side by side the two verses of one heading leave the counsellor between duty and survival: the good minister must hurt the king to save him, yet the king's anger is a tiger no one escapes, so the heading gives no single rule.

note: Kural 110 says there is no escape for one who kills a good done to him; Pazhamozhi 347 names one form of it, joining the benefactor's enemies and backbiting him.
teaches: The Kural ranks ingratitude as beyond remedy, and Pazhamozhi gives it a concrete shape in speech and alliance, likened to burning the house that fed one.
list_adds: it specifies the ingrate's act as backbiting in company with the estranged and weighs it by the past meals, which the couplet does not name.

note: Both set the millet grain against the palmyra: in Kural 104 a millet-sized kindness is reckoned palm-sized, in Pazhamozhi 187 a millet-grain's gain near at hand is preferred and the palm is the tree too slow to feed its planter.
teaches: The same millet-and-palm scale serves two judgements of value: the Kural enlarges the small out of gratitude, Pazhamozhi prefers the small because it is near and certain, so the image teaches valuing the small for moral and for prudential reasons.
list_adds: it makes the palm stand for delay rather than size, adding time to a scale the couplet uses only for magnitude.

note: Verse 18 forbids answering back so that an exchange becomes a two-sided quarrel; verse 19 forbids pushing ahead of one's turn in an exchange two have begun.
teaches: Read in sequence the two verses give a small order of debate in assembly: do not turn a speech into a contest by retort, and do not break into a contest out of turn.

note: Naladiyar 260 says the base man kicks away the subtle teaching of the learned and sets up a petty assembly with one like himself; Pazhamozhi 102 says those who refuse the good words of the keen-minded and act harshly are known to everyone.
teaches: The Naladiyar follows the refuser into a small circle of his own kind; Pazhamozhi follows him into the village's notice, so refusing counsel ends both in a narrowed company and in public notoriety.
list_adds: it adds the consequence the quatrain lacks, harsh action that makes the fool as known as a rogue bull.

note: Kural 657 says the worthy prefer utter poverty to wealth gained under blame; the friend in Akananuru 112 says the worthy, however deep in love, do not want a pleasure that comes with blame (சான்றோர் பழியொடு வரூஉம் இன்பம் வெஃகார்), and so the hero should marry.
teaches: The same rule of the worthy, refusing any gain that brings blame, governs wealth in the Kural and love in the Akananuru, and the friend turns it from a counsel of going without into an argument for marriage, which removes the blame without removing the pleasure.

note: Naladiyar 375 uses the eel that shows one end to the snake and the other to the fish for women of double conduct; Pazhamozhi 141 calls the man who courts both friends and enemies a brand burning at both ends.
teaches: Both books picture double dealing as one body with two ends, but the eel profits by fitting each side, while the brand burns whoever holds it, so Pazhamozhi makes the two-sided man a danger to both sides rather than a clever survivor.
list_adds: it moves the two-ended image from the courtesan to the go-between among friends and foes, and its proverb names the harm to the holder that the eel image does not.

note: Kural 1078 says the base, like sugar-cane, are of use only when crushed; Pazhamozhi 100 says those who have been punished go on doing evil, growing a span for every cubit cut.
teaches: Pressure may wring use out of the base, as the Kural says, but Pazhamozhi denies that it changes them: what is cut back grows again.
list_adds: its regrowth image separates getting use from the base by force and reforming them by punishment, which the couplet runs together.

note: Kural 196 calls the man who keeps up useless talk chaff among people; Acharakkovai 52 says those of unshaken mind never speak useless words, deceit, loose talk, abuse or backbiting.
teaches: The Kural judges the empty talker by what his talk shows him to be, while the Acharakkovai names the cause of not talking so, a steady mind, so useless speech appears as a symptom of an unsettled one.
list_adds: It makes useless speech one of five kinds with deceit, wanton talk, abuse and backbiting, all kept off by a single inner steadiness, where the Kural treats useless talk on its own.

note: 37 treats Death as the overpowering thing no plea escapes; 39 calls dying easy beside the hard work of character.
teaches: Within one chapter the work views death from two sides, as the terror that drives penance and as the easy thing beside lasting virtue, and the pair shows death's weight depends on what it is measured against.

note: 379 says a patron's gifts are great by his own worth; 380 says givers themselves know the measure of their worth and need no prompting.
teaches: 379 states that the giver's worth sets the gift; 380 adds that the giver knows that measure himself, so the true patron gives unprompted and the poet need not name or press him.

note: Naladiyar 284 says a thousand gather like crows while there is wealth and none asks after one in want; Pazhamozhi 134 says a thousand eat at a man's house while he lacks nothing, and in the Kali age the ruined have no friends.
teaches: The two share the thousand who feed on the prosperous, but Pazhamozhi places the desertion in the Kali age, turning the quatrain's account of poverty into a mark of a fallen time.
list_adds: its proverb with the Kali age frame adds a cause in the age itself, where the quatrain gives only the man's change of fortune.

note: Acharakkovai 90 sets rules toward the பார்ப்பார், from whose hand a cow is not taken, and the புலை, to whom leavings are not held out; Sivavakkiyar asks what a Paraiyar woman and a Brahmin woman are, since no mark on flesh, skin or bone divides them.
teaches: Read against each other, the rule that ranks two birth-groups by what may pass between their hands meets a denial that the body carries any rank, so the purity rule is shown to depend on a mark the Siddhar says is not there.

note: Naladiyar 93 says wealth gathers when its time to gather comes, whether one gives or withholds; Pazhamozhi 233 says the same of those who serve kings, by the vengai that flowers only on its day.
teaches: The quatrain uses the timing of wealth to remove the miser's excuse, and Pazhamozhi uses it to remove the courtier's hope, so the same rule frees the giver to give and tells the servant of kings his service cannot hasten his reward.
list_adds: it carries the quatrain's rule from the giver's house to the king's court and gives it the image of a tree that flowers only on the right day.

note: Kural 96 says sweet speech of good things makes அல்லவை wane and aram grow; Pazhamozhi 364's proverb says that when aram is done, அல்லவை leave, provided it is given with discernment of the fit place.
teaches: The two share the pair aram and அல்லவை but run the cause differently: in the Kural speech grows aram and wears down evil, in Pazhamozhi aram itself, placed with discernment, drives evil out, so aram is the fruit in one and the agent in the other.
list_adds: it sets good hereafter, growth of wealth and the going of evil together as fruits of one well-placed aram, with discernment as their condition, where the couplet names one fruit of speech.

note: Kural 708 says it is enough to stand and look at the face of those who read the inward; Pazhamozhi 145 says for those who know faces the face suffices to know intention, as a mirror shows one's unseen limbs.
teaches: The Kural speaks of the petitioner who needs only show his face to a perceptive master, and the Pazhamozhi gives the reason it suffices: the face works as a mirror that makes the unseen inward visible.
list_adds: its mirror image supplies the mechanism the couplet assumes, and its proverb frames face and mind as offspring and source.

note: Acharakkovai 31 forbids passing between brahmins (பார்ப்பார்) as between gods; Tirumanthiram 231 denies the name of brahmin to those who lack truth, knowledge, restraint and devotion.
teaches: The Acharakkovai's deference attaches to the birth-name with no condition, while the Tirumanthiram makes the name itself depend on inner qualities, so the second would void the rule's deference for a brahmin who lacks them.

note: Kural 806 says those who keep within bounds do not give up an old friendship even when it brings ruin; Pazhamozhi 85 says the worthy do not change toward cherished friends who lack good qualities, because the friendship was made before the village.
teaches: The Kural makes constancy a mark of the man who keeps bounds; Pazhamozhi adds a reason outside him, the village that witnessed the bond, so loyalty becomes a public obligation as well as a private virtue.
list_adds: its proverb names the friend's bad character outright and answers it with feeding as a duty, a concrete act the couplet does not specify.

note: In Kural 1167 the woman swims love's flood without seeing a shore and at midnight is the only one awake; in Kuruntokai 329 she cannot sleep in midnight's thick dark, thinking of the man on the desert road.
teaches: The couplet gives the midnight wakefulness as a bare state; the poem gives it a content, the road he took buried under fallen iluppai flowers, so the pair shows the sleepless mind of separation travelling the absent man's road.

note: 376 says habitual givers relieve dependents even with nothing left; 381 names Pari's daughter giving gold in a drought.
teaches: 376 states the rule in general with a horse; 381 gives it a named case from the most famous house of givers, so the chapter pairs the principle with its exemplar.

note: Kural 174 says those of faultless sight who have conquered the senses will not covet on the plea 'we have nothing'; Pazhamozhi 78 says the worthy do not covet others' goods even when hunger bends them.
teaches: The Kural rules out need as an excuse by the coveter's self-mastery; the Pazhamozhi makes the distance between the worthy and another's goods a fact of nature, like sea and forest, so non-coveting appears as character, not effort.
list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's conquest of the senses into a fixed separation that needs no struggle.

note: Kural 873 calls one who alone takes on the enmity of many worse than mad; Pazhamozhi 303 tells the man facing enemies not to trust himself and to rely on numbers, even of poor allies.
teaches: The couplet forbids the lone stand, the proverb verse supplies its positive rule, that number outweighs merit in war, so worthless allies are still worth having.
list_adds: it adds what the couplet lacks, a ranking of number above quality in allies, and a warning against self-admiration.

note: Pazhamozhi 266 says those who have eaten the king's food cannot shirk his work; 267 says those who have not yet been rewarded cannot refuse it either, since the one who commands will feed.
teaches: Read together the two verses close both exits from service: the servant who has been paid owes the work, and the servant who has not been paid owes it too, so reward never becomes a condition the servant may set.

note: Kural 717 says the learning of the learned shines among those who can examine words faultlessly; Pazhamozhi 258 says the fierce king's council shows a counsellor's breadth of learning as the flood shows the mountain's rain.
teaches: Together they make the assembly a gauge as well as a stage: the Kural needs fit judges for learning to shine, and the Pazhamozhi adds that what pours out there is the measure of what was stored unseen.
list_adds: its flood-and-rain proverb turns the couplet's claim about where learning shines into an inference from visible effect to hidden quantity, and sets it in a king's dangerous court.

note: Purananuru 290 has a warrior's king give him toddy before drinking himself, and the warrior will take the spear meant for the king; Pazhamozhi 266 turns the toddy already drunk into the reason a king's man cannot shrink from his task.
teaches: Held together they show the heroic custom of the king's toddy hardening into a courtier's proverb of obligation: what the war poem offers as honour freely returned, the ethics verse states as a debt that forbids hesitation.

note: Kural 228 asks whether the hard-eyed hoarders do not know the joy of giving; Pazhamozhi 218 says whether such hoarders fear sin or not makes no difference.
teaches: The pair close the hoarder's two exits: he lacks the joy of giving, and his fear of sin, which might have stood in for it, counts for nothing without the act.
list_adds: its proverb of the blind eye, the same shut or open, rules out piety without giving, a point the couplet's appeal to pleasure does not reach.

note: Purananuru 93 describes the rite of cutting with a sword the body of a king who died of sickness, so that he goes where battle-slain warriors go; Akananuru 61 opens with the saying behind that rite (blessed are those who die at others' hands, not seized by Death) as the reason a man leaves home.
teaches: Together they show the warrior's creed about a good death working at two scales: as a royal funeral rite in puram, and in akam as a proverb that sends an ordinary man away from his wife to strive.

note: Kural 505 makes one's own deeds the only touchstone of greatness and smallness; Pazhamozhi 142 says one part seen of a person, like one ladle from the pot, suffices to judge the whole.
teaches: Together they turn the Kural's touchstone into a method of sampling: one need not watch all a person's deeds, since a single act examined stands for the whole as one ladle stands for the pot.
list_adds: its cooking image and proverb add the claim that a small sample is enough, which the couplet's touchstone does not say.

note: Naladiyar 64 says the excellent do not flare up when the low confront them with unfit words; Pazhamozhi 61 says the small who confront the great with insolence walk to their death.
teaches: The pair separates the great man's calm from the offender's fate: the great may not burn with anger, yet the insolent small man is lost all the same, so his safety never rested on their temper.
list_adds: it moves the scene from the great man's response to the offender's end, with the proverb's dazed traveller as the measure of his danger.

note: Kural 715 calls not speaking first among elders the best restraint; Acharakkovai 60 says that on the road with eminent elders one does not ride, wear sandals or shade oneself.
teaches: The Kural's deference to elders lies in speech, the Acharakkovai's in the body on the road, so respect is shown both by holding back the word and by sharing the elder's hardship.
list_adds: It turns deference into three bodily refusals, of mount, sandals and shade, which the Kural's single rule about speaking first does not cover.

note: Kural 410 sets the unlearned to the learned as beasts to men; Pazhamozhi 150 calls wise the man who finishes his task even if he has learned nothing.
teaches: Read together, the two give rival measures of a person: the Kural ranks by what one has studied, Pazhamozhi by what one has completed, and on its reading the unlearned doer outranks the idle learned.
list_adds: its proverb moves rank from learning and age to finished work, a criterion the couplet does not admit.

note: Kural 957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the spot on the moon; Pazhamozhi 80 says one fault of the exalted is a lamp on a hill while the many faults of the small never show.
teaches: The Kural shows the fault against the bright moon; the Pazhamozhi adds the other side of the scale, that the small man's long-matured faults stay hidden, so visibility, not guilt, is what height changes.
list_adds: it sets the one fault of the great against the many of the small, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Verse 22 bars laying the bed along the roof-ridge; verse 30 bars the head to the north and the corners when lying down.
teaches: Read together, the bed is governed by two separate direction rules, one tied to the house's ridge and one to the compass, so the code fixes sleep by both the building and the quarters.

note: Kural 118 praises leaning to no side like a level balance; Pazhamozhi 243 applies that to the king's dealing with rich and poor and pictures the lean as milk and water.
teaches: The couplet's balance shows only that something tilts; the pairing names who gains and loses, the rich getting milk and the poor water from one royal source.
list_adds: it moves the worthy man's balance into the king's court and names the two parties, rich and poor, that the couplet leaves unnamed.

note: Both use the chisel that will not cut even into a tender shoot unless struck; the Naladiyar applies it to the base, Pazhamozhi 169 to any agent left to do a task.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes the unstruck chisel a mark of base character, but Pazhamozhi uses the same saying of the employer's duty to everyone he employs, so the image shifts blame from the worker's nature to the master's need to keep directing.
list_adds: the quatrain uses the chisel to sort people into kind and harsh-ruled; the Pazhamozhi makes it a rule for the master after the handing over, a stage the quatrain never reaches.

note: Kural 955 says an old family does not part from its nature when what it can give has shrunk; Pazhamozhi 81 says a man of a giving house keeps up ஒப்புரவு without wealth, and adds that he does so though untended and unfed.
teaches: The Kural treats the shrunken means as the only test; Pazhamozhi adds neglect, so the inherited nature is shown to hold without either resources or nurture.
list_adds: its proverb of the unfed calf that still becomes a bull makes the claim one of nature against upbringing, which the couplet does not raise.

note: Kural 185 says backbiting exposes the meanness of the backbiter; Pazhamozhi 56 says the target of hired lies has no cause for grief, since the charge is false.
teaches: Held together, the two verses show slander's weight falling wholly on the speaker: the Kural says it exposes him, Pazhamozhi that it leaves the innocent target nothing to grieve.
list_adds: it adds the slanderer's motive, food from one's enemies, and the victim's side, which the couplet on the backbiter does not consider.

note: Kural 972 holds birth alike for all living beings and distinction to come from the work done; Pazhamozhi 147 says one's own birth-group (தஞ்சாதி) shows through any concealment, as in the keeper's daughter.
teaches: The pair sets two views of what makes a person's standing side by side: for the Kural deeds make the difference, for this verse birth leaves a mark no change of house can hide.
list_adds: its exemplum and proverb make birth an ineradicable trait shown in a habit of eating, where the couplet makes birth equal and conduct the divider.

note: Naladiyar 227 says the worthy see no fault in those they have joined, and those who bring out a friend's wrongs are lower than he; Pazhamozhi 130 says those who chose friends after sifting do not blame them among many, as no one tells a shameful dream.
teaches: The quatrain ranks exposing a friend as worse than his wrong; Pazhamozhi gives the reason through the dream: a friend chosen by oneself is part of oneself, so publishing his fault is publishing one's own shame.
list_adds: its proverb of the shameful dream adds why the exposer is shamed, which the quatrain asserts without a reason.

note: Purananuru 341 tells of a father who will not give his young daughter even when the king pleads and takes up arms with his tiger-like kin, torn between her wedding tomorrow and death; Pazhamozhi 326 says even the girl's brothers will refuse the king and the only outcome is battle.
teaches: The Sangam poem holds the refusal as a tragic choice and grieves for the town's beauty; the ethics verse keeps the heroic memory but removes the dilemma, so the refusal becomes a fixed rule of a proud house and war the only remedy, said with a kitchen proverb.

note: Pazhamozhi 374's tank does not quickly run dry; 378's well springs fresh each time it is drawn.
teaches: The tank says giving does not soon exhaust stored wealth; the well says drawing on it renews it, so within one chapter the claim rises from endurance to replenishment.

note: Kural 882 says fear the bond with kin-like enemies more than sword-like ones; Pazhamozhi 298 counts the false intimate's harm in two worlds and ranks the open enemy above him by the proverb of blindness and dim sight.
teaches: The pair shows why the kin-like enemy is worse: the open foe is a known lack one guards against, while the false friend's harm reaches even one's standing in the next world.
list_adds: its rhetorical question and proverb turn the couplet's warning into a ranking of two harms, with the open enemy placed above the false friend as blindness above clouded sight.

note: Naladiyar 141 says the well-born in rags keep their principles, as a starving lion will not eat grass; Pazhamozhi 376 says the habitual giver, wasted, still relieves his dependents, as a thin great horse shows in harness.
teaches: Both use a noble animal reduced by want; the Naladiyar's lion shows what the noble will not do, Pazhamozhi's horse what he still does, so poverty is shown to test both refusal and service.
list_adds: it turns the quatrain's refusal into a positive act, relieving others' distress, so the proof of nobility in want becomes giving rather than abstaining.

note: Kural 122 says to guard restraint as wealth, since life has no greater gain; Pazhamozhi 387 sets self-possession above uncounted wealth, good birth, royal property and a king's praise, for both worlds.
teaches: The couplet's metaphor of restraint as wealth becomes a contest here: self-mastery is weighed against real wealth, lineage and court honour and wins in this life and the next, so the figure is cashed out as a ranking.
list_adds: it names the rivals that restraint outranks, wealth, birth, royal goods and royal recognition, and extends the claim over both lives.

note: Elathi 7 counts sweet speech with mingling, a seat and good food in the host's gift; Pazhamozhi 338 isolates the word given at the guest's leaving.
teaches: Elathi joins the sweet word to food in one welcome, and Pazhamozhi shows the welcome can fail at its last moment, when the departing guest is dismissed without it.

note: Naladiyar 348 lists the base as harsh, without kindly regard and scornful of all; Pazhamozhi 123 names the same traits and adds the absence of fear of evil deeds and a verdict of hell.
teaches: The quatrain describes and stops; Pazhamozhi takes nearly the same portrait and passes sentence, so the pairing shows the description turning into a judgement.
list_adds: its proverb closes the portrait with a verdict, making such men hell's own, where the quatrain gives only the list.

note: Kural 808 praises those whose intimacy is strong enough not to listen to reports of a friend's lapse; Pazhamozhi 131 says one does not burn against a friend one has made even for faults seen with one's own eyes.
teaches: The Kural guards the friend against hearsay; Pazhamozhi goes further, to faults one has witnessed, and grounds the restraint in having made the friend oneself, as one does not watch one's own calf die.
list_adds: its proverb of the dying calf extends the couplet's case from reported faults to seen ones and gives the reason, that the friend is one's own.

note: Kural 428 calls not fearing what should be feared folly and fearing it the work of the knowing; Pazhamozhi 323 denies that the fool's daring, resting on ignorance of dangers, is daring, and grants that knowing brings great fear.
teaches: The couplet makes fear a mark of wisdom in general; Pazhamozhi carries it to the soldier and draws the hard consequence, that the brave man is one who knows the danger and so feels the fear, making courage a matter of holding against it rather than lacking it.
list_adds: it moves the claim into the soldier's domain and turns it against a kind of courage, ruling out the fearless fool as brave, which the couplet does not say.

note: Kural 335 urges good deeds before the hiccup stops the tongue; Pazhamozhi 361 shows those who wait until illness to begin aram and find it of no use.
teaches: The Kural sets the deadline at the death rattle; Pazhamozhi sets it earlier, at the first sight of illness, and says aram begun then fails because the means is not to hand, as the stone is not when the dog comes.
list_adds: its dog-and-stone proverb adds that the late giver lacks the means as well as the time, a cause the couplet's deadline does not give.

note: Kural 69 has the mother rejoice when her son is called worthy; 183 has the mother's heart turn toward the accomplished child among children of one womb.
teaches: Where the Kural shows a mother's joy at one son's public praise, the Purananuru admits the harder consequence, that learning makes her favour one child over his brothers, so the pair shows that the honour of learning reorders even family love.

note: Porunaratruppadai says Karikalan received his inheritance while still in the womb; Pazhamozhi 239 tells of a Chola's son who survived burning, mounted the great elephant and in the end ruled justly, a prince tradition identifies as Karikalan.
teaches: If the traditional identification holds, the same accession is told once as a birthright fixed before birth and once as a survival against fire, and the pair shows the ethics work turning a praised royal memory into proof that a living man can still come to anything.
list_adds: it uses the heroic memory not to praise the king but as a proverb's evidence, so the Chola's rise becomes a general lesson about survival.

note: Naladiyar 140 says worldly learning without the books of wisdom is clamour that removes no confusion; Pazhamozhi 3 compares learning that leaves confusion to a lamp bought that gives darkness.
teaches: The quatrain says which learning fails to clear confusion; the proverb adds the cost, that such learning is a price paid for darkness.
list_adds: its lamp-buying image frames learning as a purchase to be tested before paying, which the quatrain's judgement of book against book does not.

note: Naladiyar 280 counts guarding wealth among its bitter sufferings (காத்தலும் ஆங்கே கடுந்துன்பம்); Pazhamozhi 200 says the wealth one guards guards its owner in return, like the thicket and the tiger. The tension holds on the plain reading of both: the Jain quatrain treats guarding as a cost, the proverb as a mutual defence.
teaches: The two books judge the same act of keeping wealth oppositely: for the Naladiyar the guard is one more place of suffering, for Pazhamozhi it is what makes wealth a shelter, so the dispute is whether wealth is a burden on its owner or a defence of him.
list_adds: its proverb makes guarding reciprocal, which turns the quatrain's one-way burden into an exchange of protection.

note: Thirikadugam 55 counts a friendship that does not keep a weighty secret as a spy; Pazhamozhi 180 says that even among pleasant friends no one keeps back what he heard.
teaches: Together they show that the leaking friend is not a rare traitor but the common case, which is why a counted work can number him among the spies inside one's circle.

note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by going the outer way if household life is lived in virtue; Pazhamozhi 389 asks what use is a body that does not renounce once friends, peace, marriage and the house are achieved.
teaches: The two rhetorical questions face each other: on the reading that the Kural's 'outer way' is renunciation, it makes a virtuous household sufficient, while the Pazhamozhi makes the finished household only the stage before the renunciation that alone gives the body its use.
list_adds: it lists the household's tasks (friends made, enemies quieted, a wife joined, a house set up) as completed, so household life becomes a sequence that ends, not a sufficient path.

note: Kural 541 defines justice as acting without favour to anyone; Pazhamozhi 241 names the hardest case of that 'anyone', one's own people.
teaches: The couplet's யார்மாட்டும் is abstract; the pairing shows where impartiality is actually tested, at the king's own kin, and names the failure there as softness of eye.
list_adds: its proverb turns கண்ணோடாது into a portrait of the king who fails it, the soft-eyed man who cannot punish, so the rule gains a named vice the couplet does not give.

note: 166 says service should be won by affection, not forced; 169 says even entrusted work needs striking like a chisel.
teaches: The two adjacent counsels separate winning a helper from running him: affection is the way to gain his will, but once the task is his, the master's prompting is still needed, so gentleness at the start does not excuse absence later.

note: Naladiyar 368 says the old wealthy and the worthy decline while concubines' sons and the base flourish, the world upside down; Pazhamozhi 122 says the worthy withdraw while the unrestrained rise, the gourd sinking and the stone floating.
teaches: Both read social inversion through an image, but the Naladiyar mixes birth and wealth into its ranks while Pazhamozhi measures only by speech and restraint, showing the complaint can be made on conduct alone.
list_adds: it drops the quatrain's birth and wealth markers and ranks by conduct, and its proverb calls the inversion impossible in nature, not merely a turned umbrella.

note: Kural 879 says to cut the thorn tree while young; Pazhamozhi 286 keeps the timing and adds a second step, stripping the young enemy of his friends.
teaches: The pair gives two parts of one tactic: the Kural's when (before the thorn hardens) and the Pazhamozhi's how (leave the tree alone so it cannot become a forest).
list_adds: it joins early action to isolation from allies, a pairing the couplet's single tree image does not make.

note: Naladiyar 94 asks for daily giving before eating, even a grain's worth, to anyone; Acharakkovai 21 names who must be served before the meal.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes giving before eating a matter of amount, however small, while the Acharakkovai makes it a matter of persons, so the two together fix both how little suffices and to whom it is owed.
list_adds: It replaces the Naladiyar's unnamed recipient with five named dependants of the house, human and animal.
