note: Kural 126 says that drawing in the five senses like a tortoise protects for seven births; Acharakkovai 65 says the five are hard to hold even for the worthy, so they must not stay alone with their nearest kinswomen.
teaches: Where the Kural trusts restraint of the senses as a power one can gain, the Acharakkovai doubts it even in the worthy and replaces it with a rule that removes the occasion, so self-mastery is backed by avoidance.
list_adds: It names mother, daughter and sister as the case, so the doubt about restraint is pressed to the women least suspected, a limit the couplet never tests.

note: Pazhamozhi 7 says only the learned know the learned; 8 says the goodness of the good is known only by those better than they.
teaches: Read in sequence the claim tightens from peer to superior: learning can be judged by equals, but goodness only by one who exceeds it.

note: Kural 893 says, in grim irony, that one who wants ruin should offend the able; Pazhamozhi 61 has the small man offend the great because his senses are dazed and he cannot see his death.
teaches: The Kural frames offending the great as a choice of ruin, Pazhamozhi as blindness: held together they show the offence as willed in form and unseen in fact, the offender choosing what he cannot see.
list_adds: its proverb replaces the couplet's mock instruction with the dazed traveller, making the offender's fault a failure of sight rather than of will.

note: Kural 152 says to bear with excess always (என்றும்) and better to forget it; Pazhamozhi 63 asks whether a man who errs again after a first fault will be borne, and answers with the plantain that bears once.
teaches: Against the Kural's 'always', Pazhamozhi sets a count: forbearance covers the first offence, and the repeated one is outside it, so the pair raises whether forbearance is unlimited or once given.
list_adds: the plantain proverb puts a number on forbearance, one bunch and no second, where the couplet sets no limit.

note: Naladiyar 369 condemns those whose hearts do not ease the pain dear ones tell them; Pazhamozhi 133 says the sufferer should tell his want to one who will remove it, as the sick do not hide disease from the physician.
teaches: The quatrain speaks to the friend who hears; Pazhamozhi speaks to the friend who suffers and tells him to choose a hearer able to cure, so the pair completes the exchange of telling and easing from both ends.
list_adds: its proverb of patient and physician adds the sufferer's duty to disclose, which the quatrain assumes.

note: Kural 946 grounds not eating to excess in health and joy; Acharakkovai 23 bars excess even when the food is choice, among rules of posture and place.
teaches: The same restraint has two grounds: in the Kural it pays in pleasure and freedom from disease, in the Acharakkovai it is decorum, binding even when the food tempts, so moderation is both prudence and conduct.
list_adds: It sets overeating beside eating lying down, standing, in the open and on the bed, so excess becomes a breach of form like a wrong posture rather than a danger to health.

note: Kural 158 says to defeat those who wrong one in excess by one's own fitness; Pazhamozhi 53 says the long feud dies of itself as grass does when paddy is grown.
teaches: The Kural states that rightness defeats excess and Pazhamozhi shows how: like a crop crowding out weeds, one's own good work starves the enmity without any act against the enemy.
list_adds: its farming proverb gives the mechanism, crowding out rather than fighting, that the couplet's language of victory leaves unstated.

note: Naladiyar 238 is a vow to put one's life in a distressed friend's hands; Pazhamozhi 137 condemns the friend who went off to penance instead of fighting beside his friend.
teaches: The vow and the story are the two halves of one rule: the Naladiyar says what the friend owes in the hour of danger, Pazhamozhi shows a famous figure who withheld it and calls his religion a late shoulder.
list_adds: it supplies a named failure for the quatrain's oath, so the duty to risk one's life is shown being broken by a pious withdrawal rather than by cowardice.

note: Naladiyar 340 says learning and birth win honour when others praise them but bring mockery when a man praises them himself; Pazhamozhi 65 condemns self-praise of a deed not yet accomplished.
teaches: Read together they give two grounds against self-praise: the quatrain's man owns real merits and is still mocked for voicing them, while Pazhamozhi's man claims a result that does not exist yet, so the second fault is falsehood on top of vanity.
list_adds: its proverb of selling uncaught birds adds the time element the quatrain lacks: praise claimed before the work is done is a sale of what one does not have.

note: 394: Kuttuvan gives a killer elephant, and when the frightened bard returns it gives a bigger one, ashamed the first seemed small; Kural 221: true giving is giving to those who have nothing.
teaches: The Kural defines a gift by the receiver's want, but Kuttuvan's elephants are sized to the giver's honour and are useless to a hungry bard, so the poem shows a royal giving that the Kural's definition would hardly count as ஈகை at all.

note: Kural 1008 likens the wealth of the unloved to a poison tree fruiting in the middle of town; Pazhamozhi 214 likens the wealth of the irresolute to a mango that fruits and draws the stick.
teaches: The same fruiting tree cuts two ways: in the Kural the fruit is useless to the town, in Pazhamozhi it is coveted and brings blows on the tree, so wealth harms either its neighbours or its holder.
list_adds: it moves the fault from the owner's being unloved to his lacking tested resolve, and turns the tree from an emblem of uselessness into a target.

note: Naladiyar 226 asks whether anyone cuts off his own hand because it poked his eye, to say one does not cast off a friend for a hurt; Pazhamozhi 76 praises a king who did cut off his own hand for its fault.
teaches: The same act is absurd as a response to a friend's offence and noble as a response to one's own moral fault, so the pair separates forgiving others from judging oneself.
list_adds: its story turns the quatrain's absurd hypothetical into a real and admired deed, by making the fault the king's own.

note: Kural 752 says all honour the rich and all scorn the poor; Pazhamozhi 199 says even the compassionate praise the rich and gives the reason in its proverb, that two take from the fortunate.
teaches: The Kural states the fact; Pazhamozhi names whom 'all' includes, even those whose compassion should look to need, and explains the praise by interest, since everyone shares in what the rich hold.
list_adds: it divides the Kural's 'all' into the compassionate and the rest and supplies a motive, a reason the couplet does not give.

note: Both use the simile of a poor man's youth (பொருள் இல்லான் இளமை, 38 line 15; the waste's trees in 10): poem 10 measures a withered landscape by it, poem 38 the girl's face drooping after a night of fear.
teaches: The paalai poet and Kapilar draw on one stock of moral similes, but Kapilar moves it from the land to the woman's body and pairs it with its opposite (the gracious man's wealth), so the girl's face becomes a landscape that his coming can drought or rain on, which is the kali form's way of turning a moral maxim into a lover's argument for marriage.

note: Pazhamozhi 89 says the poverty of the great is better than the wealth of the small, as old ghee never sinks below buttermilk; Pazhamozhi 204 says the fallen great are not insulted by the mean.
teaches: Together the two verses build the book's case that greatness is not measured by wealth: 89 ranks the poor great above the rich small in worth, and 204 adds that others still treat them so, since the tiger's head is safe from dogs.

note: Purananuru 116 shows Pari's daughters after his fall, in a thorn-fenced hut counting salt carts; Pazhamozhi 381 shows Pari's daughter giving a bard gold in a drought.
teaches: The Purananuru remembers the daughters as the dispossessed; Pazhamozhi keeps one of them as a giver who feeds a bard even when rain fails, so the ethics work turns the elegy of Pari's house into proof that his giving outlived his fortune.

note: Kural 814 prefers solitude to allies like an untrained horse that throws its rider in battle; Pazhamozhi 163 describes those who stir their own side into a quarrel and flee first.
teaches: The couplet's ally fails at the decisive moment; Pazhamozhi adds that the same man often made the battle, so the desertion is the second half of a single betrayal that begins with words.
list_adds: its proverb of the broken food-bowl names the fault as ingratitude to one's own support, where the couplet only weighs such company against being alone.

note: Both have the small or unlearned offend the great and end in an image of unseen danger: 61 a dazed man who does not see his death, 62 a man who thinks an erukku shrub hides him from an elephant.
teaches: Read together, the two proverbs name the two blindnesses of the offender: he does not see the danger at all, or he sees it and wrongly trusts a cover.

note: Kural 510 says that both trusting without examining and doubting one already trusted bring endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 95 says that once you have seen a man speak evil you should never trust him again.
teaches: Pazhamozhi names the case where withdrawing trust is not the fault the Kural warns of: one evil word plainly seen is taken as proof of a nature, as neem stays bitter whoever eats it.
list_adds: it adds a specific condition, evil speech plainly seen, that overrides the couplet's warning against doubting the trusted.

note: Naladiyar 110 says that since what was set at the start cannot change, there is no reason to grieve when ruin comes; Pazhamozhi 240 says those who know what is to be done do not fear their distress when fearful things come.
teaches: Both ask for calm before what fate brings, but the quatrain grounds it in the fixity of the lot while Pazhamozhi grounds it in knowing what to do, so the pair shows two routes to the same composure, resignation and readiness.
list_adds: it rests calm on knowing one's course of action, with an image of an elephant sheltering its mate, rather than on the quatrain's sum that cannot be altered.

note: Naladiyar 72 bids silence before the unfit words of those not one's equals because the world counts a retort as disgrace; Pazhamozhi 55 bids the same silence because silencing strangers is as futile as bolting a public hall.
teaches: The pair gives two different grounds for one silence, reputation in the Naladiyar and futility in Pazhamozhi, which shows the counsel can rest on prudence alone without appeal to honour.
list_adds: its proverb replaces the quatrain's appeal to the world's judgement with the plain impossibility of shutting an open hall.

note: Kural 892 says disregard of the great brings ills through the great, with the conduct itself as agent; Pazhamozhi 48's image of the hand hurt by pinching rock makes the same point that the great need not act.
teaches: The proverb's mountain gives the couplet's grammar an image: the great do nothing and the attacker's hand is hurt by its own act against something harder, however easy the attack looks.
list_adds: it adds the apparent ease of the attack (நற்கெளி தாகி விடினும்) and a proverb that shows why the ease deceives.

note: Kural 988 says poverty is no disgrace to one with the firmness of worth; Acharakkovai 50 says the learned do not mock or deride the poor.
teaches: The disgrace of poverty is denied from two sides: the Kural says the poor man of worth carries none, and the Acharakkovai says the learned onlooker must not lay it on him.
list_adds: It sets not deriding the poor among the habits of the learned listener, beside not blaming and not sleeping among crowds, so respect for the poor becomes part of learned decorum.

note: Kural 849 says one who shows things to the unseeing becomes unseeing himself while the other keeps what he saw; Pazhamozhi 37 says even the subtly learned cannot turn back one who has taken a wrong course.
teaches: The Kural mocks the would-be teacher; Pazhamozhi removes the blame from him, since even the wisest fail when the pupil's resolve is fixed like a drum's sound.
list_adds: it raises the adviser to the great and the keenly learned to show the failure is not his, and its drum gives the cause: a mind sounds only what it has resolved.

note: Kural 552 likens a sceptred king's demand to a robber's 'hand it over'; Pazhamozhi 246 follows the extorted wealth into the king's gifts.
teaches: The couplet stops at the taking; the pairing shows the robbery disguised as largesse, so a king can be both robber and giver at once.
list_adds: it sets refuge-seekers harmed, crooked rule, excess levy and later favour in one sequence, so the extortion of 552 is followed to its use.

note: Kural 85 asks whether the field of one who feeds guests even needs sowing; Pazhamozhi 330 gives the same unfailing yield to the house, but credits the hospitality to the wife who reads the husband's unspoken sign.
teaches: The pair shows the promise of endless plenty for the hospitable house resting in practice on the wife, whose silent understanding of her husband is what keeps the guests fed.
list_adds: its proverb of a water-lift in the sea replaces the unsown field with an inexhaustible source, and it adds the wife's reading of signs, which the couplet does not mention.

note: Kural 280 says shaving or long hair are not needed if one gives up what the world blames; Pazhamozhi 339 also sets aside the sect's marks and says what penance is: an even mind under the blade and the sandal.
teaches: The Kural removes the outward marks by a negative test, and Pazhamozhi supplies a positive one, equanimity toward harm and honour, as the substance the marks pretend to.
list_adds: its yoke-pin proverb gives the inward test an image of balance the couplet lacks, centring penance on a mind pulled equally both ways.

note: Both men speak to the heart that stands behind them (பின்நின்று): in 3 it drives him from behind toward wealth (பின்நின்று துரக்கும்), in 19 it plans to stay behind with her (பின்நின்று ஒழியச் சூழ்ந்தனை).
teaches: The heart at the man's back is a fixed paalai figure that can push either way, toward the road or toward home, so in these poems the heart is not one side of the debate but the place where the debate happens.

note: Kural 510 says trusting without examining brings endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 183 gives the case of a ruler who gave without weighing the one who came and lost the world.
teaches: Together they show that the couplet's untested trust covers generosity too: the open-handed king who does not weigh the asker suffers the very trouble the Kural assigns to careless trust.
list_adds: its story turns the couplet's abstract fault into a royal gift, so the failure to examine is shown in the act the ethics books most praise, giving.

note: Pisirandhaiyar tells the Pandya to take his due like an elephant fed paddy in balls, not one loosed in the field; Pazhamozhi 244 gives the same rule of revenue through the bee that takes and leaves.
teaches: The Sangam poem warns one king of the ruin a greedy collection brings on him and his land; the ethics verse lifts the warning into a general rule of royal taking that should leave no mark at all.

note: Muthumozhikkanchi 26 says those under an unjust king do not openly censure him; Pazhamozhi 247 says they have no recourse at all.
teaches: The pair gives the reason for the silence: the people do not speak against the unjust king because, with the protector himself the taker, there is no one higher to cover them.

note: Kural 882 says not to fear sword-like enemies but the bond with kin-like ones; Pazhamozhi 297 gives the reason as distance, the flood afar against the debt in one's own house.
teaches: The Kural gives the ranking of the two dangers; the Pazhamozhi explains it, since the open enemy works from outside and far off while the false friend consumes the house from within.
list_adds: it sets a flood, a natural force, against a household debt, so the ranking turns on nearness rather than on the enemy's strength.

note: Naladiyar 110 says what was fixed at birth does not shrink or grow and so asks why grieve at ruin; Pazhamozhi 135 turns the same fixed term against a friend turned murderer, who cannot shorten it.
teaches: Together they show the fixed-term doctrine working in two directions: the Naladiyar uses it to quiet grief over loss, while Pazhamozhi uses it to quiet fear of betrayal, making fate a shelter against human malice.
list_adds: its proverb pictures Death as the guard of a life until its portion is eaten, so the fixed span becomes protection from a plotting friend rather than a reason for calm at ruin.

note: Both picture Death as an eater: Nanmanikkadigai 40 says it does not take its food at anyone's bidding, Pazhamozhi 135 that it guards a man until his eating is done.
teaches: Put together, Death's refusal to eat at command explains the Pazhamozhi consolation: no plotter can order Death to take a man early, so the same appetite that cannot be bribed cannot be hurried either.

note: The Kural says the fivefold sense-knowledge is fruitless without true understanding; Manimekalai tells the materialist, who trusts the senses alone, that true things are hard to know without true understanding.
teaches: The couplet's general claim becomes a debating move: the heroine uses its contrast between sense-knowledge and true understanding to show that a perception-only rule cannot reach even one's parentage.

note: Kural 788 says friendship clears distress there and then, like the hand catching a slipping garment; Pazhamozhi 137 shows a friend who chose penance over battle, help offered when the festival is over.
teaches: Read with the Kural's 'there and then', the Balarama story shows that timing is the whole of friendship's help, so even a holy act done for the friend fails if it replaces help at the moment of need.
list_adds: it sets an epic case and a proverb of lateness against the couplet's simile of speed, and ranks the friend's present help above pious works done on his behalf.

note: Kural 699 says the clear-sighted do not do the unacceptable on the thought that they are in favour; Pazhamozhi 283 says that when a king bears an offence with visible displeasure, going on to offend again is a boil on a hump.
teaches: Together they mark two false grounds for presuming: favour in the Kural and forgiveness in Pazhamozhi; the ethics verse adds that the king's patience, shown with displeasure, is a warning the offender misreads as licence.
list_adds: it adds a sequence the couplet lacks, a first offence borne and then repeated, and a proverb of harm piled on harm.

note: 241 demands that the king turn hard-eyed and punish; 256 praises rulers who are not quickly angered even by great harm.
teaches: Together the two separate severity from haste: the king must punish wrong without favour, but the rulers people shelter under are those slow to anger at harm done to them.

note: 159 will refuse an elephant given grudgingly and take a kunri seed given gladly; Kural 1057 says the heart rejoices on seeing those who give without scorn.
teaches: The Kural names the asker's joy at a gift without contempt; 159 turns it into a rule of conduct for the asker, who must refuse a grudging gift even while his family starves, so the manner of giving decided whether a bard could accept at all.

note: Kural 506 warns against trusting those cut off from kin, since ties make a person accountable; Pazhamozhi 177 says kinship or friendship is no ground for trusting anyone with one's weak point.
teaches: Together they show ties as a necessary but not sufficient condition of trust: the kinless are not to be trusted, yet kin are not to be trusted with one's exposed point either, since even a god acted for his own ends.
list_adds: its proverb grounds the limit in a universal claim proved from a god's conduct, so the couplet's reliance on attachment meets a rule that self-interest outruns every bond.

note: Kural 1263: she lives on, longing for the return of the man who went desiring victory with his resolve as his only companion. Kar Narpathu 7: the friend says he went to give to seekers and crush foes, and the rain will bring him back.
teaches: The couplet's woman treats his heroic aim as the rival that left her behind, while the friend names the same aim, giving and conquest, as a reason to trust he will return in the rains: one motive is a grievance in the Kural and a guarantee in the venba.

note: Pazhamozhi 303 says nothing is mightier than numbers; 307 says one capable man kills the hundred because division is in everyone.
teaches: The book's two proverbs meet: numbers win in the field, but a host can be undone by one man who works its divisions, so number is strength only while it is united.

note: Kural 883 says to fear the enemy within and guard against it; Pazhamozhi 308 says the discerning gain by winning over the enemy within their enemy.
teaches: What the Kural tells one to fear at home the proverb verse tells one to seek in the enemy's camp, so inner enmity is a single force judged by whose house it is in.
list_adds: its doubled proverb, liquor by liquor and thorn by thorn, gives the principle that like cures like, which the couplet's potter's-cutter image lacks.

note: Kural 90 warns the host that a guest wilts at a changed face; Pazhamozhi 337 turns the duty on the guest: the great should not stay with the poor, whom hospitality strains beyond their means.
teaches: Read together, hospitality has two delicate parties: the guest who wilts at a cold look and the poor host who would wound himself to feed a great guest.
list_adds: its sparrow proverb names the host's cost, which the Kural's chapter on hospitality never counts, and makes restraint a guest's virtue.

note: Pazhamozhi 302 counsels silence before the strong and pressing the weak; 300 says the great gain nothing from enmity with the low.
teaches: Read together the book separates the weak, who may be overrun, from the low, who are not worth fighting, so strength and standing are two different measures of an enemy.

note: Pazhamozhi 136 says those cherished as a store against bad days fail one in trouble; Pazhamozhi 341 says even the smallest companion may save one.
teaches: Within one book help is shown to come from where it is not counted on, the crab, and to fail where it was banked on, the cherished friend.

note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander, like a lamp's inner flame; Pazhamozhi 77 says the worthy do not join slanderers who pose as protectors but turn away at once like a crow from a bow.
teaches: The quatrain gives the inner response to slander, steadiness, and the Pazhamozhi the outer one, flight, so the worthy are shown both unmoved by the slanderer and unwilling to stay in his company.
list_adds: it names the slanderer's disguise, speaking as if guarding one, and answers it with withdrawal rather than endurance.

note: Kural 113 bids one let go at once any gain that comes from leaving fairness, even if it brings good; Pazhamozhi 213 says the good do not even desire such gain, and gives the reason in the proverb.
teaches: The Kural's command assumes the unfair gain may truly bring good; the proverb denies even that, so renouncing it becomes good sense rather than sacrifice.
list_adds: its proverb and the image of the onrushing wave add a mechanism, that the gain's apparent growth is the first stage of its loss, which the couplet leaves out.

note: Kural 850 says one who says 'it is not' to what the world says is will be reckoned a demon; Pazhamozhi 108 names one such denial, of the next world, and its practical upshot.
teaches: The couplet leaves blank what is denied; the pairing fills it with the next world and shows the denier's error as a bad exchange, not only a social stigma.
list_adds: it fills the couplet's blank with a named denial and a proverb that judges it by what is lost, not by the world's verdict.

note: Kural 987 says worth is useless unless it does good even to those who did harm; Pazhamozhi 59 says worth (சால்பு) comes from enduring such people rather than punishing them.
teaches: The pair sets two thresholds for nobility: Pazhamozhi grants சால்பு to one who merely endures the wrongdoer, while the Kural asks that the wrongdoer also be done good.
list_adds: it sets enduring against punishing and gives each its fruit, renown against nothing, where the couplet asks a third thing, doing good.

note: Naladiyar 283 says bees do not go to the hill where the kanthal has not flowered, so the poor have no kin; Pazhamozhi 198 says no one who dug a tank sought out the frogs, so the rich need not seek those who need them.
teaches: Read together, the two nature images state one law from both sides: people are drawn by what can be had, so the rich are sought without seeking and the poor are left without kin, and Pazhamozhi presents as a comfort what the Naladiyar presents as a grief.
list_adds: it states the attraction from the side of the owner, who may wait, where the quatrain states it from the side of the poor man who is abandoned.

note: Both proverbs turn on உறற்பால, what is bound to befall: 229 proves it by the moon's harm, 230 by an elephant that went to a man of Karuvur.
teaches: Read together the same word covers both directions of fate, harm that strikes the highest and good that finds a man who did not seek it, so உறற்பால in this chapter is neutral lot, not misfortune only.

note: Both rank the poverty of the worthy above others' wealth through an image of what is drunk or eaten: the Naladiyar's small well beside the sea, Pazhamozhi's old ghee beside buttermilk.
teaches: The images argue differently for the same ranking: the Naladiyar's well is preferred because it can be used, Pazhamozhi's ghee because its kind does not change with age, so one rests the claim on use and the other on nature.
list_adds: it measures the worthy against the small rather than against those ignorant of the next world, making the ranking one of character rather than of foresight.

note: Kural 772 says carrying a spear that missed an elephant is sweeter than an arrow that hit a hare; Pazhamozhi 319 scorns petty men who keep quiet before the strong and overrun the weak.
teaches: Both measure valour by its target rather than its success, and Pazhamozhi names the opposite type the couplet only implies: the man who chooses hares, silent before the guard and pitiless to the helpless.
list_adds: it adds the social side the couplet lacks, the bully's two faces toward strong and weak, and the razor image of sharpness wasted on what offers no resistance.

note: Naladiyar 17 says youth falls like fruit, so do not desire a woman for her eyes; Kalittokai 15 says wealth can be made any day but youth cannot be brought back, so do not leave her.
teaches: From the same fact that youth passes, the moralist counsels turning from desire and the love poet counsels holding fast to it, so the two books read the brevity of youth as a reason for opposite lives.

note: Naladiyar 98 says to give to those who cannot repay is duty and giving to those who repay is only a loan; Pazhamozhi 226 says giving to those who do not rejoice in kindness is all loss.
teaches: Together they say what a gift may and may not ask in return: no repayment, but gladness, so a recipient who cannot repay is fit and one who will not rejoice is not.
list_adds: it adds a condition the quatrain lacks, the recipient's joy in the kindness, without retracting its rule against seeking return.

note: Kural 659 says what is taken with tears goes with tears; Pazhamozhi 213 says evil gains perish as they seem to thrive.
teaches: Together the two make ill-gotten wealth self-cancelling twice over: it leaves the way it came, and its swelling is the very shape of the leaving.
list_adds: it sets the claim as a choice the good make in advance, refusing to want such wealth, where the couplet only forecasts its end.

note: Naladiyar 195 calls good and bad caste mere words and makes lineage from austerity, learning and effort; Pazhamozhi 147 says one's own சாதி breaks through concealment.
teaches: Within the same group of ethics works the Naladiyar denies that caste has substance while the Pazhamozhi treats it as a nature that betrays itself, so the group holds no single view of birth.
list_adds: its story gives birth an observable trait, which is just what the quatrain denies birth has.

note: Kural 750 says a fort with every excellence is nothing for those without excellence in action; Pazhamozhi 285 names the missing excellence as courage and adds allies to the fort as a support that fails without it.
teaches: Read together, the outer defences of a ruler, walls and allies alike, are shown to depend on one inner thing, and the Pazhamozhi names that thing as freedom from fear.
list_adds: it sets strong allies beside the fort as a second outer prop and lets the proverb make fear the single cause that empties both.

note: Kural 229 calls eating alone from one's hoard worse than begging; Acharakkovai 39 bars cooking for oneself alone and requires the house offering to be fed first.
teaches: The Kural condemns eating alone by its bitterness, while the Acharakkovai moves the bar back to the hearth, so the fault begins when the pot is set on the fire for oneself.
list_adds: It sets the bar on solitary cooking beside a purity rule for the kitchen and an offering rule, so sharing becomes part of the ritual order of the house.

note: Kural 657 sets the utter poverty of the worthy above wealth gained under blame; Pazhamozhi 89 sets the poverty of the great above the wealth the small have reached, calling that wealth shameful.
teaches: The Kural condemns wealth for how it was got; Pazhamozhi condemns it for who holds it, so the pair shows two grounds on which wealth can rank below poverty.
list_adds: the old-ghee proverb concedes the great man's decline and ranks him above the fresh lesser thing anyway, a turn the couplet's plain ranking lacks.

note: Pazhamozhi 222 shows a man who seems about to help and then dashes the asker's hope; 225 says an honest refusal is no fault but that killing hope forfeits the next world.
teaches: Read together, the pair say the wrong is not in refusing but in raising hope and then crushing it, and 225 names the price of what 222 depicts.

note: Kural 43 names five the householder must tend (ancestors, gods, guests, kin, self); Acharakkovai 21 names five who must be fed before the householder eats: guests, elders, the cow, caged creatures and children.
teaches: Read together, the Kural's general duty to five becomes a sequence at the meal, and the circle of dependants widens from kin and gods to animals and captives, while the self drops off the list.
list_adds: It turns a list of duties into an order of serving, and it puts the cow and the caged creature beside guests and elders as claimants on the same meal.

note: Naladiyar 345 says a dog fed from a golden bowl still eyes leftovers, so honouring the base does not change their deeds; Pazhamozhi 105 says giving the small the honour due to the great is like laying a seat for a dog.
teaches: Both use the honoured dog, but the Naladiyar faults the dog, which stays a dog, and Pazhamozhi faults the one who honours it, who has also taken the honour from the great.
list_adds: it moves the blame from the honoured base to the giver and adds the loss to the great whose due was given away.

note: Kural 1007 likens the non-giver's wealth to a beautiful woman growing old alone; Pazhamozhi 217 likens it to losing the eye together with its beauty.
teaches: Both images make unused wealth a beauty wasted, but the Kural's beauty fades unseen while Pazhamozhi's is destroyed with the organ, so one is waste by neglect and the other by injury.
list_adds: its proverb replaces slow fading with sudden destruction, matching its frame of kings who vanished like a festival dance.

note: Kural 796 says ruin has one benefit, that it measures one's people to full length; Pazhamozhi 134 says in the Kali age the ruined have no friends.
teaches: The Kural treats ruin as a rod that sorts true friends from false; Pazhamozhi reports what the rod finds in this age, nothing at all, so the couplet's consolation becomes a bleak verdict.
list_adds: its proverb gives the result of the measuring the couplet describes, the thousand eaters reduced to none.

note: Kural 451 says greatness fears small company while smallness takes it at once as kin; Pazhamozhi 113 says fostering and living with the shameless is binding worms into a wound.
teaches: The couplet explains why the great fear such company, and the pairing supplies what they fear: harm that grows under one's own care, sealed in by the very bandage of fellowship.
list_adds: its proverb makes one's care for the base the means of one's injury, a mechanism the couplet's fear leaves unstated.

note: Kural 426 says understanding lives as the world lives; Pazhamozhi 195 closes on running with the town's way, but first asks for repeated private scrutiny of what one has seen without heeding others.
teaches: The pair shows that going with the world is the end of a private test, not a substitute for it: Pazhamozhi puts one's own repeated examination before conformity, as the Kural's chapter sets 423 beside 426.
list_adds: it ranks the counsels in order, not abandoning dependants, not leaving the renouncers' path, examining for oneself, and only then conforming, so conformity comes last.

note: Kural 693 tells the king's servant that once suspicion has arisen nobody can clear it; Pazhamozhi 335 carries the same irreversibility into a friend's house, where the town's rumour leaves no witness.
teaches: The pairing shows one rule about suspicion working at court and in the town alike: since it cannot be undone, the only defence is avoiding the occasion, even for the innocent.
list_adds: its flood-and-dam proverb gives the couplet's 'hard for anyone' a cause, the swell of public talk, and moves it from the king's suspicion to the neighbours'.

note: Kural 694 says to suppress whispers and shared smiles before the great; Acharakkovai 73 bars laughter, yawning, hawking and sneezing before them.
teaches: The Kural bars the laugh as a sign that may be misread; the Acharakkovai puts it with yawning and sneezing, which carry no meaning, so the presence of the great governs the body itself and not only what it signals.
list_adds: It joins a meaningful act, laughter, to involuntary ones, so the couplet's guard against misread signs becomes a guard on the body as such.

note: Naladiyar 141 says the well-born keep their principles though their clothes are rags; Pazhamozhi 329 says the household should keep a bright outward show even in ruin, since the world reads want from dress.
teaches: The two divide dignity in poverty between inner principle, which must never fall, and outward appearance, which the Naladiyar lets go and the Pazhamozhi insists on keeping for the world's eyes.
list_adds: its proverb about the clothed never being asked if they have eaten adds the social reason for outward show, which the quatrain's lion image of inner nature ignores.

note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Pazhamozhi 255 says giving high dignity to the unrestrained is putting a firebrand in a monkey's hand.
teaches: The couplet counts the folly as the king's; the proverb shows it burning outward, since the monkey with fire harms everything near it, not only the one who handed it over.
list_adds: it moves the fault from ignorance to want of restraint and adds wealth to the trust given, so the harm is power and means in an unruly hand.

note: Innaa Narpathu 26 counts telling one's own trouble to those who do not care (பரியார்க்குத் தாமுற்ற கூற்று) as painful; Pazhamozhi 133 says one should tell one's want to one moved with care (பரிந்து) who will remove it.
teaches: The two say the same thing from two sides, the painful telling to the uncaring and the fitting telling to the caring healer, so together they make the listener's care the condition of disclosure.

note: Kural 1078 says the base yield use only when crushed; Pazhamozhi 101, on the reading that அலப்பின் means 'if pressed', says the base do wrong when pressed and also when left alone. The conflict depends on that reading of line 1.
teaches: The two disagree on whether pressure works on the base at all: the Kural makes it the one way to get good from them, Pazhamozhi makes it one more occasion for harm, like the jackal that feeds in any year.
list_adds: it sets the pressed and the unpressed case side by side and finds harm in both, removing the couplet's one remedy.

note: Naladiyar 329 says the small-minded think of the next world only in want and illness; Pazhamozhi 108 gives the base man who denies it outright and urges the fill of desire.
teaches: The pair sets two degrees of the same neglect, forgetting the next world when able and denying it as a creed, and Pazhamozhi's proverb names the cost the Naladiyar leaves implied, brick eaten in tears.
list_adds: it quotes the denier's own words and answers them with an image of the trade he offers, where the quatrain only describes the forgetter's timing.

note: Kannaki cites the Chola who crushed his own son under the chariot for a cow's grief; Pazhamozhi 242 tells the same episode and adds that the worthy had hidden the deed.
teaches: Kannaki uses the episode to shame a king who killed without inquiry; Pazhamozhi makes it a rule about age, so one exemplum serves both as indictment and as maxim.

note: Kural 691 says those who serve quarrelsome kings should be like men warming at a fire, neither too far nor too near; Pazhamozhi 265 says the experienced never even think of what would anger the mighty king, for nothing escapes his force.
teaches: The pair shows the fire's danger from inside the servant's mind: the Kural regulates distance, and the Pazhamozhi says the only safety is never to give the king's anger cause, even when he is in the right.
list_adds: its doubled proverb of deer before tiger and straw before wind adds that once the king's anger rises there is no escape at any distance, so the caution moves from posture to thought.

note: Naladiyar 68 says the worthy's anger cools of itself like heat taken on by boiled water; Pazhamozhi 51 uses the same heated water to say the well-born's heat, while it lasts, cannot burn the house.
teaches: Read together, the boiled-water image answers two questions: the Naladiyar says the worthy's anger does not last, Pazhamozhi says it does no harm even at its height.
list_adds: its proverb shifts the image from the cooling of the heat to the house that survives it, so harmlessness is added to brevity.

note: Both proverbs of this heading turn on a dog's bite: in 45 the abused dog bites its master, in 49 the worthy man does not bite back the dog that bites him.
teaches: The heading uses the dog from both sides, as the weak who will strike back when cornered and as the base whom the worthy will not answer, so the same bite warns the strong and restrains the worthy.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 15 calls bearing a wrong greatness and counts living so that enmity ends as good; Pazhamozhi 53 says how the enmity ends: by tending one's own good rather than by force.
teaches: The counted verse names ending a feud as a good to aim at, and Pazhamozhi shows that the aim is reached by not aiming at the enemy at all, since the feud withers on its own.

note: Kural 969 praises those who, like the yak, give up life when honour is at stake; Pazhamozhi 293 tells the weak to survive by doing anything at all.
teaches: The two give opposite answers on whether life may be bought with loss of standing: the Kural's man of honour dies rather than live shamed, while the Pazhamozhi counts staying alive as the greater good.
list_adds: its என்செய்தே யாயினும் and the promise of the bangle make survival a positive aim, where the couplet makes life itself forfeit to honour.

note: Kural 478 says a small income brings no ruin if outgo is not wider; Pazhamozhi 201 says a small income gathered daily grows great, like drops into a flood.
teaches: The pair gives two answers to the small income: the Kural makes it safe by limiting what goes out, Pazhamozhi makes it great by what accumulates over time, so a narrow channel is both a limit to respect and a source that time can enlarge.
list_adds: it adds the daily repetition and a second image of gathered light, turning the couplet's balance of channels into growth by accumulation.

note: Verse 21 names five to be fed before one eats; verse 39 bars cooking for oneself alone and requires the house offering to be fed first.
teaches: Together they show that the code puts others before the eater at both ends of the meal: in cooking (39) and in serving (21), with the house offering added to the living claimants.

note: Kural 124 praises the restrained man who does not stray from his station (நிலை); Acharakkovai 49 says dress, gait, slack speech and rebuke must fit one's standing (நிலைமை), learning, manliness and family.
teaches: The Kural's 'not straying from one's station' is shown in concrete outward marks, and the Acharakkovai's addition of family as a measure shows how that station can be read as rank of birth.
list_adds: It names four outward behaviours, two of them faults, and four measures they must fit, so keeping one's station becomes a fitting of dress, walk and speech to learning and lineage.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from deeds; Pazhamozhi 51 credits freedom from anger to those excellent by birth (பிறப்பினால் மாண்டார்). The tension holds on reading பிறப்பு in 51 as lineage rather than nature.
teaches: The pair shows two accounts of where restraint comes from: the Kural makes worth follow what one does, while Pazhamozhi makes a virtue of conduct the mark of a good birth.
list_adds: it sets the great by birth against the very small and makes forbearance the sign that separates them, the ranking the couplet refuses.

note: Kural 400 calls learning the imperishable wealth and says other things are not wealth; Pazhamozhi 33 grants that jewels and riches do return to the fortunate, and ranks understanding above them because it never leaves.
teaches: Where the Kural denies other goods the name of wealth, the Pazhamozhi verse concedes their worth and their power to come back, and rests understanding's superiority on its independence from fortune.
list_adds: it names the rival goods, priceless jewels and wealth, and gives them a real but conditional permanence, so the ranking is argued rather than asserted.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the work one does; Pazhamozhi 103 says those who come down in a base line have no one of good character among them. The conflict holds on the reading of 972's செய்தொழில் as conduct or work rather than hereditary occupation.
teaches: The pair puts the period's two accounts of character side by side: the Kural makes worth follow deeds and denies birth a role, Pazhamozhi makes it follow descent so firmly that a whole line is written off.
list_adds: its monkey proverb treats a line of descent as a species, the very ranking by birth that the couplet rejects.

note: Kural 803 asks what use long friendship is if one does not accept a friend's liberty as if one had done it oneself; Pazhamozhi 132 says the faultless take a friend's faults as their own.
teaches: The Kural asks one to treat a friend's liberties as one's own acts; Pazhamozhi carries the same identification to his faults, so what began as tolerance of intimacy becomes sharing of blame.
list_adds: its proverb of one's patience as two's friendship extends the couplet from liberties to wrongs.

note: Kural 978 says greatness bows while smallness adorns itself with self-admiration; Pazhamozhi 9 ties self-praise to not knowing the restraint of the learned.
teaches: The Kural sets self-admiration against greatness as a trait; Pazhamozhi makes it a symptom of shallow learning, so boasting becomes evidence of what one has not learnt.
list_adds: it moves the claim from greatness in general to learning and gives the full-pot proof that the deeply filled make no noise.

note: Kural 698 tells those who serve a king not to belittle him as young; Pazhamozhi 6 shows elders doing just that and the young Chola answering them.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule to the courtier; the story shows the king's side, meeting contempt for his youth with a disguise and a sound judgement.
list_adds: it supplies the episode and the cause of the king's competence, his family's craft, which the courtier's rule leaves unstated.

note: Kural 220 grants for argument that ruin may come by ஒப்புரவு and calls it worth buying with oneself; Pazhamozhi 377 denies that anyone has ever become poor by giving.
teaches: The Kural meets the objection by accepting the cost; Pazhamozhi meets it by denying the cost exists, so the two show two answers to the fear that giving ruins, one heroic and one reassuring.
list_adds: its proverb flatly denies the premise the couplet entertains, and places the claim of ruin in the mouths of the takers rather than the giver.

note: Kural 448 says a ruler without those who rebuke him perishes; Pazhamozhi 353 says hurtful counsel should be heard from kin, whose treading, like a mother's, does not lame.
teaches: The pair moves the needed rebuker from the king's council into the family and gives a reason the couplet lacks for bearing him: the bond guarantees the hurt does no harm.
list_adds: its mother-bird proverb explains why rebuke is bearable, which the couplet only declares necessary.

note: Kural 320 says all pains rest on those who caused pain; Pazhamozhi 43 uses the same word, நோய், in its proverb and applies it to the man who hurts someone because they will forgive.
teaches: The pairing shows the rebound of pain is independent of the victim's response: forgiveness on one side does not stop the return of pain on the other.
list_adds: it names the excuse the couplet does not, that the victim will bear it, and makes gods and the steadfast fall under the same rule.

note: Naladiyar 127 asks who can examine another's mind, since minds and deeds differ; Pazhamozhi 146 opens with nearly the same words (ஒருவர் ஒருவர்தம் உள்ளத்தைத் தேரும்) and grants the difficulty, but answers that people take the colour of their kin.
teaches: The two share the question almost word for word and part on the answer: the Naladiyar leaves the mind unknowable because conduct misleads, while the Pazhamozhi finds an outside mark, lineage, that it trusts more than conduct.
list_adds: its proverb turns the Naladiyar's closing despair into a method, making kin the visible plumage of a hidden nature.

note: Kural 521 says honouring old ties when all is lost is found only in kin; Pazhamozhi 352 extends it to kin who were hostile before, and sets them against outsiders who were favoured.
teaches: Together they show that kin loyalty in ruin does not rest on remembered kindness: even a hostile kinsman stands behind, so the bond is of family, not of debt.
list_adds: its contrast of ஒருகுடியார் with பிறர் treated as gold gives the couplet a counter-case, the favoured outsider who still will not come in.

note: Kural 57 says confinement is no use and a woman's own நிறை is the best guard; Pazhamozhi 336 restates this and adds the obverse, that a woman without that restraint is not amended by force however hard.
teaches: The couplet shows only that the inner guard is better; the verse makes the outer guard useless in both cases, needless for the restrained and powerless over the unrestrained.
list_adds: its dog's-tail proverb supplies the second case the couplet does not state, so the claim covers both the woman with restraint and the woman without it.

note: On the reading that புலை names the outcaste person, Acharakkovai 6 makes the sight of a birth-group polluting; Kural 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction comes from deeds.
teaches: The conflict holds only if புலை is a person and செய்தொழில் means conduct, so the pairing shows how the caste force of each verse rests on one disputed word.

note: Kural 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming are not shaken by affliction; Pazhamozhi 205 applies that foresight to one's own wealth and to the prosperity of one's kin.
teaches: The Kural's foresight is a general shield against calamity; the snail that stores water shows it as stockpiling for a known dry season, so foresight becomes provision for kin as well as self.
list_adds: it joins one's own wealth and the kin's prosperity as one object of forethought, which the couplet leaves unnamed, and gives the snail as the instance.

note: Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle endlessly (தொலைவில்லா) of grammar and astrology the greatest fools; Acharakkovai 92 tells one to fix the day of a rite from the unfailing (தொலைவில்லா) அந்தணர், whose word never errs.
teaches: The same word, தொலைவில்லா, marks the Naladiyar's endless and foolish astrology and the Acharakkovai's unfailing reckoners, so the two books take opposite views of consulting the day before acting.
list_adds: It sets the reckoning of days in a contrast between two birth-groups, so the question becomes whose reckoning to trust, not whether to reckon.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 9 says a debtor's tongue dies when he once sees his creditor; Pazhamozhi 212 says the borrower asked to repay grows angry as if at an enemy.
teaches: The Sirupanchamoolam gives the debtor's shame and Pazhamozhi his anger, and Pazhamozhi ties the anger to the lender's long delay, so shame is seen to turn into resentment once a loan has lain unclaimed.

note: Both prove excellence by a light in the sky: in 27 the moon that the many stars cannot equal, in 32 the sun that no hand can cover.
teaches: The two sky proverbs give the excellent man two properties at once, that a crowd cannot outshine him and a hand cannot put him out.
list_adds: 32 turns 27's contest of brightness into one of concealment, so the image moves from comparison to suppression.

note: Akananuru 59: on the road for wealth an elephant bends a yaa tree so its young mate can eat, yet the man forgets her; Kuruntokai 255: on that road the elephant strips the yaa tree to feed its whole hungry herd, and the men went to fulfil their duty.
teaches: The same road-sign is turned two ways by the friend: feeding one mate in Akananuru 59 shames the man who forgets his wife, while feeding the whole herd in Kuruntokai 255 matches the man's duty to his household, so the friend can use the elephant to reproach the journey or to justify it.

note: Kural 774's hero sends his spear away with an elephant and laughs as he pulls one from his own body; 274's warrior hurls his spear at the oncoming elephant and, weaponless, takes the enemy's attack upon his body.
teaches: The Kural's couplet compresses a set scene that the Purananuru gives at length with dress and enemy horse, which shows that Valluvar's chapter on martial pride was built on stock battle episodes the audience already knew from heroic song.

note: 69 says the noble's light is his own and the covering will not cling; 72 says it is the discerning who see the gem through the mud.
teaches: Read together, worth that survives misfortune needs two things: its own shine and an eye that can find it under the dirt, so the verse after 69 hands the burden from the noble to the beholder.

note: Kural 411 ranks the wealth of the ear first among all wealth; Pazhamozhi 5 ranks hearing above learning itself.
teaches: The Kural ranks hearing against wealth, Pazhamozhi against study, so together they set listening at the head of both outer and inner goods.
list_adds: it moves the ranking from wealth to learning and names what hearing cures, the well-frog's belief that its own water is the only water.

note: Kural 153 calls bearing with fools the strength of strengths; Pazhamozhi 57 says the learned do not retort to the unlearned, for no one gores back a cow.
teaches: The Kural calls forbearance toward fools a strength, and Pazhamozhi gives the ground of that strength: a learned man who retorts makes himself the equal of an animal, so restraint keeps the rank between them.
list_adds: its proverb makes the fool a beast whose offence cannot be returned, a ranking the couplet's paradox of strength does not draw.

note: Naladiyar 226 asks whether anyone cuts off his own hand because it poked his eye, so a friend who hurts should not be cast off; Pazhamozhi 140 says breaking with one who breaks is the remedy.
teaches: The images decide the rule: the Naladiyar makes the friend one's own limb, so cutting him off is self-harm, while Pazhamozhi makes the broken friendship an ailment, so the cut is the cure.
list_adds: the medicine proverb answers the quatrain's body image with one of cure, turning the same separation from mutilation into healing.

note: Naladiyar 71 says to speak nothing to a fool and slip away; Pazhamozhi 52 gives the same withdrawal as the answer to a man of unquenchable anger and grounds it in his untrustworthiness.
teaches: Together they show that withdrawal, not endurance, is the counsel for two cases, the fool and the man of lasting anger, and Pazhamozhi supplies the reason: neither can be trusted with one's words.
list_adds: it carries the quatrain's withdrawal from the fool to the man of lasting anger and adds a proverb that names distrust as the ground.

note: Kuruntokai 320: on the dune of drying fish and prawns she has not even one day's laughter with the shore lord to be blamed for, yet the town gossips. Kainnilai 54: on the same drying-ground he lied to her and enjoyed her beauty. On a plain reading one heroine denies what the other confesses.
teaches: The prawn-drying ground serves one heroine as the scene of an innocence the town will not credit and another as the scene of her seduction, so the stock place of neythal kalavu could carry either a defence before the town or an accusation of the lover.

note: Kural 696 asks the king's counsellor to know the mood and the time before saying what is needed; Pazhamozhi 275 says those who speak to kings at the right moment achieve everything, and that a hunchback inside is better than a minister outside.
teaches: The pair shows that the couplet's timing depends on access: one who knows the right moment is useless unless he is in the room when it comes, so the menial with the inner rooms can outdo the minister the Kural addresses.
list_adds: its proverb ranks a hunchbacked attendant above a minister, adding a ranking by nearness that cuts across office, which the couplet's advice on timing does not consider.

note: Kural 719 tells the able speaker not to speak in a mean assembly even by slip; Pazhamozhi 24 condemns the man who does the reverse, silent before the good and boastful before the mean.
teaches: The pair fixes both halves of the rule: the Kural forbids good speech wasted on the mean, Pazhamozhi shows the inverted vice, where the mean assembly gets self-praise and the good assembly gets nothing.
list_adds: it joins silence among the good and self-praise among the mean as one fault and gives it a single image of cowardice.

note: Kural 892 says disregard of the great brings ills that do not leave; Pazhamozhi 291 gives an exemplary case, the demon who took enmity with the great without heed and was caught in battle.
teaches: The Kural's general warning gains a named example and a sharper premise, that the offender's own might, even might won by penance, does not change the outcome.
list_adds: it adds the exemplum and the point that the offender was himself great, which the couplet's plain contrast of the great and the heedless leaves out.

note: Naladiyar 350 says small bullocks never learn to draw the cart however well fed; Pazhamozhi 167 says forcing work from a slack man is ploughing with an idle old bullock.
teaches: The quatrain says care cannot supply a missing capacity; Pazhamozhi adds that pressure cannot either, so between them neither feeding nor driving makes the unfit beast or man do the work.
list_adds: it turns the quatrain's verdict on the base into a rule for the employer about sloth and the use of force.

note: Kural 529 says kin who left return when the cause of discord is gone; Pazhamozhi 351 says kin who seem never to help will help at last, as rain falls after holding off.
teaches: The couplet makes the return of kin wait on removing a cause, while the rain proverb makes it as sure as weather, so delay in kin's help is no proof of its absence.
list_adds: its rain proverb gives kin help the certainty of a natural cycle and sets it against strangers who never help.

note: Thirikadugam 51 says deceivers stay deceivers even when they keep close and that examination shows them; Pazhamozhi 194 shows deceivers who keep close, appearing attached by day while stealing by night.
teaches: The pair says both that closeness proves nothing and what the examination must look for: the gap between the day's show of attachment and the night's acts.

note: Kural 473 says many who did not know their strength rose on zeal and were broken midway; Pazhamozhi 317 says that even capable men who rush on an unequal foe come to harm, like a hand struck on stone.
teaches: The couplet blames ignorance of one's own strength; Pazhamozhi adds that being able (ஆற்றுவாரேனும்) is not enough, since what counts is the match (நிகர்) with the enemy, so the weighing is relative, not absolute.
list_adds: it shifts the measure from the self's strength to the comparison with the enemy and gives the image of injury to the striker, which the couplet's broken-midway leaves general.

note: Kural 849 says the one who shows things to the unseeing becomes unseeing himself while the other keeps what he saw; Pazhamozhi 94 says not to counsel the obstinate, who keep what they took up.
teaches: The Kural describes the failed lesson and Pazhamozhi draws the rule from it, adding the cause: the obstinate are already dyed, so the teacher has no blank cloth to work on.
list_adds: its indigo proverb explains why the lesson fails, a first colour that has set, and turns the couplet's observation into a counsel not to speak.

note: Pazhamozhi 32 says those of wide strength cannot be hidden, as no hand hides the sun; Naladiyar 105 shows the palm-tall great shrinking to millet size and hiding their brightness through former deeds.
teaches: The pair limits the proverb's confidence: no man can cover real greatness, but the Naladiyar shows it dwindling from within through old deeds, so it is safe from suppression, not from fate.
list_adds: its moss and raised hand make concealment a deliberate act by others, which separates it from the self-hiding the quatrain attributes to deeds.

note: Kural 1067 begs all beggars not to beg of those who conceal; Pazhamozhi 224 says those who beg of hard-minded men get nothing, like seeking alms in a monastery.
teaches: The Kural gives the warning; Pazhamozhi gives the reason in an image, that the hard rich man yields no more than renouncers who own nothing.
list_adds: its proverb equates the hard-hearted rich with those who themselves live on alms, a comparison the couplet does not draw.

note: Kural 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum that proclaims every secret heard; Pazhamozhi 178 likens the choosing of a mean confidant to putting the stick to the drum.
teaches: The drum image moves from the base man to his chooser: the Kural blames the drum for sounding, Pazhamozhi blames the one who sets the stick to it, so the leak begins in a bad choice of confidant over worthy kin.
list_adds: it sets the mean confidant against kin rich in excellence, turning the couplet's description of the base into a fault of selection by the one who confides.

note: Kural 503 says even those who have studied hard books and are flawless are rarely without some blankness; Pazhamozhi 171 says even one who has learnt and is rid of faults should not get a task without clear practical knowledge.
teaches: The verbal echo (learned and faultless) makes the pair a step: the couplet admits learning leaves gaps, and Pazhamozhi draws the employer's conclusion that learning and faultlessness alone do not qualify a man for a task.
list_adds: it adds the decision the couplet leaves open, that the work should wait rather than go to the learned but incapable.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 60 counts going before those who are not one's own as laughable; Pazhamozhi 290 says why, with the child crying to be carried by those who would not let it follow.
teaches: The counted line names the act as laughable; the proverb shows what makes it so, the asking for closeness from people who deny even distance.

note: Naladiyar 164 says those who anger the great do not escape even in a fortress, as the snake in its crevice dreads thunder; Acharakkovai 69 lists the small signs of displeasure one must not show before the great.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives the reason the Acharakkovai's courtesies are owed: the great one's anger reaches anywhere, so the rule not to sulk or contradict is a defence, not only a manner.
list_adds: It breaks the single danger into a list of guarded acts, sulking, facing, private talk and contradiction, so the quatrain's dread becomes a code of gestures.

note: Kural 508 warns that trusting an outsider (பிறன்) without examining him brings lasting trouble; Pazhamozhi 206 refuses even eminent men and kin the trust of one's goods until they are tested.
teaches: The Kural's danger is the untested stranger; Pazhamozhi removes the exemption kinship might seem to give, so testing applies inside the family too, and adds that the loss of entrusted wealth cannot be reversed.
list_adds: it names the two pretexts for trust, standing and kinship, and sets both aside, which the couplet does not, since it speaks only of the outsider.

note: Thirikadugam 23 calls giving, faultless conduct and a mind free of possessions a rope that binds good deeds; Pazhamozhi 371 calls penance and aram practised falsely a rope that binds oneself.
teaches: The same rope image holds merit fast in Thirikadugam and holds the person fast in Pazhamozhi, so whether giving and penance are a rope that secures good or one that ties up the doer turns on sincerity.

note: Kural 445 says counsellors are the ruler's eyes and must be chosen with care; Pazhamozhi 260 says one who has not made many around him his eyes is helpless in distress like a lute with cut strings.
teaches: Read together, the eyes the Kural asks a ruler to choose are shown at the moment they are missing: in a crisis the king without them still has his state but can make no response, as a stringless lute keeps its body and loses its sound.
list_adds: it adds the number, many rather than one, and the crisis in which the lack is felt, with an image of form left without function.

note: Kural 879 says cut a thorn tree while young before it wounds the hand; Pazhamozhi 308 removes a thorn with a thorn.
teaches: Both read the enemy as a thorn, but the Kural deals with it by timing, cutting early, and the proverb by means, setting one thorn against another.
list_adds: it adds a second way of handling the thorn, by its own kind, beside the couplet's way of cutting it young.

note: Kural 376 says what is not one's own will not stay though guarded, nor what is one's own leave though thrown away; Pazhamozhi 231 shows a palmyra guarded all night whose fruit still falls to the one it is due to.
teaches: The pairing turns the couplet's abstract 'guard' into a watchman shouting through the night under a tree, and adds a second person the couplet lacks, the passer-by who gets the fruit, so the loss of the guarder is someone else's unearned gain.
list_adds: it gives the couplet a scene with two people, guard and receiver, so fate's allotment is seen as a transfer, not only a keeping or a losing.

note: Purananuru 117 says Pari's land kept its rain even when Venus ran to the south and other evil signs appeared; Patitruppattu 13 says that in the king's guarded land Venus does not run into the burning quarter and rain stands where it is wanted.
teaches: Read together, the two show two views of the omen: the lament makes a just ruler's land immune to the bad sign, while the Chera praise has the good ruler prevent the sign itself, so royal virtue was imagined as reaching even the planets' course.

note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to a village tank full of water; the verse makes the gift of water itself the first of five charities.
teaches: The Kural's tank is a figure for wealth all may draw on; the verse makes it literal and the lowest step of a scale that ends in founding temples and halls.

note: Kural 1075 says fear is the conduct of the base; Pazhamozhi 97 says the base do not care about the great blame that falls on them.
teaches: The pair separates two fears: the base may be held in line by fear of punishment, as the Kural says, but blame, which works on others through shame, has no hold on them at all.
list_adds: its proverb of eating fearlessly at a house of mourning shows what the base do not fear, the judgement of others, which the couplet leaves out.

note: Kural 1051 says that if the worthy giver withholds, the blame is his and not the asker's; Pazhamozhi 384 shows a never-refusing giver hiding what he has because many ask one thing, and puts the fault on the crowd of askers.
teaches: The Kural places the blame for withholding on the giver; Pazhamozhi names a case where withholding comes from pity for those who would be turned away, so the blame moves to the number of askers.
list_adds: its proverb adds the askers' number as a cause of withholding, a condition the couplet's single asker and single giver leave out.

note: Kural 312 says not hurting in return even those who hurt in hatred is the stand (கோள்) of the stainless; Pazhamozhi 49 uses the same word, கோள், for the worthy's refusal to retaliate but grounds it in the offender's likeness to a dog.
teaches: The two give the same rule different grounds: the Kural states non-retaliation as purity of the stainless, Pazhamozhi bases it on the offender's lowness, so the restraint becomes a mark of rank.
list_adds: its proverb ranks the offender with a dog, a contempt the couplet does not express, and limits the case to offenders lacking worth.

note: In 200 Kapilar offers Pari's daughters to Vichikko as a suppliant and brahmin; in 201 he offers them to Irungovel as their father's friend, naming himself அந்தணன், புலவன்.
teaches: Read together, Kapilar's two offers show him grounding the same gift in different claims, his standing as suppliant and brahmin in 200 and his friendship with their father in 201, so the reader sees how a bard, not a kinsman, asserted the right to give a dead patron's daughters.

note: Naladiyar 219 ranks enmity above the friendship of the undiscerning; Pazhamozhi 298 ranks open enmity above the attachment of those who do not care for one.
teaches: The quatrain blames the friend's lack of understanding, the proverb verse his lack of care, so two different faults in a friend both make plain enmity the better lot.
list_adds: it sets the ranking within strategy of enmity rather than among a list of lesser evils, and grounds it in harm done here and hereafter.

note: 124 says friends take each other as a whole body; 132 says the faultless take a friend's fault as their own.
teaches: The union pictured in 124 as one body is given its moral cost in 132: if the friend is one's own whole body, his faults are one's own too.

note: Kural 894 says that when the weak do harm to the strong it is like beckoning Death; Pazhamozhi 294 says the small inflaming the victorious ends in no good.
teaches: The Kural's image makes the attack fatal; the Pazhamozhi's bees warring with the mountain make it pointless as well, an assault that cannot even reach its target.
list_adds: it adds futility to danger: the bees' quarrel with the hill shows the attack does nothing to the strong, not only that it destroys the weak.

note: Kural 363 says there is no fine wealth like not wanting, here or hereafter; Pazhamozhi 273 uses the same word வேண்டாமை to say that a king's servant who asks nothing even in hardship is given all he wants.
teaches: Together they show the renouncer's highest wealth being turned into a courtier's method: the Kural's not-wanting is its own reward, while Pazhamozhi makes it the means by which a king's servant is given everything, so the same virtue serves release and preferment.
list_adds: it carries the couplet's claim from the chapter on cutting off desire into service at court and adds the case of hardship (அல்லுறினும்), where not asking is hardest.

note: Naladiyar 345 says a dog fed from a golden bowl still watches for others' leftovers, so honouring the base does not change their deeds; Pazhamozhi 170 says setting the base on a task and sitting back is setting a cat to guard fish heads.
teaches: The quatrain states the base man's fixed appetite; Pazhamozhi turns it into a charge against the employer, whose fault is not only the choice but sitting idle afterwards, so the base nature becomes the master's loss.
list_adds: it moves the quatrain's observation into the employer's domain and adds the second fault of leaving the agent unwatched.

note: Kural 160 ranks those who fast below those who bear harsh words; Valayapathi 66 calls a vow (நோன்பு) without forbearance (பொறைமை) darkness.
teaches: The Kural only ranks fasting below forbearance, but the fragment makes forbearance the condition without which a vow is worthless, a stronger claim that turns a ranking into a dependence.

note: Kural 507 says trusting the ignorant out of fondness brings every folly; Pazhamozhi 104 says clearing out the fit to raise up the useless base is like felling the jackfruit to plant the kanjirai.
teaches: The Kural warns against the wrong appointment, Pazhamozhi counts its double cost: the base raised and the fit removed, a sweet tree lost and a bitter one planted in its place.
list_adds: its orchard proverb pairs the promotion with a removal, so the folly is an exchange of good for bad rather than a single mistaken trust.

note: Purananuru 200 presents Pari's daughters as the children of the man who gave his tall belled chariot to a jasmine creeper that never sang for him; Pazhamozhi 74 cites the same gift as hearsay of old givers.
teaches: The heroic poem uses the chariot to the creeper to claim a husband for the daughters, while the ethics verse turns the same act into a maxim that knowing folly adorns the worthy, so the patron's deed becomes a proof text.
list_adds: it sets Pari's chariot beside a second giver's mantle and names both as foolishness, a judgement the bardic poem never makes.

note: Both verses urge acting at once against an enemy; 286 speaks of an enmity still young, 287 of one that has already struck.
teaches: Together they cover enmity before and after its first blow, and say that in neither case does waiting help, once because the enemy grows, once because he escapes.

note: Kural 510 warns against trusting one not examined; Pazhamozhi 52 names unquenchable anger as a sign that a man fails the test and is to be avoided.
teaches: The pairing turns the Kural's general rule on examined trust into a usable test, since a man whose anger never cools shows by it that he is never clear and so not to be trusted.
list_adds: it names one observable trait, anger that never cools, as the mark of the untrustworthy that the couplet leaves unspecified.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 4 says a proud raised neck (ஏக்கழுத்தம்) in one who has nothing to be proud of draws the laughter of the good; Acharakkovai 91 says a raised neck (ஏக்கழுத்து) is blamed even in the forest, since there are always those older than oneself.
teaches: Sirupanchamoolam faults the raised neck when it lacks ground, but the Acharakkovai faults it anywhere, even unseen, so the pair separate pride as absurdity from pride as disrespect to elders.

note: Kural 638 makes it the duty of the one at the king's side to tell him his good even when he destroys counsel; Pazhamozhi 259 says the king's faults are laid on those beside him, since no doll is unlike its maker.
teaches: The pair gives the duty of plain counsel its sanction: because the world reads the king as his counsellors' making, the one who stays silent shares the guilt of what the king does.
list_adds: its doll-and-maker proverb adds the consequence the couplet leaves unsaid, that blame for the king's wrongs passes to his attendants.

note: Naladiyar 220 says parting after closeness hurts even from a deadly snake, so test friends first; Pazhamozhi 126 says parting hurts even from a demon, so do not abandon those one has joined.
teaches: The same image of a painful parting from a dangerous companion yields opposite advice: the quatrain draws caution before the bond, Pazhamozhi draws loyalty after it, and together they show the image argues for testing first and keeping afterwards.
list_adds: its proverb is used after the bond is formed, where the quatrain uses the same thought before it, so the pair divides friendship into two stages.

note: Naladiyar 223 says it is right to bear with friends even when they do great wrong and closes with ஒருவர் பொறையிருவர் நட்பு; Pazhamozhi 132 closes with the same proverb after saying the faultless take a friend's fault as their own.
teaches: The two works close on the same proverb but frame it differently: the quatrain asks the injured friend to bear the wrong, while Pazhamozhi has the faultless friend own it as 'our fault', so the one who bears becomes the one who shares the blame.
list_adds: it applies the shared proverb to a different act, owning the fault rather than enduring the injury.

note: Elathi 15 counts not burning against those dear as one's eyes (கண்போல்வார்க் காயாமை) among five good things; Pazhamozhi 131 says one does not burn against (காய்ந்தீயார்) a friend one has made even for faults seen with one's own eyes.
teaches: The counted verse lists the restraint as one good among five; Pazhamozhi sets the hardest condition on it, faults seen with one's own eyes, and argues it by the calf one would not see die.

note: Naladiyar 369 says those whose hearts do not ease the pain a dear one tells them had better leap from a cliff; Pazhamozhi 127 says the remedy for a dear one's distress is not accomplished by words.
teaches: The quatrain makes a heart moved by a friend's pain the minimum of friendship; Pazhamozhi sets the bar higher, since feeling expressed in speech still leaves the tank empty, so the pair moves from compassion to remedy.
list_adds: its proverb ranks deed above sympathy where the quatrain asks only that the heart be moved.

note: Naladiyar 201 says a man's distress vanishes on seeing kin who ask after him; Pazhamozhi 350 says good kin are those who remove distress by deeds.
teaches: Read together, the comfort of kin has two measures, being asked after and being helped, and the Pazhamozhi verse ranks the deed as what makes kin good.
list_adds: it defines good kin by their act (வினைமரபின் நீக்கும்) and makes them a remedy at hand, where the quatrain heals by presence alone.

note: Sirupanchamoolam 16 says that before the worthless anger is good and nobility bad, as good meat is wasted in a biting dog's mouth; Pazhamozhi 109 says good done to the graceless base puts the doer in danger.
teaches: Holding them together shows the two halves of one counsel: Sirupanchamoolam says kindness to the base is wasted, Pazhamozhi that it is also dangerous, the tiger's face being closer than the dog's mouth.

note: Kural 959 says a sprout shows the soil and speech shows the lineage one was born in; Pazhamozhi 146 runs the inference the other way, using lineage to read the hidden mind, as land shows in a bird's colour.
teaches: In the Kural lineage is what is inferred from speech, and in the Pazhamozhi lineage is the evidence from which the mind is inferred, so the pair shows kin serving as both sign and signified in this ethics.
list_adds: its bird image matches the Kural's soil image but makes kin the key to another's mind rather than the thing to be found.

note: Kural 995 says scorn hurts even in jest; Pazhamozhi 54 adds that the hearer takes the jest as abuse and the harm returns on the jester, like a rat burnt by the lamp it seized.
teaches: The Kural looks at the pain a jest gives the hearer, Pazhamozhi at the anger it rouses and the cost to the jester, so together they show a mocking word wounding both ends.
list_adds: its proverb turns the couplet's concern for the hearer into a warning about self-harm, the rat burnt by its own theft.

note: Elathi 35 promises kingship to one who feeds the renouncers, the powerless, the unknown, the dead or bereaved (இறந்தார்), the destitute and the young; Acharakkovai 100 frees from ஆசாரம் the stranger, the destitute, the old, the young and one who has lost a life.
teaches: The two books name nearly the same weak persons, but the Elathi makes them claims on the giver's food while the Acharakkovai lifts the rules of conduct from them, so the vulnerable are owed help in one code and excused in the other.

note: Kural 887 says a family with inner enmity is not joined though it fits like box and lid; Pazhamozhi 305 shows how an enemy creates that enmity, by flattering one brother that the two together need no one.
teaches: The Kural describes inner enmity from inside the house that suffers it, the proverb verse from the hand that plants it, so the pair shows both the seam and the wedge.
list_adds: it supplies the act of sowing discord, with its quoted boast and bone-among-dogs image, which the couplet's picture of a split family leaves unsaid.

note: Kural 220 says ruin through ஒப்புரவு is worth buying even by selling oneself; Pazhamozhi 82 names the concrete form of that cost, borrowing to do what is due, and the excuse it refuses, waiting for a better time.
teaches: Read together they show the Kural's startling price, selling oneself, as the far end of an ordinary practice the worthy actually follow: going into debt rather than postponing a duty.
list_adds: its pun on கடன் as debt and duty makes the cost and the obligation one word, which the couplet keeps as ruin set against gain.

note: Kural 230 says death is sweet when giving is out of reach; in Kalittokai 61 the friend says the girl, who would find it better to die than live unable to give to suppliants (ஈதல் இரந்தார்க்கு ஒன்று ஆற்றாது வாழ்தலின் சாதலும் கூடுமாம்), would give him whatever he lacks.
teaches: The friend's offer turns the Kural's maxim into a trap for the household: once the lover presents himself as a suppliant for grace rather than wealth, the giving ethic obliges the girl to yield.

note: Kural 667 says not to despise anyone for their form, since the great chariot has its linchpin; Pazhamozhi 202 uses the same words (எள்ளாமை வேண்டும்) of one whose small beginnings are known in town, since the market calf may become a bull.
teaches: The two give different grounds for the same rule: the Kural's small linchpin matters now by where it stands, while Pazhamozhi's calf matters later by what it grows into, so contempt can err about function or about time.
list_adds: it moves the rule from bodily size to known origin or capital, and grounds it in growth over time rather than in present function.
