note: Kural 720 likens holding forth before those not of one's group to nectar spilled in a dirty yard; Pazhamozhi 25 likens counsel spoken among dull men to sifting flour in the sea.
teaches: The two waste images differ in what is lost: the Kural's nectar is fouled where it falls, Pazhamozhi's flour simply vanishes, and Pazhamozhi names the hearers as fools rather than outsiders, so the loss comes from incapacity, not from difference of group.
list_adds: it narrows the couplet's 'those not of one's group' to the dull and complacent and makes the counsel itself (உறுதி), not display, what is lost.

note: Kural 595 says a water-flower rises to the water's depth and a man's height to his mind; Pazhamozhi 379 uses the same image to say a patron's gifts are great by the measure of his worth.
teaches: The Kural measures a man's rise by his inner drive; Pazhamozhi applies the image to giving, so the size of a gift becomes a reading of the giver's worth and not of the suppliant's rank.
list_adds: it carries the image from striving to giving and sets it against the foolish view that gifts follow the receiver's rank, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 10 says the base are bound with iron after goading while the worthy are bound by courtesy; Pazhamozhi 116 says the qualityless cannot be restrained by words.
teaches: Together they mark a limit of persuasion: courtesy binds the worthy, but words are wind to the base, so only force is left, as the Nanmanikkadigai says outright.

note: The materialist calls knowledge of former births the delusion of possession or dream; in kaathai 9 Manimekalai, carried off by the deity in sleep, knew her former birth without error.
teaches: The materialist's objection names the very conditions of the heroine's own knowledge, so the epic's story stands as her unspoken answer to him.

note: Acharakkovai 1 makes eight virtues the seed of ஆசாரம்; Acharakkovai 100, the last verse, names nine persons freed from it: the stranger, the destitute, the old, the young, the bereaved, the frightened, one who has eaten, one on the king's work and the bridegroom.
teaches: Read as the book's frame, the pair show the code bounded at both ends: it grows from virtues that bind everyone, but its rules lapse for those whom ignorance, weakness, fear, grief or duty prevent from keeping them.

note: Naladiyar 164: a snake in a rock crevice still dreads thunder, and those who anger the great are not safe in a fortress; Pazhamozhi 62: the provoker hides behind an erukku shrub and goads an elephant.
teaches: Set side by side, the two hiding places run from the strongest to the weakest, a rock crevice and a fortress against a shrub, and both fail, so no shelter of any strength protects against the great.
list_adds: its proverb makes the shelter absurdly thin and the offender the one who starts the charge, where the quatrain's snake only fears.

note: Naladiyar 279 says the base yield only when strong men press them, like a cow milked by force; Pazhamozhi 224 says those who stand and beg before the hard-minded get nothing.
teaches: Read together, the hard-hearted are moved by force but never by entreaty, so the beggar's mode of asking is the one sure to fail.
list_adds: it fixes the asker's posture, standing before them (முன்னின்று இரந்தார்), as the thing that yields nothing, where the quatrain sets yielding gladly against yielding under force.

note: Kural 319 says hurts done to others in the forenoon come back in the afternoon; Pazhamozhi 46's proverb keeps the forenoon and afternoon but has the man only see (கண்டான்) another's ruin, and addresses the heart.
teaches: Together they move the rebound from the deed to the inner wish: the Kural times the return of harm done, Pazhamozhi applies the same timing to a cruel thought voiced in the heart.
list_adds: addressing the rebuke to the heart and using 'saw' for 'did' extends the couplet's rule from acts to wishes.

note: Purananuru 39 tells a Chola that, with ancestors who destroyed the hanging fort, killing is not his own fame; Pazhamozhi 155 recalls the same Chola feat of the fort in the sky.
teaches: The puram poem treats the hanging fort as inherited glory a descendant cannot claim, while the ethics verse turns it into a lesson anyone can use: the fort fell to force applied by the right means.

note: Kural 276 calls those who deceive as if renounced while unrenounced in heart the hardest of all; Pazhamozhi 371 extends false practice to aram as well as penance and says it binds the deceiver in both worlds.
teaches: The Kural judges the false renouncer by his cruelty to others; Pazhamozhi turns the harm back on him, a rope he ties on himself, and carries the blame into the next life, so the fraud is self-ruin as much as an injury.
list_adds: it pairs penance with aram as the two things that can be falsely kept and this life's blame with the next, which the couplet, speaking only of renunciation, does not.

note: Kural 1000 says great wealth got by a man without courtesy spoils like good milk in a faulty vessel; Pazhamozhi 209 says wealth placed in the hands of a man not of good family is grass fed to a sluggish ox.
teaches: The Kural blames the holder's character for spoiling his own wealth, while Pazhamozhi turns this into a rule for the owner who chooses a keeper, and makes birth rather than courtesy the test.
list_adds: it carries the couplet's claim from the man who owns wealth to the man to whom wealth is entrusted, and its proverb makes the loss a waste with no return rather than a spoiling.

note: Natrinai 142: returning, the man tells his charioteer of the young woman of mullai-fitting chastity who rejoices when a guest comes even at night. Ainthinai Aimpathu 10: returning, he tells the charioteer to hurry to see her who stands with the bolt of her chastity drawn shut, hand to cheek.
teaches: The same speaker on the same road imagines the wife's chastity as an open door to guests in one poem and as a shut bolt in the other, so the pair shows karpu as both the household's hospitality and its closing against the world while the husband is away.

note: Thirikadugam 4 names living openly before enemies and taking by the hand one once enraged as the doings of a man about to die; Pazhamozhi 295 says those who swagger and enrage the steadfast become crows' food.
teaches: Both verses treat a way of behaving toward enemies as a sign of death already on its way, the counted work by naming it, the Pazhamozhi by showing the boaster's end as carrion.

note: Naladiyar 131 says the beauty of hair, garment border and saffron is not beauty and only learning's is; Pazhamozhi 26 keeps the ornaments but makes understanding the garment they must follow.
teaches: The quatrain discards outward adornment, while the Pazhamozhi verse keeps it and ranks it, so outer graces are not worthless but parasitic on the inner one.
list_adds: its string of jewels, sandal and garlands is not dismissed but placed in an order, ornaments after the cloth, which the quatrain's flat denial lacks.

note: Naladiyar 219 ranks abuse above praise of qualities one does not have; Pazhamozhi 66 says praise must be pushed away even when it comes from one's own kin.
teaches: The quatrain makes unfit praise worse than abuse in general; Pazhamozhi carries the refusal to the hardest case, the affectionate praise of one's own people, and gives the reason in the image of a jewel that is one's own and still does not fit.
list_adds: the proverb's own-but-unfitting jewel names the source the quatrain leaves open, one's own kin, and makes the test fit rather than giver.

note: Pazhamozhi 208 counts guarding earned wealth oneself a duty and handing it to the worthless a folly; Pazhamozhi 368 says that even wealth guarded with care is outnumbered by those who eye it.
teaches: Read together the book's two verses on custody limit each other: 208 says keep it yourself, 368 says keeping it never wins, so custody is a duty under the wealth heading that the aram heading turns into a reason to give.

note: Pazhamozhi 196 says the senseless are best cut off with wealth, a gift's thrust being stronger than a spear's; 310 puts giving second among the means of ending enmity.
teaches: The earlier verse gives the gift as a weapon by itself; 310 sets it in a sequence with words, division and force, so the book's praise of the gift becomes one stage of a method.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 49 says living apart from one's companions is hard for the well-born; Pazhamozhi 355 says living long together in one place, even for brothers, is painful.
teaches: Held together, the two verses name a real dilemma of kinship: separation is hard and long cohabitation painful, so kin are best close but not under one roof.

note: Verse 6 bars a falling star from the sight of one in எச்சில்; verse 51 bars a falling star, lightning, harlots' finery and the low sun from anyone who wants to keep his radiance.
teaches: The same sight is barred on two grounds in the book, once as a matter of pollution and once to guard one's lustre, so the gaze rules do not rest on pollution alone.

note: Pazhamozhi 191 says sweet speech never brings anyone into trouble; Thirikadugam 24 names a courtesan's sweet words as a mire that sinks those who step in.
teaches: Read together they show the proverb holds for the speaker, not the hearer: one's own sweet speech is safe, but another's sweet speech may be bait, so sweet speech protects the one who uses it and can trap the one who trusts it.

note: Naladiyar 170 says the fitting quality of one who has some excellence is restraint; Acharakkovai 71 says those of good family do not spread out their wealth, learning, lustre and virtue before the lord.
teaches: The Naladiyar makes restraint the proper dress of excellence in general; the Acharakkovai names the place where it is tested, before the lord, and the risk of failing it, being taken for an enemy.
list_adds: It names four excellences, wealth, learning, lustre and virtue, as alike to be kept silent before the lord, and gives a reason, looking like an enemy, that the quatrain lacks.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 26 names as sweet the worth of not killing the hope of those who come in desire; Pazhamozhi 222 shows the hope-killer at work, feigning kindness and then withholding.
teaches: The counted verse names the virtue bare; Pazhamozhi shows its opposite as a staged deceit, the gift dangled like grass tied at a beast's neck.

note: Kural 509 bids one trust no one without examination; Pazhamozhi 182 applies this even to the affectionate and says the unexamined truster perishes.
teaches: The pairing extends the Kural's rule to the case where it is hardest to keep, affection, and fixes the stake at death rather than mere trouble.
list_adds: it ranks the hostile, who need no testing because they are plainly not to be told, below the affectionate, who must be tested, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

note: Verse 16 names the king, teacher, mother, father and elder brother as the குரவர் to be worshipped as gods; verse 58 ends by keeping the குரவர் on one's right.
teaches: Verse 16 says the elders are to be worshipped like gods, and verse 58 gives one bodily form of that worship, the circling to the right otherwise paid to the divine.

note: Kural 409 says the unlearned, though born high, have not the worth of the learned born low; Pazhamozhi 73 says the well-born, though they learn nothing, are far better than those who know other things.
teaches: The two books rank the same pair, birth and learning, in opposite order, so the ethics group does not agree on whether lineage can stand in for study.
list_adds: its proverb makes the well-born the very source of what learning would bring them, so instruction is superfluous rather than merely outweighed.

note: Purananuru 203 tells a king that refusing a returning suppliant with 'you took before' is cruel and that protecting suppliants is his duty; Pazhamozhi 84 says those who took in seekers do not cast them off as worthless.
teaches: The puram poem closes the excuse of past giving and the ethics verse closes the excuse of the seeker's unworthiness, so together they show the protector's duty answering two different pretexts for withdrawal.

note: Naladiyar 213 holds up the dog that wags its tail with its master's spear in its body as the loyal friend; Pazhamozhi 45 says even a dog shut in and beaten bites its owner.
teaches: The same animal marks the limit of loyalty: the Naladiyar praises the dog's endurance of injury, Pazhamozhi shows that cornering and steady abuse break even that endurance.
list_adds: its proverb adds the condition, the shut door and repeated beating, under which the quatrain's model of loyal endurance fails.

note: 291 warns against enmity with the great themselves; 292 extends the warning to enmity with those who depend on the great.
teaches: Read in sequence, the reach of a great man's protection is shown to cover his dependents, so the danger of provoking him begins one step before he is touched.

note: Naladiyar 347 says the base, though they have come into wealth, are known by their deeds, as a golden sandal is still for the foot; Pazhamozhi 106 says the worthless whom a patron lifts out of distress into faultless prosperity do not become men of good family.
teaches: The Naladiyar says wealth does not change deeds; Pazhamozhi adds that it does not change rank either, even when the wealth is a patron's gift and is used without fault.
list_adds: it names the patron's favour as the source of the wealth and denies the base the standing of குடி, a claim of rank the quatrain does not make.

note: Naladiyar 325 says it is a wonder if one who reviles another before an assembly survives when the reviled stays silent; Pazhamozhi 75 says the worthy say no wounding word in an assembly because any speaker is answered.
teaches: The quatrain gives the rare case, the reviled keeping silence, and the proverb the ordinary one, the retort, so between them reviling in company is shown to rebound whether it is answered or not.
list_adds: its proverb extends the rule to the highest speaker, Mal himself, so no rank exempts a reviler from reply.

note: The Siddhar song says forest, rags and begging bowl gain nothing without inner love; Pazhamozhi 339 says the sect's mark is not penance without an even mind.
teaches: Both deny that garb makes the ascetic, but they put different things in its place, love for the Lord in the Siddhar and Jain-style equanimity in Pazhamozhi.

note: Kural 763 says a host of rats roaring like the sea perish at the cobra's breath; Pazhamozhi 249 says a gathered enemy army is nothing to a firm-minded king, one stone for a thousand crows.
teaches: The couplet locates the strength in the cobra alone; the pairing traces it to the king's undivided mind, so numbers fail against resolve, not only against force.
list_adds: its condition, a king not divided in mind, gives the source of the one's power over the many that the couplet's image takes for granted.

note: Kural 134 says a brahmin's birth is ruined when his conduct fails, though a forgotten Veda can be relearned; Acharakkovai 61 says the four-Veda knowers, come by heaven's order, are honoured as one's own elders.
teaches: The Kural makes the brahmin's standing hang on conduct and treats the Veda as recoverable, while the Acharakkovai grounds his honour in the Veda and a heavenly origin and names no condition of conduct, so the two disagree on what earns the rank.
list_adds: It places the Veda-knowers inside the circle of one's own elders, so reverence for a birth-group is folded into filial reverence, which the couplet never does.

note: Kural 720 says speaking before those not of one's own kind is nectar spilt in a dirty yard; Pazhamozhi 30 says the discerning do not even enter among those who have no regard for them.
teaches: The couplet counts the waste after one has spoken in the wrong company; the Pazhamozhi verse moves the judgement earlier, to not going in at all, and makes that avoidance itself a mark of understanding.
list_adds: its jackal that keeps out of the reapers' sight turns the couplet's rule of speech into a rule of where to be seen, with the danger as well as the waste.

note: Verse 61 honours the four-Veda knowers as one's own elders; verse 64 puts பார்ப்பார் first among eight to whom one yields the road.
teaches: Verse 64 turns 61's honour into a gesture on the road and sets the brahmin at the head of a line of the burdened, the sick and cows, so rank by birth is enacted with the same act as care for the weak.

note: Pazhamozhi 51 says the well-born's heat, like hot water, cannot burn the house; 58 says that abuse returned is the very act of setting the house on fire.
teaches: Read side by side, the two verses draw the line between heat felt and heat spoken: anger held inside does no harm, while anger turned into a retort burns down one's own house.

note: Kural 696 says to speak knowing the mood and the time, what is needed and not disliked; Acharakkovai 76 says to speak at the right moment with few syllables that hold the whole sense.
teaches: The Kural asks for the right time and the right matter; the Acharakkovai adds the right length, so speech before the great is judged by moment, content and brevity together.
list_adds: It lists four faults of manner, haste, going on, falsehood and sprawl, before giving the positive rule, so the couplet's advice is defined against its failures.

note: Kopperunchozhan, the poet of Kuruntokai 53, is the king of Purananuru 216, who tells the doubters that his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar wants no lie that would spoil his fame and will come to share his death. In Kuruntokai 53 his friend-speaker holds a lover to an oath sworn before the hill-goddesses, which he has broken.
teaches: Read together, the king's two voices weigh faith two ways: in puram a friend never met keeps faith with no oath at all, while in his akam poem a lover breaks faith despite an oath sworn before goddesses, so the poet who staked his death on unsworn friendship knew how little a sworn word could hold in love.

note: Pazhamozhi 146 reads a hidden mind by kin; Pazhamozhi 148 reads it by the company kept, without inquiry or witnesses.
teaches: Within one heading the book offers two outward marks of an inner nature, the group one is born into and the group one chooses, and 148 adds that the second applies even to renouncers who have left their kin.

note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken when slandered; Acharakkovai 52 says those of unshaken mind never backbite.
teaches: Held together the two verses make one steady mind both unmoved by slander and unwilling to slander, so steadiness works in both directions of backbiting.
list_adds: It sets backbiting last in a list of five faults of speech that the same unshaken mind avoids, where the Naladiyar shows only that mind receiving slander.

note: Naladiyar 135 says learners have few days and so must choose what to learn; Pazhamozhi 1 locates those days in youth and says that once past they cannot be used at all.
teaches: Together they make two limits on learning, a short life that forces choice and a closing season of youth after which no choice remains.
list_adds: its proverb of toll and wages turns the quatrain's shortness of days into a deadline, a payment that lapses once the work is past.

note: Verse 20 sets the eater's direction, posture and silence; verse 25 sets the order of the food by taste, sweet first and bitter last.
teaches: Verse 20 governs only the eater's body, and verse 25 completes the meal code by governing the food's sequence, so the rule reaches what is eaten as well as how.

note: Kural 633 names three skills of the minister, dividing others, holding one's own and reconciling; Pazhamozhi 310 names four means of ending enmity, sweet words, gifts, division and measured force.
teaches: The two lists overlap only in division: the Kural's are skills of joining and parting, the proverb verse's a sequence ending in force, so they show two ways of ordering statecraft.
list_adds: it puts the means in an order, words and gifts first and force last and in due measure, which the couplet's three skills do not rank.

note: Kural 1052 says asking is a pleasure if what is asked comes without suffering; Pazhamozhi 375 calls excellent the giver who reads the asker's mind and gives what he wants.
teaches: The Kural conditions the asker's pleasure on getting without pain; Pazhamozhi locates the means in the giver, who spares that pain by reading the need from the asker's manner and giving the fit thing, not stones for the bowl.
list_adds: its begging-bowl proverb adds that the gift must match the need, a requirement on what is given that the couplet does not make.

note: Kural 133 makes conduct itself the substance of noble birth and its lapse low birth; Pazhamozhi 34 keeps old lineage as a good already held and makes conduct an addition upon it.
teaches: Read together they show two models of lineage: in the Kural birth is earned by conduct, in Pazhamozhi conduct enriches a birth already counted as excellent.
list_adds: its proverb of milk upon ghee makes conduct a second richness laid on lineage, a layering the couplet's identity of the two removes.

note: Kural 1070 says the asker's life goes out at the word of refusal; Pazhamozhi 225 says refusing what one cannot give is no disgrace, and that the fault lies in keeping the asker in hope and then not sharing.
teaches: The Kural weighs every refusal by the asker's death of spirit; Pazhamozhi exempts the honest refusal and reserves the blame for the one who holds out hope and withholds.
list_adds: it divides refusal into the honest 'I have none' and the hope kept alive and killed, a distinction the couplet, which condemns concealment as such, does not make.

note: Naladiyar 213 says hold close those like a dog, which wags its tail with its master's spear in its body, and leave those like an elephant; Pazhamozhi 128 says a befriended dog brings in a good hare.
teaches: Both take the dog as the model friend but for different virtues: in the quatrain it is loyal even when wounded, in Pazhamozhi it is useful as a hunter, so the same animal serves a test of character and a reckoning of gain.
list_adds: its proverb keeps the quatrain's dog but changes its merit from loyalty to yield.

note: Kural 524 makes living surrounded by kin the fruit of wealth; Pazhamozhi 355 says even brothers living long in one dwelling is painful.
teaches: The pair separates being surrounded by kin from sharing a roof with them: the Kural's ideal holds only at a distance, for even brothers wear on one another at close quarters.
list_adds: its proverb that even the goddess of fortune is a bad housemate puts a limit of nearness and time on the couplet's praise.

note: Both name the road after death with செல்வுழி: Naladiyar 328 mocks the fool who does not tie on its provisions; Pazhamozhi 359 shows the worthy making great wealth a protection for it.
teaches: The Naladiyar sets clutching wealth against provision for the road; Pazhamozhi's cane both chewed and boiled into jaggery lets the same wealth serve now and keep for later, so present use and provision are not opposed.
list_adds: its cane-and-jaggery proverb holds enjoyment and provision in one use of wealth, where the quatrain sets the grip on wealth against the provision.

note: Kural 791 says nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry; Pazhamozhi 128 says there is no need to insist on worthy friends and one should take anyone's friendship, since a befriended dog brings in a hare.
teaches: On a plain reading the two disagree on whether a friend must be tested first: the Kural fears the bond one cannot leave, while Pazhamozhi counts the profit even a low friend brings, so the pair shows two grounds of valuing friendship, by its risk and by its yield.
list_adds: its proverb measures a friend by what he brings in, a ground of judgement the couplet does not use, and so drops the inquiry the couplet requires.

note: Kural 821 calls the friendship of those close without inner consent an anvil for striking when the chance comes; Pazhamozhi 120 calls the arrogant, concealing men one has honoured gravel in a sandal.
teaches: The two images of hidden ill will differ in timing: the Kural's waits for its moment to strike, Pazhamozhi's galls at every step, so the false intimate is shown as both a threat and a constant wearing.
list_adds: its proverb turns hidden hostility into a present, continuous injury, where the couplet looks to a single future blow.

note: Naladiyar 53 lists home, youth, beauty, repute, wealth and strength as impermanent and says the best renounce them; Pazhamozhi 391 lists wealth, lustre, strength, beauty, youth and birth and says they give no escape from Death.
teaches: Two nearly identical lists of six goods lead to different conclusions: the Naladiyar argues from their passing to renunciation, the Pazhamozhi only to their powerlessness before Death, leaving the remedy to the verses around it.
list_adds: it adds birth (இற்பிறப்பு) and lustre to the goods that fail and drops home and repute, so lineage too is placed among the things Death ignores.

note: Thirikadugam 24 makes the bowing of hardened enemies a mire; Pazhamozhi 289 says favours shown to enemies set against reconciliation do not take.
teaches: The two verses look at a false peace from both sides: the enemy's submission cannot be trusted, and one's own kindness cannot change him, so neither party's gesture ends a settled enmity.

note: Both are Kapilar's friend speaking to the hill lord about his night visits: in 18 she asks him to come by day instead, to the kanthal grove; in 12, by its colophon after day meetings have been stopped, she refuses the night as well and demands marriage.
teaches: The two poems show the friend's options closing one by one, night refused for day and then day lost to confinement, so the only path left is marriage, the end both poems are built toward.

note: Both call desire for another man's wife பேதைமை; the Kural says it is absent in those who have seen aram and porul.
teaches: The Innaa list explains the shared word by its company: the folly is that of a venture beyond one's strength, like a valourless king in battle, which those the Kural describes would never attempt.

note: Kural 436 says a ruler who removes his own fault and then sees others' has no fault; Pazhamozhi 38 uses the same pair of own fault and others' fault to mock anyone who corrects others first.
teaches: Held together, the Kural's condition for a king's just correction becomes in Pazhamozhi a rule for anyone, and the reversed order is made ridiculous rather than unjust.
list_adds: it carries the king's condition into common life and adds the goat that cures others' wind and not its own, turning a rule into a jest.

note: Kar Narpathu 4: the season is the medicine for her pallor. Kural 1265: the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with full eyes; on a plain reading the two disagree about what cures pasalai.
teaches: The friend claims the sign of his return heals the pallor and the Kural's woman holds that only the sight of him will, so the couplet reads as the heroine's answer to the whole method of the Kar Narpathu's friend.

note: Kural 423 asks for the truth of whatever is heard from any mouth; the proverb of Pazhamozhi 185 asks that even what one saw be weighed before it is spoken.
teaches: The pair extends testing from what one hears to what one has seen and from judging to speaking: the Kural doubts others' report, the proverb doubts one's own eyes as a ground for testimony.
list_adds: it moves the test from the hearer's understanding to the witness's speech before a king, adding the shame that makes a worthy man hold back.

note: Naladiyar 76 says one should not abandon those one has mingled with, since parting is hard even for beasts; Pazhamozhi 126 uses nearly the same words and closes with the proverb that parting hurts even from a demon.
teaches: The quatrain grounds staying in patience with a friend's hurts, while Pazhamozhi drops the hurts and adds that parting is painful even from a demon, so the reason to stay becomes the bond itself, whatever the companion is worth.
list_adds: its proverb adds a claim the quatrain lacks: the pain of parting does not depend on the friend being good.

note: Iniyavai Narpathu 34 names as sweet leaving the friendship of worthless people even when they embrace one; Pazhamozhi 128 says one should take friendship whoever's it is.
teaches: Within the same group of works the counted verse and the proverb verse take opposite sides on befriending the unworthy, which shows the group does not speak with one voice on choosing friends.

note: 396 praises Ezhiniyathan of Vattaru, whose land has the toddy-drinking Kosar; Akananuru 216 names Athan Ezhini, lord of Selli, among whose people the young Kosar make garlands, and compares the parathai's pain to the elephant his spear pierced.
teaches: If the two Ezhinis are one chief (both are named with the Kosar), akam remembers him by a war wound inflicted on an elephant, used as a courtesan's image of suffering, while puram remembers him as feeder of the kinless, showing how a patron's two reputations were divided between the genres.

note: Kural 1043 says poverty destroys at once one's ancient descent and dignity; Pazhamozhi 204 says the great known to the land, though fallen poor, keep their standing, since no dog sniffs at a tiger's head. The tension depends on reading the couplet's தொல்வரவு as inherited standing, as its marks do.
teaches: The two disagree on whether poverty can strip inherited greatness: the Kural says it takes descent and dignity together, while Pazhamozhi holds that renown already known to the land outlasts the wealth that won it.
list_adds: its proverb of the dog and the tiger's head adds the onlookers, the mean who do not dare, where the couplet speaks only of what the poor man loses.

note: Both close the heading with ingratitude; 346 is plotting ruin, 347 is backbiting in league with enemies.
teaches: The two proverbs split ingratitude's harm: cutting one's own branch ruins the traitor, burning the house one ate in ruins the benefactor.

note: Kural 345 asks what further tie (தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்) is left to those cutting off birth, when even the body is excess; Pazhamozhi 395 asks the same question (தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்) of those who left children and wealth, and answers with the elephant whose tail sticks.
teaches: The Pazhamozhi repeats the Kural's very question, and its proverb supplies what the couplet's 'even the body is excess' leaves unpictured: the danger after renunciation is not the great ties but a small remnant that holds the whole back.
list_adds: it names what was given up, dear children and earned wealth, and adds the image of the stuck tail, which ranks the last small tie as the real obstacle.

note: Kural 764 makes an army one that cannot be turned by subversion (அறைபோகாது); Pazhamozhi 312 asks whether one who would give his body for the king could join his enemies.
teaches: The couplet names the quality, incorruptibility, as a property of the army; Pazhamozhi grounds it in the single soldier's willingness to die, so loyalty becomes the consequence of a readiness to give the body rather than a separate virtue.
list_adds: its two-bulls proverb gives a reason the couplet lacks: enmity so settled that the two cannot even share a ford, so desertion is shown as unnatural rather than only forbidden.

note: Naladiyar 189 sets the pure heart unshaken against cruel slander; Pazhamozhi 42 says the evil tongue never runs short and spares not even a god.
teaches: Pazhamozhi shows how far slander reaches, even to Mal's saving act, which is why the Naladiyar's steadiness must hold against slander that cannot be avoided.
list_adds: its example of a god called a cowherd shows slander turning a saving act into a slight on rank, a case beyond the quatrain's general slanderer.

note: Naladiyar 278 says the miser's heirs do not give once the wealth is theirs; Pazhamozhi 215 says that the miser's kin too cling and grow tight while he lives.
teaches: Read together, miserliness is shown as a household trait passed sideways to kin in life and down to heirs after death, not a private vice.
list_adds: it pairs not giving with not enjoying and sets the kin's clinging in the same breath, so the hoard is shown corrupting the whole circle around it.

note: Kural 282 says that even thinking of stealing another's goods is wrong; Acharakkovai 38 bars thinking of seizing, along with lying, slander and envy.
teaches: The Kural's thought-crime is confined to theft, and the Acharakkovai extends the same inward standard to speech faults and envy and names its sanctions, suspicion, hell and the deity's wrath.
list_adds: It groups seizing with lying, slander and envy, so faults of hand, tongue and heart are all forbidden at the stage of thought.

note: Kural 555 makes the tears of those who cannot bear their affliction the weapon that wears away a ruler's wealth; Pazhamozhi 47 uses the same phrase of tears wept unable to bear it, and makes them Death to any strong oppressor.
teaches: Read together, the victims' tears pass from wearing down a king's wealth to killing the oppressor, and from the king's subjects to four named kinds of the defenceless anyone strong might torment.
list_adds: it lists four kinds of victims, the ill-favoured, the friendless, the poor and those taken as foes for a word, where the couplet names none.

note: Kural 104 says those who know the fruit take a millet's good as a palm; Pazhamozhi 344 asks the knowing to plan always for the good of one who gives them a measure of grain.
teaches: The Kural enlarges a small kindness in the mind, and Pazhamozhi turns that into lasting service toward a provider, framed as a return no trade can match.
list_adds: it moves the couplet from a single favour to a standing tie of maintenance, and its trade proverb puts gratitude in the language of profit.

note: Both use grass and a beast to show that the well-born keep their nature in hardship: the lion will not chew creeping grass, the bull's calf grows into a bull though it grazes where there is no grass.
teaches: The same pasture image argues in two directions: the Naladiyar's lion refuses what is beneath it, while Pazhamozhi's calf needs nothing from the pasture at all, so lineage is shown both as refusal and as self-sufficient growth.
list_adds: it turns the image from what the well-born will not do to what they become regardless, and ties it to the act of ஒப்புரவு rather than to principle in general.

note: Kural 57 asks what use the guarding of women by confinement is, since the best guard is their own steadfastness; Acharakkovai 95 lists the wife among four things a man guards like gold.
teaches: The Kural moves the guard of a wife inside her, while the Acharakkovai keeps it in the husband's hands beside his body and his deposits, so the pair show two views of where a wife's keeping lies.
list_adds: It puts the wife in one list with the man's body, a deposit and his savings, so she is guarded as a possession.

note: Pazhamozhi 342 addresses renouncers who eat flesh; 343 addresses those who kill in rage and lack grace.
teaches: The adjacent verses carry the bar on flesh from the renouncer's path to anyone without grace, and give it two roots: leftover appetite and anger.

note: Naladiyar 187 says even enmity with the wise brings dignity while intimacy with the mean brings grief; Pazhamozhi 300 says enmity with the low brings the great nothing.
teaches: The two say from opposite sides that the worth of an enemy is the measure of the quarrel: a wise foe honours one, a petty foe only costs.
list_adds: it adds the hazard the quatrain leaves out, that the petty enemy can still do great harm, as a light shower brings a flood.

note: Kural 535 says the man who slipped by not guarding beforehand grieves afterwards over his own error; Pazhamozhi 210 says neglecting what one had and searching to get it back later is catching a peacock with butter.
teaches: The Kural leaves the negligent man with regret, while Pazhamozhi follows him into his attempt to undo the loss and shows the attempt itself as absurd, so the cost of neglect is wasted effort as well as grief.
list_adds: its proverb mocks the method of recovery, a stage the couplet does not reach, and fixes the neglect on wealth one already had.

note: Kural 612 warns against letting a task die midway; Pazhamozhi 366 applies this to aram and says an aram broken off midway is worse than one never begun.
teaches: The Kural guards any task against abandonment; Pazhamozhi makes the rule sharper for aram, ranking the half-done gift below not giving at all, and puts the remedy in the planning that keeps many from being burdened.
list_adds: it ranks the abandoned aram below never beginning, a ranking the couplet does not make, and ties firmness of plan to sparing others the burden.

note: 109 warns against doing good to the graceless base; 113 against fostering and living with the shameless.
teaches: Read in order the two verses rise from a single favour to a shared life, and the danger rises with them from a tiger's sudden bite to a wound eaten from within.

note: 107 has the base set the great level with themselves in speech; 122 has the unrestrained rise while the worthy withdraw.
teaches: The two verses give the same inversion at two scales, one man's insolent equal talk and a whole order where stone floats, and show the first as the seed of the second.

note: Pazhamozhi 90 denies that good company changes the base; 106 denies that a patron's favour and prosperity change them.
teaches: Read in sequence the chapter closes both routes of reform it considers, the influence of good companions and the gift of fortune, so the base man's nature is fixed against both.

note: Nanmanikkadigai 28 says that as one learns ignorance lessens, step by step toward truth; Pazhamozhi 2 says the earnest learner finds himself the more unlearned at each step.
teaches: Read together, ignorance shrinks in fact while the learner's sense of it grows, so the Nanmanikkadigai's ladder is climbed only by one who feels farther from the top.

note: Both verses forbid the worthy to answer the low in kind; 49 says it is not their way, 50 says it wastes their strength.
teaches: Side by side the two give two separate reasons for the same restraint: retaliation would lower the worthy to the dog's act (49), and it would spend great means on a little jackal (50).

note: Akananuru 296 says the man's bathing in the great Vaiyai with the dark girl has become gossip in Koodal (அலர்ஆ கின்று, அது பலர்வாய்ப் பட்டே); thirattu 2.51-56 shows a woman wearing a garland from the flood openly, for the land to know (நாடு அறியப் பூ மாலை அப்பி), and the town's gossip following (ஊர்த்து அலர்).
teaches: The fragment shows how the gossip the Akananuru friend throws at the man was made: a love token worn in plain sight at the river festival, chosen by the woman as display, so the akam reproach of public shame rests on a festival custom in which the other woman wanted to be seen.

note: Both use the jackal as the creature that reads its ground: in Kural 500 it kills the elephant stuck in mud, in Pazhamozhi 30 it keeps out of the reapers' sight.
teaches: Held together, the jackal's cunning has two faces, striking where the ground favours it and vanishing where it does not, and the Pazhamozhi verse gives the second to the wise.
list_adds: it turns the Kural's lesson of place in war into a lesson of social company, applied to the discerning person rather than the commander.

note: Kural 441 bids one weigh their worth and take the friendship of the wise who know virtue; Pazhamozhi 261 says to test by discussion those who weigh good and ill and hold them firm, as bull rubs against bull.
teaches: The pair names the means of the Kural's weighing, testing in set speech, and its fruit, a support that runs both ways as two bulls prop each other.
list_adds: its bull proverb makes the tie between chooser and chosen mutual, where the couplet speaks only of what the chooser gains.

note: Kural 43 makes tending ancestors, gods, guests, kin and oneself the householder's chief duty; Acharakkovai 48 names the days of gods, ancestors, wedding, festival and sacrifice as days for aram and for feeding guests.
teaches: The Kural's standing duties to gods, ancestors and guests are turned by the Acharakkovai into dated occasions, showing how a general householder's duty becomes a festival calendar.
list_adds: It replaces the Kural's five persons owed care with five kinds of day, so the duty is counted by occasion, and the guest is fed as an addition to the day's aram.

note: Kural 696 bids one know the king's mood and the time and say what is needed and not disliked; Pazhamozhi 264 says the wise, finding the king's favourable moment, will even use guile, as mothers soothe children with the moon.
teaches: Together they show how far reading the king's mood can go: the Kural stops at saying the welcome needful thing, while the Pazhamozhi lets the counsellor treat the king as a child to be steered by a pleasing deception.
list_adds: its mother-and-moon image adds deceit to the couplet's tact and casts the king as a child, a ranking of counsellor over king the couplet avoids.

note: Pazhamozhi 311 praises the worthy who, having weighed it, meet the foe whether they or the enemy win; 317 calls attacking without being the enemy's match a harm, like striking a stone.
teaches: Read together, the weighing in 311 does not license fighting any foe: courage indifferent to outcome is admired, but 317 bars the charge against a clearly superior enemy, so the chapter separates accepting risk from courting certain defeat.

note: Pazhamozhi 6 has a young Chola who judges well despite his youth; 242 has a son not spared despite his youth.
teaches: Read together the two Chola stories make youth irrelevant from both sides of the court: it neither disqualifies the judge nor excuses the accused.

note: Pazhamozhi 40 makes reproach a disease that wastes the man it strikes; 41 says great reproach does not exist for those who do not heed it.
teaches: Together they show that blame wounds only those who care for their name, so the disease of verse 40 is itself a mark of the man worth curing.

note: Kural 293 says not to lie about what one's own heart knows, for the heart will burn its owner; Pazhamozhi 76 makes the king his own witness (தனக்குக் கரியாவான் தானாய்) who judges his hidden fault and cuts off his hand.
teaches: The Kural makes the heart the witness that punishes a lie; the Pazhamozhi shows a king acting on that witness and carrying out the sentence on his own body, so self-witness becomes self-justice.
list_adds: its proverb names the opposite motive, 'no one will see', and the story shows the inner witness overruling it in a king with no accuser.

note: Naladiyar 300's tiger starves rather than eat a kill fallen on its left side; Pazhamozhi 70's tiger starves rather than graze grass. Both make the tiger's hunger the test of the excellent.
teaches: The two tigers refuse different things, one a proper meal improperly placed and one a meal beneath its kind, so honour is shown both in rejecting the base and in rejecting the ill-fitting.
list_adds: its proverb ties the refusal to poverty (ஒற்கம்) and to holding one's station, where the quatrain ties it to honour weighed against heaven.

note: Naladiyar 203 says the great never refuse to bear those who depend on them; Pazhamozhi 348 says bearing them is useless unless their trouble is felt as one's own.
teaches: The pair adds an inner condition to the duty of support: carrying dependants as a branch carries fruit is not enough if their trouble is not felt as one's own.
list_adds: its proverb of pounding husk turns support without fellow feeling from a virtue into wasted labour.

note: Naladiyar 208 says true intimates enter the fire with you like the smith's poker; Pazhamozhi 354 says one taken as kin follows wherever his kinsman goes, as thread follows the needle.
teaches: Both use a craftsman's tool for loyalty, but the poker proves itself in danger and the thread by following, so kin loyalty is shown as obedience to another's course whatever it costs.
list_adds: its needle and thread make loyalty a matter of following the kinsman's lead, where the quatrain's smithy tools sort friends by their behaviour in the heat.

note: Kural 417 says men of deep heard learning do not speak folly even when mistaken; Thirikadugam says friendship with such men clears the tangle of words.
teaches: The couplet says kelvi keeps its owner's own speech clear; the verse adds that it clears others' confusion, so the virtue passes to the friend.

note: 245 says even prosperous subjects should not bear excess levy; 246 says a king's favours funded by excess levy are like feeding a creature its own crest.
teaches: The two close both escapes for over-taxing: the subjects' prosperity does not justify it, and the king's later generosity does not redeem it.

note: Kural 711 bids the speaker know the assembly and examine the matter before speaking; Pazhamozhi 17 names what is to be known, the hearers' desire about the matter, and calls speech that misses it a losing case.
teaches: Read together, knowing the assembly turns out to mean reading its appetite: the Kural asks for discernment, and Pazhamozhi says that discernment is of desire, so a true speech the hearers do not want is already lost.
list_adds: its bee image and proverb make the hearers' want the measure and recast unsuited speech as a defeat carried into the contest.

note: Kural 874 praises one who conducts himself taking enmity as friendship; Pazhamozhi 309 says an oppressor whose victim does not fall should come over to him in friendship.
teaches: The couplet makes turning enmity into friendship a mark of character, the proverb verse makes it a move forced by a failed attack, so the same turn can be virtue or prudence.
list_adds: it adds the occasion and the motive, a missed arrow and the need for guard, which the couplet's praise of character does not give.

note: Both use the Kazhar legend of Aathi Manthi and Attan Atthi; 222 names Maruthi, who restored the lover and entered the sea, 236 has Manthi searching town after town.
teaches: One legend served two speakers: the friend holds up Maruthi's fatal deed as a fame to win, the wife holds up Manthi's lament as her own shame, so the story was a shared stock the poets bent to opposite purposes.

note: Kural 805 says that when friends do what hurts one should read it as folly or great intimacy; Pazhamozhi 140 says one should not act as one who knew them of old but break with them as they broke.
teaches: The two give opposite rules for the old friend who turns unfriendly: the Kural asks for a generous reading of the hurt, Pazhamozhi denies old acquaintance any claim and prescribes the break as a cure.
list_adds: its proverb treats breaking off as a medicine, so ending the friendship becomes a remedy rather than a failure of the patience the couplet asks.

note: Naladiyar 191 says kin live at ease on what their relative gives, like crops below a tank; Pazhamozhi 349 says the patron's trust in them means nothing unless he sees they do not go in want.
teaches: The pair makes provision the substance of the kin bond: the quatrain shows kin living on the giver, and the proverb verse denies that trust without the meal is any bond at all.
list_adds: its proverb that all is false but cooked food puts feeding above every other proof of kinship, which the quatrain assumes without arguing.

note: Kural 612 warns against letting a task die midway, since the world's regard follows how one deals with unfinished work; Pazhamozhi 161 says what broke off unfinished has no increase and what does not exist has no name.
teaches: Pazhamozhi states as a law of naming what the Kural states as social regard: the half-done work does not earn a poor name but no name at all.
list_adds: its four parallel clauses rank the finished, the broken-off and the capable, ending in the proverb that the undone has no name.

note: Naladiyar 189 says the pure in heart stay unshaken by cruel slander like a flame in a lamp; Pazhamozhi 284 says the wise do not join those agitated by slander spoken to the king, but work out how he may see through it.
teaches: The pair moves steadiness under slander from one's own mind to the court: the Naladiyar's pure heart is not moved when slandered, and Pazhamozhi's wise courtier is not moved when another is slandered before the king, and also helps the king see clearly.
list_adds: it gives the steady one a task beyond composure, clearing the king's judgement, and sets him against a crowd of stilt-dancers moved by alarm.

note: Kural 847 says the man without understanding who lets slip the precious secret (அருமறை) harms himself; Pazhamozhi 181 says telling the precious secret (அருமறை) to the small-hearted is cotton carded on a palm-top.
teaches: The pair names one concrete way the secret slips: handing it to a small heart, and the image shows why the harm the Kural calls self-inflicted cannot be recalled once done.
list_adds: it opposes the noble keepers to the small-hearted hearers, adding to the couplet's lone fool a ranking of who can hold a secret at all.

note: Both set the silent fighter against the talker: in 311 those who rage within the fort with many words, in 313 the idle who talk and blame the king while the doers stand silent.
teaches: The pair shows the chapter's double charge against talk in war: it is wasted when made from safety, and it becomes slander when the talker turns it on the king.

note: Kural 127 says those who do not guard the tongue suffer from the fault of their words; Pazhamozhi 114 shows the hiding fool betrayed by his own evil speech, like the frog in the sand.
teaches: Pazhamozhi adds what the Kural does not consider, that the unguarded tongue undoes even a man who has hidden himself, so concealment is no substitute for restraint of speech.
list_adds: its proverb sets hiding against speaking and lets speech win, a contrast the couplet's single command lacks.

note: Kural 371 says the fate of gain produces tireless effort and the fate of loss produces sloth; Pazhamozhi 237 says the fortunate need no effort and the striving of the unfortunate is fruitless.
teaches: The Kural keeps effort as fate's instrument, while Pazhamozhi makes it idle on both sides, so the pair shows two ways of subordinating effort to fate: as its product, or as beside the point.
list_adds: it pairs the two lots as the couplet does but cuts effort loose from them, so the fortunate prosper without it and the unfortunate strive in vain.

note: Pazhamozhi 230's proverb repeats almost word for word Naladiyar 109's last line, that wanted or not what is bound to come can hardly be kept from touching one; the Naladiyar applies it to unwanted evil, Pazhamozhi to an elephant that went to a man of Karuvur.
teaches: The pair shows a saying shared between the two works, and that Pazhamozhi re-aims it: the quatrain's line is a warning that unwanted evil cannot be fended off, and the elephant story makes it a promise that unsought good cannot be missed.
list_adds: it takes the quatrain's closing line as a proverb and backs it with a named episode, turning a general warning into a story of fortune arriving.

note: Naladiyar 70 says the high do not answer the low with their own mouths; Pazhamozhi 116 says it is hard to restrain loose talkers by speech at all.
teaches: The Naladiyar's refusal to answer the base is a matter of dignity, and Pazhamozhi adds a practical ground: answering is useless, since words cannot catch wind.
list_adds: its proverb gives a reason of futility beside the quatrain's reason of rank.

note: Pazhamozhi 179 permits telling a secret once the hearer's love is known; Naladiyar 127 asks who has the power to know another's mind, since mind and deed differ.
teaches: Held together they show the condition Pazhamozhi sets may never be met: if love cannot be read from conduct, the counsel to wait for known love becomes a counsel of near-total silence.
list_adds: the Naladiyar quatrain denies the knowledge of minds that Pazhamozhi's proverb of the hunting trail presupposes can be had.

note: Kural 504 tells the employer to examine both good qualities and faults and take what predominates; Pazhamozhi 165 says not to voice an unsteady helper's faults but to take the benefit.
teaches: The couplet's weighing of faults happens in the employer's mind; Pazhamozhi adds that once the helper is in use, saying the faults aloud is itself a fault, so the examination must stay silent.
list_adds: its proverb of the holed appam turns the weighing into a rule of speech: the faults are counted in choosing and not counted again in the using.

note: Kural 694 tells one to suppress whispers and shared smiles in the presence of the great; Acharakkovai 97 says one speaks before the great only with folded hands or a covered mouth and does not look into their eyes.
teaches: The Kural forbids the small private signs that the great may read as against them, and the Acharakkovai prescribes the posture of the mouth, hands and eyes, so together they show restraint before the great as a whole bodily discipline.
list_adds: It names the hands, the mouth and the eyes in turn, so the Kural's ban on two signs becomes a full posture of address.

note: Kural 898 says those who seem to stand forever vanish with their line (குடியொடு) when the hill-like are slighted; Pazhamozhi 64 says the house (குடி) of the crooked perishes while the great only tremble and grieve.
teaches: Both make the offender's line the casualty, but Pazhamozhi has the great grieve rather than strike, so the ruin of the family comes from the offence itself and not from the great man's wrath.
list_adds: it makes the offenders the great man's own long-standing people and gives the great dread and grief, where the couplet gives them only height.

note: Kural 67 names the father's good to his son as setting him first in the assembly; Pazhamozhi 331 makes the father's task the child's conduct and warns that a child badly formed afflicts the one who formed him.
teaches: Together they give the father's duty a reward and a penalty: the well-formed son is set before the assembly, the ill-formed one turns on the father like a made thing become a demon.
list_adds: its proverb of the doll that becomes an afflicting spirit to its maker adds the cost of failure, which the couplet's statement of the duty leaves unsaid.

note: 65 forbids praising oneself before the deed; 66 forbids settling into praise even from one's own people.
teaches: The two adjacent verses close off praise from both the self and the circle nearest the self, leaving only praise that fits the deed and comes from beyond one's own people as worth keeping.

note: In 189 the lord of the gentle shore has come and her eyes have become good; in 190 the same மெல்லம் புலம்பன் is the one who made her many-petalled eyes weep.
teaches: Placed side by side in the decade with the same name for the man, the two poems make the heroine's eyes a gauge wholly in his hands, healed by his coming and wet by his absence, and the neythal image follows them, dusted with gold in one and cut down in the other.

note: Kural 510 says doubting one who has been trusted brings endless trouble; Pazhamozhi 174 says that if an appointee proves bad he should be let go without public exposure.
teaches: The couplet warns against doubt of a trusted man; Pazhamozhi takes the harder case where the doubt is proven, and still counsels quiet removal, so the concern in both is the damage done by open distrust.
list_adds: it adds the case the couplet does not face, the appointee who has truly failed, and the manner of removing him.

note: Kural 938 lists what gambling destroys: wealth, truth, compassion; Pazhamozhi 356 shows by the Bharata that dice between kin destroy kinship itself.
teaches: The couplet's loss of compassion becomes, in the epic case, brothers' sons turned into strangers and enemies, so the worst stake at dice is the bond with the other player.
list_adds: its Bharata story names a loss the couplet's list leaves out, the player's kin turned ஏதிலர்.

note: 125 condemns re-telling a friend's words in a twisted sense; 130 says a chosen friend is not blamed among many.
teaches: Read together the two verses govern what one says of a friend to others: neither distort his words nor publish his faults, so a friend's speech and his failings are both kept from the crowd.

note: Kural 875 says one alone against two enemies should take one as an ally; Pazhamozhi 304 says against a stronger enemy one should find someone to harass him from behind.
teaches: The couplet makes an ally out of an enemy one already has, the proverb verse recruits a new enemy for one's enemy, so both turn the enemy's own surroundings into one's defence.
list_adds: its ram-and-dog proverb adds the tactic of a rear threat, which halts an advance without meeting it head on, something the couplet's alliance does not name.

note: Kural 678 and Pazhamozhi 29 close on the same proverb, binding an elephant with an elephant; the Kural applies it to using one task to achieve another, Pazhamozhi to winning a wise man through a wise man.
teaches: The pair shows one proverb serving two ethics: in the Kural a rule of method for tasks, in Pazhamozhi a rule of persons, that only an equal can draw in an equal.
list_adds: it moves the elephant image from the ordering of tasks to the gaining of people, and names the kings who practise the capture.

note: Kural 223 says not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing', and giving, belong to the well-born; Pazhamozhi 223 condemns pleading 'nothing' to those long close when one could help.
teaches: The Kural measures the plea of poverty against birth; Pazhamozhi measures it against an old bond, so the same words are a fault of lineage in one and a wound to friendship in the other.
list_adds: it adds who is asking, old intimates, and its proverb of the hacked tree says what the false plea does to the bond, which the couplet does not consider.

note: Kural 224 says being begged from is painful until one sees the asker's glad face; Pazhamozhi 226 says all that is given to those who do not rejoice in what was done is lost.
teaches: The pair make the receiver's gladness the completion of the gift: the Kural says it ends the giver's pain, Pazhamozhi that without it the gift itself is wasted.
list_adds: it turns the couplet's psychology of the giver into a judgement on the recipient, setting the ungrateful who will not stand by one in need as the wasted object of giving.
